hints: This is an age problem with two people. When time passes, each person gets older, so the sum of their ages grows for both of them.
From 5 years ago to 5 years from now is 10 years. Think about how much each of the two people adds to the sum in that time.

Similar example: 3 years ago, the ages of a father and son added up to 40. From 3 years ago to 3 years from now is 6 years. Two people each grow 6 years older, so the sum grows by 2 × 6 = 12. The sum 3 years from now is 40 + 12 = 52.

steps.text: From 5 years ago to 5 years from now is 10 years.
There are two people, the mother and the daughter. Each one grows 10 years older, so the sum grows by 20.
The sum 5 years ago was 5x. So the sum of their ages 5 years from now is 5x + 20.

notes.A: This takes 10 away. Ages grow as time passes, so the sum must go up, and it goes up for both people.
notes.B: The 20 is right, but it should be added. Going forward in time makes both people older.
notes.C: Yes! 10 years pass for two people, so the sum grows by 2 × 10 = 20.
notes.D: This adds 10 years for only one person. Both the mother and the daughter grow 10 years older.

hints: This is an age problem. First bring everyone to the same time, the present, before you compare the sums.
Find the sum of the husband's and wife's ages now. Two people each grew 6 years older since then.

Similar example: 4 years ago a father's and mother's ages added up to 50. Now their sum is 50 + 2 × 4 = 58. Father, mother and daughter add up to 66 now, so the daughter is 66 − 58 = 8 now. In 4 years she will be 8 + 4 = 12.

steps.text: 6 years ago the husband and wife together were 48. Each is 6 years older now, so add 12.
Now all three together are 63. Take away the husband and wife to get the son's age now.
Add 6 years to find the son's age 6 years from now.
The son will be 9 years old.

notes.A: Check the sum of the husband's and wife's ages now. Two people each grew 6 years older, so add 12 to 48. Then find the son's age.
notes.B: 6 is the number of years that pass, not the son's age. Find his age now, then add 6.
notes.C: Go through it step by step: the couple's sum now, then the son's age now, then 6 years on.
notes.D: Yes! The couple are 60 together now, so the son is 3, and in 6 years he will be 9.

hints: This is an age problem about two people. Bring the sum to the present first, then split it using the difference in their ages.
Find the sum of their ages now. Each of the two boys is 3 years older than he was 3 years ago.

Similar example: 2 years ago the ages of Asha and Ravi added up to 26. Now the sum is 26 + 2 × 2 = 30. Ravi is 4 years younger, so take 4 away and halve: (30 − 4) ÷ 2 = 13. Ravi is 13 now. After 3 years he will be 13 + 3 = 16.

steps.text: 3 years ago the sum was 38. Both are 3 years older now, so add 6.
Vipul is 2 years younger. Take away Nirav's 2 extra years, then share equally.
Vipul is 21 now. Add 2 years.
After 2 years Vipul will be 23 years old.

notes.A: Yes! The sum now is 44, Vipul is 21 now, and after 2 years he is 23 years old.
notes.B: 22 is half of the sum now. The two are not the same age, and the question asks for Vipul's age after 2 years.
notes.C: This is Nirav's age after 2 years. Vipul is the younger one.
notes.D: This shares the sum equally and adds 2. Vipul is 2 years younger than Nirav, so allow for that before you halve.

hints: This is a substitution problem. One letter is given through the other, so find every letter's value first.
Start with b = 3. Use a = 2b to find a before you touch 2a − b.
Similar example: if p = 3q and q = 2, find 2p − q. First p = 3 × 2 = 6. Then 2p − q = 2 × 6 − 2 = 12 − 2 = 10.

steps.text: a is 2 times b, and b is 3.
Now put a = 6 and b = 3 into 2a − b.
The value of 2a − b is 9.

notes.A: Yes! a is 6, so 2a − b is 12 − 3 = 9.
notes.B: This uses a = 3. But a is 2 times b, so find a first.
notes.C: 6 is the value of a. The question asks for 2a − b, so keep going.
notes.D: This adds b at the end. The sign is minus, so take 3 away from 12.

hints: This is a perimeter problem written with letters. The perimeter of a rectangle is 2 times (length + breadth).
First write the length using a. The length is 2 more than the breadth, and the breadth is a + 2.
Similar example: a rectangle has breadth k + 1 and its length is 3 more than its breadth. Length = k + 1 + 3 = k + 4. Length + breadth = k + 4 + k + 1 = 2k + 5. Perimeter = 2 × (2k + 5) = 4k + 10.

steps.text: The breadth is a + 2. The length is 2 more, so the length is a + 4.
Add the length and the breadth: a + 4 + a + 2 = 2a + 6.
The perimeter is 2 times this.
The perimeter is 4a + 12.

notes.A: Check the length again. It is a + 4, and both the length and the breadth are counted twice.
notes.B: This is 4 times the breadth, as if all four sides were equal. The length is 2 more than the breadth.
notes.C: Yes! Length a + 4 plus breadth a + 2 is 2a + 6, and twice that is 4a + 12.
notes.D: The numbers were doubled but the letters were not. Doubling 2a + 6 doubles both parts.

hints: This is a substitution problem with brackets. Work out each bracket first, then multiply.
Put a = 2 and b = 5 into the first bracket, a + b. Then do the same for b − a.
Similar example: if a = 3 and b = 7, find (a + b) × (b − a). First bracket: 3 + 7 = 10. Second bracket: 7 − 3 = 4. Multiply: 10 × 4 = 40.

steps.text: Work out the first bracket.
Work out the second bracket.
Multiply the two results.
The value is 21.

notes.A: This is 7 × 7. The second bracket is b − a, which is 5 − 2, not 7.
notes.B: Yes! The brackets are 7 and 3, and 7 × 3 = 21.
notes.C: This is 5 × 5. Use both letters: the brackets are 2 + 5 and 5 − 2.
notes.D: This is 7 + 3. The two brackets are multiplied, not added.

hints: This is a substitution problem. Some letters are given through other letters, so find each letter's value in order first.
Start with x = 3. Use it to find y = x − 1, then use both to find z = x + y.
Similar example: find 4x − 2y + 3z when x = 5, y = x − 2 and z = x + y. First y = 5 − 2 = 3 and z = 5 + 3 = 8. Then 4 × 5 − 2 × 3 + 3 × 8 = 20 − 6 + 24 = 38.

steps.text: y is 1 less than x.
z is x and y added together.
Now put the values in: 6x is 18, 3y is 6 and 5z is 25.
The value is 37.

notes.A: Yes! With x = 3, y = 2 and z = 5 you get 18 − 6 + 25 = 37.
notes.B: Check the value of each letter again: y is 2 and z is 5. Then 6x − 3y + 5z is 18 − 6 + 25.
notes.C: Check z again. It is x + y, which is 3 + 2. Then work out 18 − 6 + 25.
notes.D: The value is in the list. Find y and z first, then work out 18 − 6 + 25.

hints: This is a compare problem. Find the value of every expression, then pick the smallest.
Put a = 3 and b = 6 into the first expression: 4a means 4 × 3. Do the same for each of the others.
Similar example: with a = 2 and b = 5, which is least: 3a + b, 2b − a or 4a − b? 3a + b is 6 + 5 = 11. 2b − a is 10 − 2 = 8. 4a − b is 8 − 5 = 3. The least value is 3, so 4a − b is least.

steps.text: Work out 4a − b.
Work out 5b − 7a.
Work out 3b − 5a.
Work out 7a − 2b.
The smallest value is 3, so 3b − 5a has the least value.

notes.A: This one is 12 − 6 = 6. Another expression gives a smaller value.
notes.B: This one is 30 − 21 = 9. That is one of the largest values here.
notes.C: Yes! 3b − 5a is 18 − 15 = 3, the smallest of the four.
notes.D: This one is 21 − 12 = 9. Look for a smaller value.

hints: This is a compare problem. Find the value of every expression, then pick the smallest. Work out brackets first.
Put m = 2, n = 3 and p = 5 into the first expression: m × n + p. Then do the same for each of the others.

Similar example: with m = 3, n = 4 and p = 6, which is least: m × n + p, (p − m) × n or p + n − m? The first is 12 + 6 = 18. The second is 3 × 4 = 12. The third is 10 − 3 = 7. The least value is 7, so p + n − m is least.

steps.text: Work out m × n + p.
Work out (p − m) × n.
Work out (p − n) × m.
Work out p + n − m.
The smallest value is 4, so (p − n) × m has the least value.

notes.A: This one is 2 × 3 + 5 = 11. That is the largest value here.
notes.B: This one is 3 × 3 = 9. Another expression gives a smaller value.
notes.C: Yes! (p − n) × m is 2 × 2 = 4, the smallest of the four.
notes.D: This one is 5 + 3 − 2 = 6. It is close, but one expression is smaller.

hints: This is a compare problem. Find the value of each side, then choose the sign that fits between them.
Put A = 7 into the left side first: 4A means 4 × 7, then add 17. Then work out the right side.
Similar example: compare 5A + 6 and 7A − 4 when A = 3. Left side: 5 × 3 + 6 = 21. Right side: 7 × 3 − 4 = 17. Since 21 is greater than 17, the sign is >.

steps.text: Left side: put A = 7 into 4A + 17.
Right side: put A = 7 into 8A − 9.
45 is less than 47, so the sign is <.

notes.A: The left side is 45 and the right side is 47. The open end of the sign must face the bigger number.
notes.B: Yes! The left side is 45 and the right side is 47, and 45 is less than 47.
notes.C: The two sides are close but not equal: 45 on the left and 47 on the right.
notes.D: One of the signs does fit. Work out both sides and compare 45 with 47.

hints: This is a counting-back problem. Think about whether a 2-digit prime is odd or even, and how far apart even numbers are.
A 2-digit prime is odd, so the first even number before V + 38 is just 1 less. After that, each even number is 2 less than the one before.

Similar example: N + 30 is an odd number. Find the 6th even number before it. The 1st even number before it is N + 29. To reach the 6th, go back 5 more jumps of 2, which is 10. So the 6th even number before it is N + 19.

steps.text: Every 2-digit prime is odd. So the 1st even number before V + 38 is 1 less: V + 37.
Even numbers are 2 apart. From the 1st to the 13th is 12 jumps of 2.
Go back 24 from V + 37.
The 13th even number before it is V + 13.

notes.A: Yes! The 1st even number before it is V + 37, and 12 more jumps of 2 take you to V + 13.
notes.B: This goes back one jump too many. From the 1st even number to the 13th is 12 jumps of 2, not 13.
notes.C: This stops one jump early. Count again: from the 1st even number to the 13th is 12 jumps of 2.
notes.D: V + 38 is odd, so V + 14 is odd too. Start from the 1st even number, V + 37, and go back 24.

hints: This is a substitution problem with brackets. Find the value of every letter first, then work out each bracket.
Start with p = 4 and use it to find q = 2p + 1. Only then work out q − p and q + p.
Similar example: if p = 3 and q = 2p + 2, find (q − p) × (q + p). q = 2 × 3 + 2 = 8. Then q − p = 8 − 3 = 5 and q + p = 8 + 3 = 11. Multiply: 5 × 11 = 55.

steps.text: Find q using p = 4.
Work out the first bracket.
Work out the second bracket.
Multiply the two brackets.
The value is 65.

notes.A: The digits look swapped. The brackets are 5 and 13, so work out 5 × 13 again.
notes.B: Yes! q is 9, the brackets are 5 and 13, and 5 × 13 = 65.
notes.C: Check each bracket: q − p is 9 − 4 and q + p is 9 + 4. Then multiply the two results.
notes.D: Check q first: 2 × 4 + 1 = 9. Then the brackets are 5 and 13, and you multiply them.

hints: This is a compare problem. Find the value of each letter, then the value of each expression, and pick the greatest.
Start with p = 4. Find a = 2p − 1 first, then y = a + 2.
Similar example: p = 2, a = 2p + 1 and y = a + 3. So a = 5 and y = 8. Then a + y − p is 5 + 8 − 2 = 11, and 3p + y − a is 6 + 8 − 5 = 9. The first one, a + y − p, is greater.

steps.text: Find a from p = 4.
Find y from a.
Work out 3a − 2y + p.
Work out 3p + a − y.
Work out y − a + p.
10 is the greatest, so 3p + a − y has the greatest value.

notes.A: This one is 21 − 18 + 4 = 7. Another expression is greater.
notes.B: Yes! 3p + a − y is 12 + 7 − 9 = 10, the greatest of the three.
notes.C: This one is 9 − 7 + 4 = 6. That is the smallest of the three.
notes.D: The values are 7, 10 and 6, so they are not all the same.

hints: This is about writing an expression from words. Decide which operation the word 'total' asks for.
The total weight is the two weights put together. Write the weight of the apples and the weight of the bananas with the right sign between them.
Similar example: Ravi buys y kg of rice and 5 kg of flour. Total means add, so the total weight is (y + 5) kg.

steps.text: The apples weigh x kg and the bananas weigh 2 kg.
Total weight means we add the two weights.
The total weight is (x + 2) kg.

notes.A: Yes! Total means add, so x kg and 2 kg together make (x + 2) kg.
notes.B: This takes the bananas away. Total means both weights are put together.
notes.C: This is 2 times x. The 2 kg of bananas is added to the apples, not multiplied.
notes.D: This shares x into 2 parts. For a total, add the two weights.

hints: This is about writing an expression from words. The same amount is repeated every hour, so think about which operation fits.
He reads k pages in each of the 6 hours. Think of adding k six times.
Similar example: Meera walks m km every day. In 4 days she walks m + m + m + m, which is 4 times m, written 4m km.

steps.text: In 1 hour Mann reads k pages.
In 6 hours he reads 6 times as many.
He can read 6k pages.

notes.A: Yes! k pages every hour for 6 hours is 6 times k, written 6k.
notes.B: This adds 6 pages only once. He reads k pages in every one of the 6 hours.
notes.C: This shares k among 6. More hours means more pages, so multiply.
notes.D: This takes 6 away. Reading for more hours gives more pages, so multiply k by 6.

hints: This is an age expression. Decide whether his age now is more or less than his age in the future.
'8 years hence' means 8 years from now. His age now is smaller than y. Think about by how much.
Similar example: 5 years from now Anu will be p years old. She is 5 years younger now, so her present age is (p − 5) years.

steps.text: 8 years hence means 8 years from now. Then Rahul will be y years old.
Now he is 8 years younger than that, so take 8 away from y.
His present age is (y − 8) years.

notes.A: Yes! He is 8 years younger now than he will be then, so his age is (y − 8) years.
notes.B: This is his age 8 years after he turns y. Now he is younger than y, so take away.
notes.C: This is 8 times y. Years pass by adding, not by multiplying.
notes.D: This shares y into 8 parts. He is just 8 years younger now, so take 8 away from y.

hints: This is about turning words into an expression. Look for the words that tell you the operation: 'sum' and 'more than'.
First write the sum of a and b. Then think about what '4 more than' does to it.
Similar example: 7 more than the sum of p and q. The sum is p + q. 7 more means add 7, so it is p + q + 7.

steps.text: The sum of a and b is a + b.
4 more than this means add 4.
The expression is a + b + 4.

notes.A: Yes! Sum means a + b, and 4 more means add 4.
notes.B: This is 4 times the sum. '4 more than' means add 4.
notes.C: This is 4 less than the sum. 'More than' means add.
notes.D: This multiplies everything. 'Sum' means add a and b, and '4 more' means add 4.

hints: This is about turning words into an expression. Look for the words that tell you the operation: 'times' and 'difference'.
First write the difference of x and y. Then think how to show that the whole difference is multiplied by 4.
Similar example: 3 times the sum of p and q. The sum is p + q. To multiply the whole sum by 3, put it in brackets: 3(p + q).

steps.text: The difference of x and y is x − y.
4 times the whole difference needs brackets around x − y.
The expression is 4(x − y).

notes.A: Yes! The brackets show that the whole difference x − y is multiplied by 4.
notes.B: Here only x is multiplied by 4. The whole difference must be multiplied, so use brackets.
notes.C: Here only y is multiplied by 4. Put x − y in brackets and multiply all of it.
notes.D: This divides the difference by 4. '4 times' means multiply.

hints: This is a substitution problem. Swap each letter for its number. A number written next to a letter means multiply.
Put a = 3 into 5a first: that is 5 × 3. Then do the same for 3b.
Similar example: if a = 4 and b = 1, find 6a + 2b. 6a is 6 × 4 = 24 and 2b is 2 × 1 = 2. Add: 24 + 2 = 26.

steps.text: 5a means 5 times a.
3b means 3 times b.
Add the two parts.
The value is 21.

notes.B: This adds all four numbers: 5 + 3 + 3 + 2. But 5a means 5 × 3 and 3b means 3 × 2.
notes.C: This is 15 + 2. The 3b part is 3 × 2, not just 2.
notes.D: Check each part: 5 × 3 = 15 and 3 × 2 = 6. Then add them.

hints: This is about opening a bracket. The number outside multiplies every term inside.
Multiply 3 by the first term, 2b. Then multiply 3 by the second term too.
Similar example: 2(3x + 5y). Multiply each term by 2: 2 times 3x is 6x and 2 times 5y is 10y. So 2(3x + 5y) = 6x + 10y.

steps.text: Multiply the first term by 3.
Multiply the second term by 3.

notes.A: Yes! The 3 multiplies both terms: 3 times 2b is 6b and 3 times 4c is 12c.
notes.B: Only the first term was multiplied. The 3 multiplies 4c as well.
notes.C: This adds 3 to each number. The 3 outside the bracket multiplies each term.
notes.D: Check the first term: 3 times 2b is 6b.

hints: This is about opening a bracket. The number outside multiplies every term inside, and the sign between the terms stays.
Multiply 5 by the first term, 3. Then multiply 5 by the second term, 4n, and keep the minus sign.
Similar example: 4(2 − 3k). Multiply each term by 4: 4 × 2 = 8 and 4 times 3k is 12k. Keep the minus sign: 4(2 − 3k) = 8 − 12k.

steps.text: Multiply the first term by 5.
Multiply the second term by 5.
Keep the minus sign between them. So 5(3 − 4n) = 15 − 20n.

notes.A: Yes! 5 × 3 = 15 and 5 times 4n is 20n, with the minus sign kept.
notes.B: The sign changed. Inside the bracket it is minus, so it stays minus.
notes.C: This adds 5 to 3 and leaves 4n alone. The 5 multiplies both terms.
notes.D: Check the first term. 5 × 3 is 15, and it is not taken away.

hints: This is a perimeter problem with letters. A square has four equal sides.
The perimeter of a square is 4 times its side. Write that for this side, then compare with the options, which may be written in another form.
Similar example: a square has side (2x + y). Its perimeter is 4 times (2x + y), which is 8x + 4y. This can also be written as 2(4x + 2y), because 2 times 4x is 8x and 2 times 2y is 4y.

steps.text: A square has 4 equal sides, so the perimeter is 4 times the side.
Multiply each term by 4.
Now open the bracket in 2(6a + 4b): 2 times 6a is 12a and 2 times 4b is 8b. It is the same.
The perimeter is 2(6a + 4b).

notes.A: This is only 2 times the side. A square has 4 equal sides.
notes.B: 3a and 2b are unlike terms, so they cannot be added to make 5ab. Keep them apart and multiply each by 4.
notes.C: 3a + 2b cannot be joined into 5ab. Multiply each term by 4 to get 12a + 8b.
notes.D: Yes! 4 times (3a + 2b) is 12a + 8b, and 2(6a + 4b) is the same thing.

hints: This is a substitution problem. Swap each letter for its number. A number written next to a letter means multiply.
3a means 3 × a, so start with 3 × 6. Then take away b.
Similar example: if a = 7 and b = 3, then 3a − b is 3 × 7 − 3. That is 21 − 3 = 18.

steps.text: 3a means 3 times a. Put a = 6.
Now take away b, which is 7.
The value of 3a − b is 11.

notes.A: It looks like 7 was taken away twice. Take b away only once from 18.
notes.B: This is 6 + 7. But 3a means 3 × 6, so multiply first and then take away 7.
notes.C: This uses 4 lots of a. 3a means only 3 × 6.

hints: This is a substitution problem. Swap each letter for its number. A number written next to a letter means multiply.
3a means 3 × a, so start with 3 × 9. Then take away b.
Similar example: if a = 5 and b = 4, then 3a − b is 3 × 5 − 4. That is 15 − 4 = 11.

steps.text: 3a means 3 times a. Put a = 9.
Now take away b, which is 5.
The value of 3a − b is 22.

notes.B: This is 9 + 5. But 3a means 3 × 9, so multiply first and then take away 5.
notes.C: It looks like 5 was taken away twice. Take b away only once from 27.
notes.D: This uses 4 lots of a. 3a means only 3 × 9.

hints: This is a substitution problem. Swap each letter for its number. A number written next to a letter means multiply.
4b means 4 × b, so start with 4 × 2. Then add a.
Similar example: if a = 5 and b = 4, then a + 4b is 5 + 4 × 4. That is 5 + 16 = 21.

steps.text: 4b means 4 times b. Put b = 2.
Now add a, which is 9.
The value of a + 4b is 17.

notes.A: This uses only 3 lots of b. 4b means 4 × 2.
notes.B: It looks like a was added twice. Add 9 only once to 8.
notes.D: This is 9 + 2. But 4b means 4 × 2, so multiply first and then add 9.

hints: This is a substitution problem. Swap each letter for its number. A number written next to a letter means multiply.
2a means 2 × a, so start with 2 × 10. Then add b.
Similar example: if a = 5 and b = 4, then 2a + b is 2 × 5 + 4. That is 10 + 4 = 14.

steps.text: 2a means 2 times a. Put a = 10.
Now add b, which is 3.
The value of 2a + b is 23.

notes.A: This is 2 × 10, but b has not been added yet. Add 3.
notes.B: This is 10 + 3. But 2a means 2 × 10, so multiply first and then add 3.
notes.C: This uses 3 lots of a. 2a means only 2 × 10.

hints: This is a substitution problem. Swap each letter for its number. A number written next to a letter means multiply.
3a means 3 × a, so start with 3 × 10. Then take away b.
Similar example: if a = 5 and b = 4, then 3a − b is 3 × 5 − 4. That is 15 − 4 = 11.

steps.text: 3a means 3 times a. Put a = 10.
Now take away b, which is 5.
The value of 3a − b is 25.

notes.A: This is 10 + 5. But 3a means 3 × 10, so multiply first and then take away 5.
notes.B: This adds 5 at the end. The sign before b is minus, so take 5 away from 30.
notes.C: It looks like 5 was taken away twice. Take b away only once from 30.

hints: This is a substitution problem. The small 2 above a letter means the letter is multiplied by itself.
a² means a × a. Use a = 3. You do not need b here.
Similar example: if a = 5, then a² is 5 × 5 = 25.

steps.text: a² means a times a. Put a = 3.
The value of b is not needed here. The value of a² is 9.

notes.A: It looks like b was taken away. b is not needed: work out 3 × 3.
notes.B: Check again: a² means 3 × 3. The value of b is not needed.
notes.C: This adds a and b. Only a is needed: work out 3 × 3.
notes.D: Yes! a² means 3 × 3, which is 9.

hints: This is a turning problem. A left turn and a right turn undo each other, so think about the turn that is left over.
The right turn is bigger than the left turn. Find how many degrees of right turn remain after the left turn is cancelled.
Similar example: a girl faces north, turns 45° left and then 225° right. The turns leave 225° − 45° = 180° to the right. Half a turn from north is south, so she faces south.

steps.text: Turning left and then right cancel each other. The right turn is bigger.
So the man ends up turned 90° to the right from north.
A quarter turn to the right from north points east. He is facing East.

notes.A: This is where he faces after the first turn only. He still has to turn 225° to the right.
notes.B: This would be a turn of 135° to the right from north. The turn left over is 225° − 135° = 90° to the right.
notes.C: Yes! The turns leave 90° to the right, and a quarter turn right from north is east.
notes.D: North-West is on the left side of north. The bigger turn is to the right, so he ends on the right side.

hints: This is about complementary and supplementary angles. Complementary angles add up to 90° and supplementary angles add up to 180°.
Find the complement of 35° first by taking it away from 90°. Then find its supplement.
Similar example: for an angle of 20°, the complement is 90° − 20° = 70° and the supplement is 180° − 20° = 160°. Their sum is 70° + 160° = 230°.

steps.text: The complement makes 90° with the angle.
The supplement makes 180° with the angle.
Add the complement and the supplement.
The sum is 200°.

notes.A: Yes! The complement is 55°, the supplement is 145°, and 55° + 145° = 200°.
notes.B: Check both subtractions: 90° − 35° = 55° and 180° − 35° = 145°. Then add them.
notes.C: This is 145° + 35°, the supplement plus the angle itself. Add the complement and the supplement instead.
notes.D: Find both angles first: the complement is 55° and the supplement is 145°. Then add the two.

hints: This is a supplementary angle problem with parts. The angle and its supplement together make 180°.
If the angle is 1 part, its supplement is 5 equal parts. Count how many parts make 180° altogether.
Similar example: an angle is one third of its supplement. The angle is 1 part and the supplement is 3 parts, so 4 parts make 180°. One part is 180° ÷ 4 = 45°. The angle is 45°.

steps.text: The angle is one fifth of its supplement. So if the angle is 1 part, the supplement is 5 parts.
Together they make 180°, and that is 6 parts.
Find one part.
Check: the supplement is 150°, and one fifth of 150° is 30°. The angle is 30°.

notes.A: Check it: the supplement of 40° is 140°, and one fifth of 140° is 28°, not 40°.
notes.B: Check it: the supplement of 35° is 145°, and one fifth of 145° is 29°, not 35°.
notes.C: Yes! 30° and 150° make 180°, and 30° is one fifth of 150°.
notes.D: Check it: the supplement of 50° is 130°, and one fifth of 130° is 26°, not 50°.

hints: This is about types of angles. Think about how big an obtuse angle is and what its supplement must add to it.
An obtuse angle is more than 90° but less than 180°. Its supplement is what is left to reach 180°. Is that more or less than 90°?

Similar example: what kind of angle is the supplement of an acute angle? Try 40°: its supplement is 180° − 40° = 140°. An acute angle is less than 90°, so what is left is always more than 90°. The supplement of an acute angle is always obtuse.

steps.text: An obtuse angle is more than 90° and less than 180°.
Its supplement is 180° take away the angle. Taking away more than 90° leaves less than 90°.
For example, the supplement of 110° is 70°.
An angle less than 90° is acute. So the supplement of an obtuse angle is always an Acute Angle.

notes.A: The supplement would be a right angle only if the angle itself were 90°. An obtuse angle is bigger than 90°.
notes.B: Complementary describes two angles that add up to 90°. Here, ask how big the supplement is.
notes.C: A straight angle is 180° all by itself. The supplement is only the part left over after the obtuse angle.
notes.D: Yes! Taking more than 90° away from 180° always leaves less than 90°, which is an acute angle.

hints: This is about complementary and supplementary angles. Complementary angles add up to 90° and supplementary angles add up to 180°.
Find the complement of 48° first by taking it away from 90°. Then find its supplement.
Similar example: for an angle of 30°, the complement is 90° − 30° = 60° and the supplement is 180° − 30° = 150°. Their sum is 60° + 150° = 210°.

steps.text: The complement makes 90° with the angle.
The supplement makes 180° with the angle.
Add the complement and the supplement.
The sum is 174°.

notes.A: This is 10° short. The complement is 42° and the supplement is 132°. Add them again.
notes.B: Yes! The complement is 42°, the supplement is 132°, and 42° + 132° = 174°.
notes.C: Check both subtractions: 90° − 48° = 42° and 180° − 48° = 132°. Then add them.
notes.D: This is 10° too much. The complement is 42° and the supplement is 132°. Add them again.

hints: This question has two parts. Find the complementary angle and the supplementary angle of the same angle, then add them.
The complement of 48° is what must be added to 48° to make 90°. Find it first, then find the supplement in the same way with 180°.
Similar example: for an angle of 25°, the complement is 90° − 25° = 65° and the supplement is 180° − 25° = 155°. Their sum is 65° + 155° = 220°.

steps.text: The complement makes 90° with the angle.
The supplement makes 180° with the angle.
Add the complement and the supplement.
The sum is 174°.

notes.A: This is 10° short. The complement is 42° and the supplement is 132°. Add them again.
notes.B: Check both subtractions: 90° − 48° = 42° and 180° − 48° = 132°. Then add them.
notes.C: Find both angles first: the complement is 42° and the supplement is 132°. Then add the two.
notes.D: Yes! The complement is 42°, the supplement is 132°, and 42° + 132° = 174°.

hints: This is a clock angle problem. The clock face has 12 equal gaps between the numbers, and the hour hand keeps moving slowly as the minutes pass.
A full turn is 360°, so each gap between two numbers is 30°. At 20 minutes the minute hand points at 4. Now think about where the hour hand is: it has moved past 7.
Similar example: at 3:30 the minute hand is at 6. The hour hand is halfway between 3 and 4, so it is 15° before 4. From 4 to 6 is 2 gaps, which is 60°. The angle is 60° + 15° = 75°.

steps.text: Each gap between two numbers on a clock is 30°.
At 20 minutes past, the minute hand points at 4. From 4 to 7 is 3 gaps.
20 minutes is one third of an hour, so the hour hand has moved one third of a gap past 7.
Add the two parts.
The angle between the hands is 100°.

notes.A: This is the angle from 4 to 7. The hour hand has moved a little past 7 in 20 minutes, so add that bit.
notes.B: This adds too much for the hour hand. In 20 minutes it moves one third of a 30° gap, which is 10°.
notes.C: Yes! From 4 to 7 is 90°, and the hour hand is 10° past 7, so the angle is 100°.
notes.D: Count the gaps from 4 to 7 first: 3 gaps of 30°. Then add the small bit the hour hand has moved past 7.

hints: This is a turning problem on the compass. Between two neighbouring directions, such as north and north-east, the turn is 45°.
Start at south-west and move clockwise. Name each direction you pass until you reach north, and count the 45° steps.

Similar example: a boy faces north-east and turns clockwise to face north-west. He passes east, south-east, south, south-west, west and then north-west. That is 6 steps of 45°, so he turns 6 × 45° = 270°.

steps.text: The eight compass directions are 45° apart.
Clockwise from south-west he passes west, then north-west, then north. That is 3 steps.
Each step is 45°.
135° is not in the list, so the answer is None of these.

notes.A: 90° clockwise from south-west reaches north-west. He has to go one more step to reach north.
notes.B: 225° is the turn the other way round, anticlockwise. Clockwise it is shorter.
notes.C: A turn of 180° from south-west ends at north-east, the opposite direction.
notes.D: Yes! The turn is 3 steps of 45°, which is 135°, and that is not one of the listed values.

hints: This is a clock angle problem. Measure each hand's turn from the 12, and remember the hour hand keeps moving as the minutes pass.
The minute hand turns 6° every minute. Find how far it has turned from 12 in 18 minutes. Then find where the hour hand is.

Similar example: at 10 minutes past 4, the minute hand has turned 10 × 6° = 60° from 12. The hour hand has turned 4 × 30° = 120°, plus 5° more for the 10 minutes, so it is at 125°. The angle between them is 125° − 60° = 65°.

steps.text: The minute hand turns 6° each minute. In 18 minutes it is 108° from 12.
At 5 o'clock the hour hand is 150° from 12.
The hour hand moves 1° every 2 minutes, so in 18 minutes it moves 9° more.
Subtract to find the angle between the hands.
The angle is 51°.

notes.A: Yes! The hour hand is at 159° and the minute hand at 108°, and 159° − 108° = 51°.
notes.B: Check the hour hand. It starts at 150° and moves 9° more in 18 minutes, so it is at 159°. Then subtract 108°.
notes.C: Check the minute hand. It turns 6° each minute, so 18 minutes is 108° from 12.
notes.D: Check the subtraction: the hour hand is at 159° and the minute hand is at 108°.

hints: This is about supplementary angles. Two angles are supplementary when they add up to exactly 180°.
Add the two angles in each pair. Start with 62° + 128° and see whether it makes 180°.
Similar example: is 112.5° and 67.5° a supplementary pair? Add them: 112.5 + 67.5 = 180. Yes, they are supplementary. Is 95° and 75°? 95 + 75 = 170, so that pair is not.

steps.text: Supplementary angles add up to 180°, so add each pair.
Add the first pair.
Add the second pair.
Add the third pair.
Add the fourth pair.
Only the last pair makes 180°. The supplementary pair is 140.5° & 39.5°.

notes.B: 73.5° + 107.5° = 181°. That is just 1° too much.
notes.D: Yes! 140.5° + 39.5° = 180°, so this pair is supplementary.

hints: This is about the parts of a line. Think about the difference between a line, a ray and a line segment.
A line segment is a piece of a line that starts at one point and stops at another. Count the points where it stops.
Similar example: how many end points does a ray have? A ray starts at one point and goes on forever in one direction. So a ray has 1 end point.

steps.text: A line segment is a straight path between two points.
It stops at both of those points, so each one is an end point.
A line segment has 2 end points.

notes.A: Yes! A line segment stops at both sides, so it has 2 end points.
notes.B: One end point describes a ray, which goes on forever on one side. A line segment stops at both sides.
notes.C: No end points describes a line, which goes on forever both ways. A line segment stops at both sides.
notes.D: A line segment has endless points on it, but it only stops at its two ends.

hints: This is about lines and points. Picture two dots on paper and a ruler.
Mark two different points and lay a ruler so its edge touches both. Try to draw a second, different straight line through both.
Similar example: how many lines can pass through a single point? You can keep turning a ruler around that point and draw a new line each time. So endless lines pass through a single point.

steps.text: Mark two different points and join them with a ruler. You get a straight line.
Any other straight line through both points lies exactly on top of the first.
So only One line can pass through two distinct points.

notes.A: Yes! Two points fix the line completely, so there is exactly one.
notes.B: Try drawing a second straight line through both points. It falls exactly on the first one.
notes.C: Endless lines pass through a single point. Once a second point is fixed, the line cannot turn any more.
notes.D: You can always join two points with a ruler, so there is a line.

hints: This is a geometry word question. Think about what the parts of each word mean.
'Co' means together, as in co-operate. Look for the word that means together on one line.
Similar example: three or more lines that pass through the same point are called concurrent lines. The word tells you they run together through one point.

steps.text: 'Co' means together and 'linear' means on a line.
So points that lie together on the same line are called collinear points.
Three or more points on the same line are called Collinear.

notes.A: Yes! Collinear means lying together on the same line.
notes.B: Non-collinear means the points do not all lie on one line. Here they do.
notes.C: Concurrent is used for lines that meet at one point. Here we are naming points on one line.
notes.D: Parallel is used for lines that never meet. Here we are naming points on one line.

hints: This is about naming angles by size. Each name goes with a range of degrees, measured against 90° and 180°.
Compare with a right angle, which is exactly 90°. Which name is used for an angle smaller than that?
Similar example: an angle more than 90° but less than 180° is called an obtuse angle. For example, 120° is obtuse.

steps.text: A right angle is exactly 90°.
An angle smaller than a right angle, between 0° and 90°, has its own name.
An angle less than 90° is called an Acute angle.

notes.A: Yes! Acute angles are the ones smaller than 90°.
notes.B: A right angle is exactly 90°, not less.
notes.C: An obtuse angle is more than 90°. Here the angle is less than 90°.
notes.D: A straight angle is 180°, a straight line. Here the angle is less than 90°.

hints: This is about the size of a special angle. Think of the corner of a square or of your book.
A full turn is 360°. A right angle is a quarter of a full turn.
Similar example: a straight angle is half of a full turn. Half of 360° is 360° ÷ 2 = 180°, so a straight angle measures 180°.

steps.text: A full turn is 360°. A right angle is a quarter turn, like the corner of a square.
Divide the full turn into 4 equal parts.
A right angle measures 90°.

notes.A: Yes! A right angle is a quarter turn, and a quarter of 360° is 90°.
notes.B: 180° is a straight angle, which is two right angles together.
notes.C: 45° is half of a right angle.
notes.D: 360° is a full turn, which is four right angles.

hints: This is about naming angles by size. Picture what the two arms of the angle look like.
Draw an angle of 180°. The two arms point in opposite directions. What shape do they make together?
Similar example: an angle of 360° is a full turn back to the start, so it is called a complete angle.

steps.text: 180° is half of a full turn.
The two arms point in opposite directions and form a straight line.
So an angle of 180° is called a Straight angle.

notes.A: Yes! At 180° the two arms form a straight line.
notes.B: A right angle is 90°, half of 180°.
notes.C: A reflex angle is more than 180° and less than 360°.
notes.D: A complete angle is a full turn of 360°.

hints: This is about naming an angle by its size. Compare the angle with 90° and with 180°.
Is 135° more than 90°? Is it less than 180°? Use both answers to pick the name.
Similar example: what type of angle is 200°? It is more than 180° and less than 360°, so it is a reflex angle.

steps.text: 135° is more than 90°, so it is bigger than a right angle.

hints: Think about what makes a line a diameter. It has to pass through one special point of the circle.
A diameter starts on the circle, passes through the centre, and ends on the circle. From your point, how many straight lines go through the centre?

Similar example: how many radii can be drawn from the centre of a circle? A radius joins the centre to a point on the circle. There are endless points on the circle, so endless radii can be drawn from the centre.

steps.text: A diameter is a straight line that joins two points on the circle and passes through the centre.
Start at the chosen point on the circle. To be a diameter, the line must go straight through the centre.
Only one straight line can pass through two fixed points, here the chosen point and the centre.
So only 1 diameter can be drawn from a point on the circle.

notes.A: Yes! A diameter must pass through the centre, and only one straight line joins your point to the centre and carries on to the other side.
notes.B: Other lines from the point miss the centre, so they are chords, not diameters. Count only the line that passes through the centre.
notes.C: Many chords can be drawn from one point, but a diameter must pass through the centre. Only one line from the point does that.
notes.D: A whole circle has endless diameters, but each one starts from a different point. From one point, only one line goes through the centre.

hints: This is a circle problem that uses two formulas: area = π × r × r and circumference = 2 × π × r. Compare the two.
Write 3 times the circumference: 3 × 2 × π × r. Then set it beside the area, π × r × r, and see what r must be.

Similar example: the area of a circle is 2 times its circumference. 2 times the circumference is 2 × 2 × π × r, which is 4 × π × r. The area is π × r × r. Both have π × r, so the other r must be 4. The radius is 4.

steps.text: The area of a circle is π × r × r. The circumference is 2 × π × r.
3 times the circumference is 3 × 2 × π × r, which is 6 × π × r.
So π × r × r is the same as 6 × π × r. Both sides have π × r, so the r that is left must equal 6.
The radius is 6.

notes.A: Try it: with radius 5 the area is 25 × π and 3 times the circumference is 30 × π. They are not equal.
notes.B: Yes! With radius 6 the area is 36 × π and 3 times the circumference is also 36 × π.
notes.C: Try it: with radius 7 the area is 49 × π and 3 times the circumference is 42 × π. They are not equal.
notes.D: Try it: with radius 8 the area is 64 × π and 3 times the circumference is 48 × π. They are not equal.

hints: This is a circle problem with two formulas: circumference = 2 × π × r and area = π × r × r. Compare them, and read carefully whether the radius or the diameter is asked.
Set 2 × π × r beside π × r × r. Both have π × r. See what the remaining r must be, and remember the question asks for the diameter.

Similar example: the area of a circle is 5 times its circumference. 5 times the circumference is 5 × 2 × π × r, which is 10 × π × r. The area is π × r × r, so r must be 10. The diameter is 2 × 10 = 20.

steps.text: The circumference is 2 × π × r. The area is π × r × r.
They are equal. Both have π × r, so the r that is left must equal 2. The radius is 2 cm.
The diameter is twice the radius.
The diameter is 4 cm.

notes.A: Try it: a diameter of 6 cm gives radius 3 cm. Then the circumference is 6 × π and the area is 9 × π, which are not equal.
notes.B: 2 cm is the radius. The question asks for the diameter, which is twice as long.
notes.C: Yes! With radius 2 cm, the circumference and the area are both 4 × π, and the diameter is 4 cm.
notes.D: There is a value that fits. Find the radius first, then double it.

hints: The circles fill the rectangle exactly, so its length and breadth can be counted in circle widths. The width of a circle is its diameter.
Find the diameter of one circle: it is twice the radius of 7 cm. The length of the rectangle is 4 diameters and the breadth is 2 diameters.

Similar example: 10 equal circles of radius 2 cm sit in a rectangle in 2 rows of 5. The diameter is 4 cm. The length is 5 × 4 = 20 cm and the breadth is 2 × 4 = 8 cm, so the area is 20 × 8 = 160 sq cm.

steps.text: The diameter of each circle is twice the radius.
The length holds 4 circles side by side.
The breadth holds 2 circles.
Area is length times breadth. The area of the rectangle is 1568 sq.cm.

notes.A: Yes! The diameter is 14 cm, so the rectangle is 56 cm by 28 cm, and 56 × 28 = 1568.
notes.B: The sides may be right, so check the multiplying. 56 × 20 = 1120 and 56 × 8 = 448. Add these two.
notes.C: 784 is 28 × 28, which uses a length of only 2 diameters. The length holds 4 circles, so it is 4 × 14 = 56 cm.
notes.D: This is a little too big. Try 56 × 28 in two parts, 56 × 20 and 56 × 8, then add them.

hints: This is a circle problem in two parts. Use the circumference to find the radius, then use the radius to find the area. Take π as 22/7.
Circumference = 2 × π × r. Put 132 for the circumference and 22/7 for π, and find r.
Similar example: a circle has circumference 44 cm. With π as 22/7, the circumference is 44/7 times r, so r is 44 × 7 ÷ 44 = 7 cm. The area is 22/7 × 7 × 7 = 154 sq. cm.

steps.text: Circumference = 2 × π × r. With π as 22/7, this is 44/7 times r.
So r is 132 × 7 ÷ 44. The radius is 21 cm.
Area = π × r × r.
The area is 1386 sq. cm.

notes.A: Check the last multiplication. With radius 21 cm, 22/7 × 21 × 21 is the same as 22 × 3 × 21.
notes.B: The radius is 21 cm. Work out 22 × 63 again carefully.
notes.C: Find the radius first: 132 × 7 ÷ 44 = 21 cm. Then use area = π × r × r.
notes.D: Yes! The radius is 21 cm, and 22/7 × 21 × 21 = 1386.

hints: This problem joins two shapes. Find the perimeter of the rectangle first, then use the circumference formula, 2 × π × r, with π as 22/7.
Work out the perimeter of the rectangle: 2 times (length + breadth). That number is also the circumference of the circle.

Similar example: a circle's circumference equals the perimeter of a rectangle 50 cm by 38 cm. The perimeter is 2 × (50 + 38) = 176 cm. With π as 22/7, the circumference is 44/7 times r, so r is 176 × 7 ÷ 44 = 28 cm.

steps.text: Find the perimeter of the rectangle.
The circumference is also 44 cm. Circumference = 2 × π × r, which is 44/7 times r when π is 22/7.
The radius is 7 cm.

notes.A: 14 cm is the diameter of this circle. The radius is half of it.
notes.B: Check the perimeter first: 2 × (14 + 8) = 44 cm. Then find r from the circumference formula.
notes.C: Yes! The perimeter is 44 cm, and a circle of radius 7 cm has circumference 44 cm.
notes.D: This halves once too often. The radius is 7 cm, and 3.5 cm is half of the radius.

hints: This is about the parts of a circle. Each part has its own name. Think about which one starts at the centre.
Picture a line drawn from the centre straight out to the edge of the circle. It goes only halfway across.
Similar example: a line that joins two points on a circle and passes through the centre goes all the way across. It is called the diameter.

steps.text: Mark the centre of a circle and any point on the circle.
The line joining them goes from the centre to the edge. Every such line has the same length.
This distance is called the Radius.

notes.A: Yes! The radius is the distance from the centre to the circle.
notes.B: A diameter goes all the way across the circle through the centre. From the centre to the circle is only half of that.
notes.C: A chord joins two points on the circle. This distance starts at the centre.
notes.D: The circumference is the distance all the way around the circle.

hints: This is about the parts of a circle. Think about how the radius and the diameter are drawn.
Draw a diameter and mark the centre on it. Count how many radii lie along that diameter.
Similar example: a circle has diameter 12 cm. The centre cuts the diameter into two equal pieces, and each piece is a radius. So the radius is 12 ÷ 2 = 6 cm.

steps.text: A diameter goes across the circle through the centre.
The centre cuts it into two pieces, and each piece is a radius.
So the diameter is Twice the radius.

notes.A: Yes! Two radii placed end to end through the centre make a diameter.
notes.B: It is the other way round: the radius is half the diameter.
notes.C: The radius reaches only from the centre to the circle. The diameter goes right across.
notes.D: Only two radii fit along a diameter, one on each side of the centre.

hints: This is about the parts of a circle. A chord is a straight line joining two points on the circle.
Picture chords drawn across a circle. They get longer as they move closer to the centre. Where is the longest one?
Similar example: in a circle with centre O, chord PQ passes through O and chord RS does not. PQ is made of two radii end to end, so it is as long as a chord can be. RS is shorter.

steps.text: A chord joins two points on the circle.
Chords get longer as they get closer to the centre. The longest one passes through the centre.
A chord through the centre is called a diameter. So the longest chord is the Diameter.

notes.A: Yes! The chord through the centre is the longest, and it is the diameter.
notes.B: A radius goes from the centre to the circle, so it is not a chord. A chord joins two points on the circle.
notes.C: An arc is a curved piece of the circle itself. A chord is a straight line.
notes.D: A tangent touches the circle at just one point from outside. A chord joins two points on the circle.

hints: This is about the radius and the diameter of a circle. Think about how the two are related.
The diameter goes right across the circle through the centre, so it is made of two radii. Use the radius of 7 cm.
Similar example: a circle has radius 9 cm. The diameter is twice the radius, so it is 2 × 9 = 18 cm.

steps.text: The diameter is twice the radius.
Multiply the radius by 2.
The diameter is 14 cm.

notes.A: Yes! The diameter is twice the radius, and 2 × 7 = 14.
notes.B: This is half of the radius. The diameter is bigger than the radius, so multiply by 2.
notes.C: This is 3 times the radius. A diameter is made of 2 radii.
notes.D: This is 7 × 7. For the diameter, multiply the radius by 2.

hints: This question is about the names of the parts of a circle. Think about which word means the line that goes all the way around.
Picture walking along the edge of a round park until you are back where you started. Which word names that whole path around?
A similar example: the line going all the way around a square is called its perimeter. A circle has its own special word for the distance all the way around.

steps.text: The boundary of a circle is the curved line that goes all the way around it.
The length of that line has a special name. It is like a perimeter, but for a circle.
The boundary of a circle is called the circumference.

notes.A: Yes! The circumference is the line all the way around a circle.
notes.B: Area is the space inside the circle, not its edge. Think of the line that goes around.
notes.C: The diameter is a straight line across the circle through the centre. The boundary is the curved line around it.
notes.D: The radius goes from the centre to the edge. The boundary is the curved line all the way around.

hints: This asks for the area of a circle, the space inside it. The rule uses π and the radius.
Area = π × radius × radius. Put 21 in for the radius and 22/7 for π. Try dividing 21 by 7 first.
A similar example: a circle with radius 7 cm. Area = 22/7 × 7 × 7. First 7 ÷ 7 = 1. Then 22 × 1 × 7 = 154. The area is 154 cm².

steps.text: The area of a circle is π × radius × radius. The radius is 21 cm.
Divide 21 by 7 first to make the sum easy.
Now multiply 22 by 3, then by 21.
The area is 1386 cm².

notes.A: Yes! 22/7 × 21 × 21 = 1386, so the area is 1386 cm².
notes.B: This is half of the area. Something got halved along the way. Multiply 22/7 by 21, then by 21 again.
notes.C: 42 is just the diameter, 2 × 21. For the area, multiply 22/7 by the radius and by the radius again.
notes.D: This is double the area. The 2 belongs to the circumference rule. The area rule is π × radius × radius, with no 2.

hints: This asks for the circumference, the distance all the way around the circle. The rule uses π and the radius.
Circumference = 2 × π × radius. Put 35 in for the radius and 22/7 for π. Try dividing 35 by 7 first.
A similar example: a circle with radius 21 cm. Circumference = 2 × 22/7 × 21. First 21 ÷ 7 = 3. Then 2 × 22 × 3 = 132. The circumference is 132 cm.

steps.text: The circumference of a circle is 2 × π × radius. The radius is 35 cm.
Divide 35 by 7 first to make the sum easy.
Now multiply 2 by 22, then by 5.
The circumference is 220 cm.

notes.A: 70 is just the diameter, 2 × 35. To go around the circle, multiply the diameter by 22/7 as well.
notes.B: This is double the circumference. It happens if you double the radius and then multiply by 2 again. Use 2 × 22/7 × 35.
notes.C: Yes! 2 × 22/7 × 35 = 220, so the circumference is 220 cm.
notes.D: This is 22/7 × 35, which leaves out the 2. The circumference is 2 × π × radius.

hints: This asks for the area of a circle, the space inside it. The rule uses π and the radius.
Area = π × radius × radius. Put 28 in for the radius and 22/7 for π. Try dividing 28 by 7 first.
A similar example: a circle with radius 21 cm. Area = 22/7 × 21 × 21. First 21 ÷ 7 = 3. Then 22 × 3 × 21 = 1386. The area is 1386 cm².

steps.text: The area of a circle is π × radius × radius. The radius is 28 cm.
Divide 28 by 7 first to make the sum easy.
Now multiply 22 by 4, then by 28.
The area is 2464 cm².

notes.A: Yes! 22/7 × 28 × 28 = 2464, so the area is 2464 cm².
notes.B: This is double the area. The 2 belongs to the circumference rule. The area rule is π × radius × radius, with no 2.
notes.C: 56 is just the diameter, 2 × 28. For the area, multiply 22/7 by the radius and by the radius again.
notes.D: This is half of the area. Something got halved along the way. Multiply 22/7 by 28, then by 28 again.

hints: This asks for the circumference, the distance all the way around the circle. The rule uses π and the radius.
Circumference = 2 × π × radius. Put 14 in for the radius and 22/7 for π. Try dividing 14 by 7 first.
A similar example: a circle with radius 21 cm. Circumference = 2 × 22/7 × 21. First 21 ÷ 7 = 3. Then 2 × 22 × 3 = 132. The circumference is 132 cm.

steps.text: The circumference of a circle is 2 × π × radius. The radius is 14 cm.
Divide 14 by 7 first to make the sum easy.
Now multiply 2 by 22, then by 2.
The circumference is 88 cm.

notes.A: 28 is just the diameter, 2 × 14. To go around the circle, multiply the diameter by 22/7 as well.
notes.B: Yes! 2 × 22/7 × 14 = 88, so the circumference is 88 cm.
notes.C: This is 22/7 × 14, which leaves out the 2. The circumference is 2 × π × radius.
notes.D: This is double the circumference. It happens if you double the radius and then multiply by 2 again. Use 2 × 22/7 × 14.

hints: This asks for the circumference, the distance all the way around the circle. The rule uses π and the radius.
Circumference = 2 × π × radius. Put 28 in for the radius and 22/7 for π. Try dividing 28 by 7 first.
A similar example: a circle with radius 21 cm. Circumference = 2 × 22/7 × 21. First 21 ÷ 7 = 3. Then 2 × 22 × 3 = 132. The circumference is 132 cm.

steps.text: The circumference of a circle is 2 × π × radius. The radius is 28 cm.
Divide 28 by 7 first to make the sum easy.
Now multiply 2 by 22, then by 4.
The circumference is 176 cm.

notes.A: This is double the circumference. It happens if you double the radius and then multiply by 2 again. Use 2 × 22/7 × 28.
notes.B: This is 22/7 × 28, which leaves out the 2. The circumference is 2 × π × radius.
notes.C: 56 is just the diameter, 2 × 28. To go around the circle, multiply the diameter by 22/7 as well.
notes.D: Yes! 2 × 22/7 × 28 = 176, so the circumference is 176 cm.

hints: This asks for the circumference, the distance all the way around the circle. The rule uses π and the radius.
Circumference = 2 × π × radius. Put 7 in for the radius and 22/7 for π. Try dividing 7 by 7 first.
A similar example: a circle with radius 21 cm. Circumference = 2 × 22/7 × 21. First 21 ÷ 7 = 3. Then 2 × 22 × 3 = 132. The circumference is 132 cm.

steps.text: The circumference of a circle is 2 × π × radius. The radius is 7 cm.
Divide 7 by 7 first to make the sum easy.
Now multiply 2 by 22, then by 1.
The circumference is 44 cm.

notes.A: Yes! 2 × 22/7 × 7 = 44, so the circumference is 44 cm.
notes.B: This is 22/7 × 7, which leaves out the 2. The circumference is 2 × π × radius.
notes.C: This is double the circumference. It happens if you double the radius and then multiply by 2 again. Use 2 × 22/7 × 7.
notes.D: 14 is just the diameter, 2 × 7. To go around the circle, multiply the diameter by 22/7 as well.

hints: This asks for the area of a circle, the space inside it. The rule uses π and the radius.
Area = π × radius × radius. Put 35 in for the radius and 22/7 for π. Try dividing 35 by 7 first.
A similar example: a circle with radius 21 cm. Area = 22/7 × 21 × 21. First 21 ÷ 7 = 3. Then 22 × 3 × 21 = 1386. The area is 1386 cm².

steps.text: The area of a circle is π × radius × radius. The radius is 35 cm.
Divide 35 by 7 first to make the sum easy.
Now multiply 22 by 5, then by 35.
The area is 3850 cm².

notes.A: This is double the area. The 2 belongs to the circumference rule. The area rule is π × radius × radius, with no 2.
notes.B: 70 is just the diameter, 2 × 35. For the area, multiply 22/7 by the radius and by the radius again.
notes.C: This is half of the area. Something got halved along the way. Multiply 22/7 by 35, then by 35 again.
notes.D: Yes! 22/7 × 35 × 35 = 3850, so the area is 3850 cm².

hints: This asks for the area of a circle, the space inside it. The rule uses π and the radius.
Area = π × radius × radius. Put 14 in for the radius and 22/7 for π. Try dividing 14 by 7 first.
A similar example: a circle with radius 21 cm. Area = 22/7 × 21 × 21. First 21 ÷ 7 = 3. Then 22 × 3 × 21 = 1386. The area is 1386 cm².

steps.text: The area of a circle is π × radius × radius. The radius is 14 cm.
Divide 14 by 7 first to make the sum easy.
Now multiply 22 by 2, then by 14.
The area is 616 cm².

notes.A: 28 is just the diameter, 2 × 14. For the area, multiply 22/7 by the radius and by the radius again.
notes.B: This is half of the area. Something got halved along the way. Multiply 22/7 by 14, then by 14 again.
notes.C: Yes! 22/7 × 14 × 14 = 616, so the area is 616 cm².
notes.D: This is double the area. The 2 belongs to the circumference rule. The area rule is π × radius × radius, with no 2.

hints: This asks for the area of a circle, the space inside it. The rule uses π and the radius.
Area = π × radius × radius. Put 7 in for the radius and 22/7 for π. Try dividing 7 by 7 first.
A similar example: a circle with radius 21 cm. Area = 22/7 × 21 × 21. First 21 ÷ 7 = 3. Then 22 × 3 × 21 = 1386. The area is 1386 cm².

steps.text: The area of a circle is π × radius × radius. The radius is 7 cm.
Divide 7 by 7 first to make the sum easy.
Now multiply 22 by 1, then by 7.
The area is 154 cm².

notes.A: 14 is just the diameter, 2 × 7. For the area, multiply 22/7 by the radius and by the radius again.
notes.B: This is half of the area. Something got halved along the way. Multiply 22/7 by 7, then by 7 again.
notes.C: Yes! 22/7 × 7 × 7 = 154, so the area is 154 cm².
notes.D: This is double the area. The 2 belongs to the circumference rule. The area rule is π × radius × radius, with no 2.

hints: This is a counting problem. Every line segment joins a pair of points, so you are counting pairs. Be careful not to count the same pair twice.
Start with one point. How many other points can it join to? Then think about whether joining one point to another is the same segment going the other way.
A similar example: with 5 points on a circle, each point joins to 4 others. 5 × 4 = 20, but every segment got counted twice, once from each end. 20 ÷ 2 = 10 line segments.

steps.text: Each of the 8 points can be joined to the 7 other points.
This counts every segment twice, once from each end. So halve it.
You can check by adding the new segments point by point.
There are 28 line segments.

notes.A: This is 8 × 2. Each point joins to 7 others, not 2. Count the pairs of points.
notes.B: 7 is how many segments start from just one point. Count the segments from all the points.
notes.C: Yes! 8 × 7 ÷ 2 = 28 pairs of points, so there are 28 segments.
notes.D: Check your counting of pairs. Each of the 8 points joins to 7 others, and then you halve because each segment is counted twice.

hints: This is a counting problem about pairs. First find how many different pairs of players there are, then think about how many games each pair plays.
List the pairs of players. The first player can pair with three others. Keep going, without repeating any pair.
A similar example: 3 friends each play 2 games with every other friend. The pairs are first and second, first and third, second and third. That is 3 pairs. 3 × 2 = 6 games.

steps.text: Use the players' names to list the pairs: AB, AC, AD, BC, BD and CD. That is 6 pairs.
Each pair plays 2 games.
The total is 12 games.

notes.A: This is 4 players × 2 games. But games are played by pairs, so count the pairs of players first.
notes.B: Check your list of pairs. There are 6 different pairs, and each pair plays 2 games.
notes.C: This is 4 × 4. A player does not play against themselves, and each pair is counted once. Find the 6 pairs first.
notes.D: Yes! There are 6 pairs of players and each pair plays 2 games, so 6 × 2 = 12.

hints: This is a counting problem turned around. You know the number of line segments and need the number of points. Remember that each segment joins one pair of points.
Try a small number of points and count the segments. With 3 points you get 3 segments. See how the count grows each time you add one more point.

A similar example: how many points give 10 segments? 2 points give 1 segment. A third point adds 2 more, making 3. A fourth point adds 3 more, and a fifth adds 4 more. 3 + 3 + 4 = 10, so 5 points give 10 segments.

steps.text: Each new point joins to all the points already there. Build up the count one point at a time.
2 points give 1 segment. 3 points give 1 + 2 = 3 segments. 4 points give 3 + 3 = 6 segments.
5 points give 6 + 4 = 10 segments. One more point adds 5 more.
Check another way: 6 points, each joined to 5 others, with each segment counted twice.
So there are 6 points.

notes.A: 4 points give only 6 segments. Keep adding points until you reach 15.
notes.B: Yes! 6 points give 6 × 5 ÷ 2 = 15 segments.
notes.C: 5 points give 10 segments, which is not enough. One more point adds 5 more segments.
notes.D: 7 points give 21 segments, which is more than 15. Try one point fewer.

hints: This is a counting problem about arranging digits. An odd number must end in an odd digit, so start by thinking about the last place.
Which of the digits 4, 7, 6 and 9 are odd? Those are the only digits allowed in the ones place. Choose that place first, then fill the other places.

A similar example: using 2, 3 and 8 once each, how many 3-digit even numbers are there? The last digit must be 2 or 8, so 2 choices. The other two digits can go in 2 × 1 = 2 orders. 2 × 2 = 4 even numbers.

steps.text: An odd number ends in an odd digit. Here the odd digits are 7 and 9, so there are 2 choices for the ones place.
The 3 digits left over fill the other three places. They can be arranged in 3 × 2 × 1 ways.
Multiply the choices together.
There are 12 odd numbers.

notes.A: This would need 3 odd digits to choose from for the last place. Only 7 and 9 are odd, so there are 2 choices.
notes.B: 6 is the count for just one ending digit. The number can end in 7 or in 9, so double it.
notes.C: Yes! 2 choices for the last digit and 6 ways to arrange the rest gives 2 × 6 = 12.
notes.D: Check each place in turn. The last place has 2 choices, then the other places have 3, 2 and 1 choices.

hints: This is a counting problem about arranging digits. An odd number must end in an odd digit, so start by thinking about the last place.
Which of the digits 4, 7, 6 and 9 are odd? Those are the only digits allowed in the ones place. Choose that place first, then fill the other places.

A similar example: using 2, 3 and 8 once each, how many 3-digit even numbers are there? The last digit must be 2 or 8, so 2 choices. The other two digits can go in 2 × 1 = 2 orders. 2 × 2 = 4 even numbers.

steps.text: An odd number ends in an odd digit. Here the odd digits are 7 and 9, so there are 2 choices for the ones place.
The 3 digits left over fill the other three places. They can be arranged in 3 × 2 × 1 ways.
Multiply the choices together.
There are 12 odd numbers.

notes.A: This would need 3 odd digits to choose from for the last place. Only 7 and 9 are odd, so there are 2 choices.
notes.B: 6 is the count for just one ending digit. The number can end in 7 or in 9, so double it.
notes.C: 24 is how many 4-digit numbers there are altogether. Only the ones ending in 7 or 9 are odd, which is half of them.
notes.D: Yes! 2 choices for the last digit and 6 ways to arrange the rest gives 2 × 6 = 12.

hints: This is a counting problem about pairs. Each handshake is between two people, so count the pairs. Make sure each handshake is counted only once.
Think about one person first. How many other people do they shake hands with? Then remember that one handshake is shared by two people.
A similar example: 6 people each shake hands once with everyone else. Each person shakes 5 hands. 6 × 5 = 30, but each handshake was counted twice. 30 ÷ 2 = 15 handshakes.

steps.text: Each of the 15 people shakes hands with the 14 others.
Each handshake has been counted twice, once for each person. So halve it.
There are 105 handshakes.

notes.A: Check your multiplication. 15 × 14 = 210, and half of that is the number of handshakes.
notes.B: This is the count for 16 people. Each of the 15 people shakes hands with 14 others, so work out 15 × 14 ÷ 2.
notes.C: Yes! 15 × 14 ÷ 2 = 105 handshakes.
notes.D: Check your sum. Each of the 15 people shakes 14 hands, and every handshake is counted twice, so find 15 × 14 ÷ 2.

hints: This is a counting problem about arranging digits. A 4-digit number is bigger than 5000 only if its first digit is big enough. Start with the thousands place.
Which of the digits 1, 5, 3 and 7 can go in the thousands place so the number is more than 5000? Choose that digit first, then arrange the rest.

A similar example: using 2, 4 and 9 once each, how many 3-digit numbers are bigger than 400? The first digit must be 4 or 9, so 2 choices. The other two digits can go in 2 × 1 = 2 orders. 2 × 2 = 4 numbers.

steps.text: To be more than 5000, the thousands digit must be 5 or 7. That is 2 choices.
The 3 digits left can fill the other places in 3 × 2 × 1 ways.
Multiply the choices.
There are 12 numbers greater than 5000.

notes.A: 24 is how many 4-digit numbers you can make altogether. Only those starting with 5 or 7 are more than 5000.
notes.B: Check each place in turn. The first place has 2 choices, then the other places have 3, 2 and 1 choices.
notes.C: Yes! 2 choices for the first digit and 6 ways to arrange the rest gives 12.
notes.D: This would mean 3 digits can go first. A number starting with 1 or 3 is less than 5000, so only 5 and 7 can go first.

hints: This is a pictograph question. Each picture stands for more than one thing, so look at the key first.
Count how many apple pictures Monday shows. Each one stands for 5 apples.
A similar example: one star picture stands for 4 books and Tuesday shows 6 stars. 6 × 4 = 24 books.

steps.text: The key says each picture stands for 5 apples.
Monday shows 3 pictures, so multiply.
15 apples were sold.

notes.A: This is 3 + 5. Each of the 3 pictures stands for 5 apples, so multiply instead of adding.
notes.B: Yes! 3 pictures of 5 apples each make 3 × 5 = 15 apples.
notes.C: 5 is what one picture stands for. Monday shows 3 pictures.
notes.D: 3 is the number of pictures. Each picture stands for 5 apples, so multiply by 5.

hints: This question is about reading a bar graph. Think about what the height of a bar tells you.
Imagine a bar graph of marks. A child with more marks gets a taller bar. So what does the tallest bar show?
A similar example: in a bar graph of rainfall, the shortest bar belongs to the month with the least rain. The height of a bar always matches the size of its value.

steps.text: In a bar graph, the height of each bar shows how big its value is.
A bigger value gets a taller bar.
So the tallest bar represents the largest value.

notes.A: The average is found by adding all the values and sharing equally. It is not shown by the tallest bar. Think about what a taller bar means.
notes.B: A value of zero would have no bar at all. A tall bar means a big value.
notes.C: Yes! The taller the bar, the larger the value.
notes.D: The smallest value has the shortest bar. Think about what the tallest one means.

hints: This asks for the mean, which is another word for average. It is the fair share if the total were split equally.
First add all five numbers together. Then think about how many numbers there are.
A similar example: the mean of 4, 6, 8, 10 and 12. Add them: 4 + 6 + 8 + 10 + 12 = 40. There are 5 numbers, so 40 ÷ 5 = 8. The mean is 8.

steps.text: Add all the numbers.
There are 5 numbers, so divide the total by 5.
The mean is 18.

notes.A: Yes! The total is 90 and 90 ÷ 5 = 18.
notes.B: 15 is one of the numbers, but not the fair share. Add all five numbers and divide by 5.
notes.C: Check your total. The five numbers add up to 90, and then you divide by 5.
notes.D: 90 is the total of the numbers. To get the mean, divide the total by how many numbers there are.

hints: This asks for the mode. The mode is the number that appears most often in a list.
Go through the list and count how many times each number appears. A tally can help.
A similar example: in 4, 8, 6, 8, 1, 8, 6 the number 8 appears three times and 6 appears twice. Nothing appears more often than 8, so the mode is 8.

steps.text: Count how many times each number appears in 3, 5, 7, 5, 9, 5, 2.
5 appears 3 times. Every other number appears only once.
The mode is 5.

notes.A: Yes! 5 appears three times, more than any other number.
notes.B: 9 is the biggest number, but the mode is the one that appears most often. Count each number.
notes.C: 7 appears only once. Look for the number that shows up the most times.
notes.D: 3 is the first number in the list, but it appears only once. Look for the number that shows up the most.

hints: This asks for the range. The range tells you how far apart the biggest and smallest numbers are.
Find the biggest number and the smallest number in the list. You will need both.
A similar example: the range of 6, 19, 11, 3 and 15. The biggest is 19 and the smallest is 3. 19 − 3 = 16, so the range is 16.

steps.text: The biggest number is 22 and the smallest is 5.
Subtract the smallest from the biggest.
The range is 17.

notes.A: This is 22 + 5. For the range, subtract the smallest from the biggest instead of adding.
notes.B: 14 is the first number in the list. The range is the biggest number minus the smallest.
notes.C: 5 is the smallest number. The range is how far it is from the biggest number.
notes.D: Yes! 22 − 5 = 17, so the range is 17.

hints: This is a pictograph question with a half picture. A half picture stands for half of what a full one stands for.
Count the full pictures first and work out what they stand for. Then find what half a picture is worth.
A similar example: one picture stands for 8 toys, and a row shows 3 full pictures and a half. 3 × 8 = 24, and half of 8 is 4. 24 + 4 = 28 toys.

steps.text: Each full picture stands for 10 students. There are 2 full pictures.
The half picture stands for half of 10.
Add the two parts.
The row represents 25 students.

notes.A: Yes! Two full pictures make 20 and the half makes 5 more, so 25.
notes.B: This counts one full picture and a half. There are two full pictures before the half.
notes.C: This counts only the two full pictures. The half picture stands for 5 more students.
notes.D: This counts the half picture as a full one. Half a picture stands for 5 students, not 10.

hints: This asks for the difference between two bars. Difference means how much more one is than the other.
To find a difference, take the smaller value away from the bigger one.
A similar example: one bar shows 62 and another shows 40. 62 − 40 = 22, so the difference is 22.

steps.text: Difference means subtract the smaller value from the bigger one.
Bar A is 45 and Bar B is 30.
The difference is 15.

notes.A: Check your subtraction. 45 − 30 leaves 1 ten and 5 ones.
notes.B: This is 45 + 30. Difference means subtract, not add.
notes.C: This is 45 ÷ 30. Difference means subtract the smaller from the bigger.

hints: This is about chance. Think about all the things that can happen when you toss a coin.
A coin has two sides, heads and tails. Is one side more likely to land face up than the other?
A similar example: a bag has 5 red balls and 5 blue balls. Each colour has the same number of balls, so picking red has the same chance as picking blue.

steps.text: A coin has two sides: heads and tails.
Both sides have the same chance of landing face up.
So getting a head is equally likely as tails.

notes.A: Certain means it must happen every time. A coin can also land on tails. Compare the chances of the two sides.
notes.B: Yes! Heads and tails each have the same chance.
notes.C: Impossible means it can never happen. A coin does land on heads sometimes. Compare the chances of the two sides.
notes.D: Likely means it happens more often than not. Heads does not come up more often than tails. The two sides have the same chance.

hints: This asks for a total from a table. Total means add all the values together.
Add the numbers a few at a time. Look for pairs that make easy tens, like 12 and 18.
A similar example: Mon = 11, Tue = 14, Wed = 9, Thu = 16. Pair them up: 11 + 9 = 20 and 14 + 16 = 30. Then 20 + 30 = 50 in total.

steps.text: Pair numbers that make tens.
Add the other easy pair.
Now add everything.
The total is 75.

notes.A: This is 10 too few. Check that all five days are added in.
notes.C: This is 5 too many. Add again slowly, pairing 12 with 18 and 10 with 20.
notes.D: This is 5 too few. Check the ones digits when you add the 15.

hints: This is an average problem worked backwards. If you know the average and how many numbers there are, you can find their total.
First find the total of all five numbers. Multiply the average by how many numbers there are.
A similar example: the average of 4 numbers is 10, and three of them are 8, 12 and 9. The total must be 4 × 10 = 40. The three known numbers add up to 29. 40 − 29 = 11, so the fourth number is 11.

steps.text: The total of all 5 numbers is the average times 5.
Add the four numbers you know.
The fifth number is what is left.
The fifth number is 20.

notes.A: Yes! The total must be 100, the four known numbers make 80, and 100 − 80 = 20.
notes.B: 25 is one of the four numbers already given. Find the total of all five, then take away the four you know.
notes.C: 80 is the sum of the four known numbers. Take it away from the total of all five.
notes.D: 100 is the total of all five numbers. Take away the four you know to find the fifth.

hints: This is about the words we use for chance. Each word tells how sure we are that something will happen.
Think of something that must happen, like the sun rising tomorrow. Which word says there is no doubt at all?
A similar example: picking a green ball from a bag that has only red balls can never happen. An event that can never happen is called impossible.

steps.text: Some events may or may not happen. Others can never happen.
An event that will definitely happen has no doubt about it.
Such an event is called certain.

notes.A: Uncertain means we are not sure. The question says the event will definitely happen.
notes.B: Impossible means it can never happen. That is the opposite of what the question asks.
notes.C: Yes! Certain means it will definitely happen.
notes.D: Unlikely means it probably will not happen. Look for the word that means it will surely happen.

hints: This is about a pie chart. A full circle has 360 degrees at its centre, and each slice takes a share of that.
The slice is one quarter of the circle. So you need one quarter of the full turn of 360 degrees.
A similar example: a slice that takes up 1/6 of the circle. 360 ÷ 6 = 60, so its angle is 60 degrees.

steps.text: A full circle is 360 degrees.
One quarter means divide by 4.
The angle is 90°.

notes.A: 45° is one eighth of the circle. One quarter is 360 ÷ 4.
notes.B: 180° is half of the circle. One quarter is smaller than that.
notes.C: 120° is one third of the circle. For one quarter, divide 360 by 4.
notes.D: Yes! One quarter of 360° is 90°.

hints: This asks for the median. The median is the middle number once the list is in order.
First write the numbers from smallest to biggest. Do not pick the middle one until they are in order.
A similar example: the median of 8, 2, 6, 12 and 4. In order they are 2, 4, 6, 8, 12. The middle one is 6, so the median is 6.

steps.text: Put the numbers in order: 3, 5, 7, 9, 11.
There are 5 numbers, so the middle one is the third.
The median is 7.

notes.A: 3 is the smallest number. The median is the middle number after putting them in order.
notes.B: 5 is the second number in order. Count to the middle of the five numbers.
notes.C: 9 is in the middle of the list as it is written. Put the numbers in order first, then find the middle.
notes.D: Yes! In order the numbers are 3, 5, 7, 9, 11 and 7 is in the middle.

hints: This is a pictograph question worked backwards. You know the total and what one symbol stands for, and you need the number of symbols.
Think of putting the 36 books into equal groups. Each group is one symbol.
A similar example: 56 pencils are shown and each symbol stands for 8 pencils. 56 ÷ 8 = 7, so 7 symbols are needed.

steps.text: Each symbol stands for 6 books. Share 36 books into groups of 6.
Check by multiplying back.
So 6 symbols are needed.

notes.A: This is 36 − 6. You need to find how many groups of 6 fit into 36, so divide.
notes.B: This is 36 × 6. The symbols group the books, so divide instead of multiplying.
notes.C: 5 symbols show only 5 × 6 = 30 books. You need enough symbols for all 36.
notes.D: Yes! 36 ÷ 6 = 6 symbols.

hints: This is about the scale of a bar graph. The scale tells you how many students each centimetre of bar stands for.
Split the height of the bar into 3 whole centimetres and half a centimetre. Work out what each part stands for.
A similar example: the scale is 1 cm = 10 students and a bar is 4.5 cm tall. 4 cm stands for 4 × 10 = 40 students, and half a centimetre stands for 5. 40 + 5 = 45 students.

steps.text: Each centimetre stands for 20 students. Start with the 3 whole centimetres.
Half a centimetre stands for half of 20.
Add the two parts.
The bar shows 70 students.

notes.A: 3.5 is the height of the bar in centimetres. Each centimetre stands for 20 students, so multiply.
notes.B: Yes! 3.5 × 20 = 70 students.
notes.C: This is 3.5 × 10. The scale says each centimetre stands for 20 students.
notes.D: This counts only the 3 whole centimetres. The extra half centimetre stands for 10 more students.

hints: This is about chance. Think about which numbers a die can show.
List the numbers on the faces of a standard die. Is 7 one of them?
A similar example: rolling a number less than 7 on a standard die. Every face shows a number from 1 to 6, so this happens on every roll. That event is certain.

steps.text: A standard die has six faces showing 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6.
There is no face with 7 on it, so a 7 can never come up.
Rolling a 7 is impossible.

notes.A: Yes! A die has no 7, so a 7 can never be rolled.
notes.B: Certain means it happens every time. Check which numbers are on a die.
notes.C: Unlikely means it can happen, but not often. Check whether a die has a 7 at all.
notes.D: Likely means it happens often. Check whether a die has a 7 at all.

hints: This asks for a frequency. Frequency means how many times a value appears in the list.
Go through the marks one at a time. Put a tick each time you see an 8.
A similar example: in the marks 7, 2, 7, 7, 3, 7, 7, 2, 7 the mark 7 appears six times. So the frequency of 7 is 6.

steps.text: Go through the list and tick each 8: 8, 9, 8, 10, 9, 8, 7, 9, 8, 10.
The 8s are the first, third, sixth and ninth marks.
The frequency of 8 is 4.

notes.A: Count again slowly. Tick each 8 as you go so none is counted twice.
notes.B: Yes! The mark 8 appears 4 times.
notes.C: 2 is how many times 10 appears. Count the 8s instead.
notes.D: 3 is how many times 9 appears. Count the 8s instead.

hints: This is an average problem worked backwards. The average and the count of numbers together tell you the total.
First find the total of all four numbers. Multiply the average by how many numbers there are.
A similar example: the average of 3 numbers is 12, and two of them are 9 and 13. The total must be 3 × 12 = 36. The two known numbers add up to 22. 36 − 22 = 14, so the third number is 14.

steps.text: The total of all 4 numbers is the average times 4.
Add the three numbers you know.
The fourth number is what is left.
The fourth number is 28.

notes.A: 25 is the average, not the missing number. Find the total of all four, then take away the three you know.
notes.B: Check your adding. 20 + 30 + 22 = 72, and that comes off the total of 100.
notes.C: Yes! The total must be 100, the three known numbers make 72, and 100 − 72 = 28.
notes.D: Check the total first. Four numbers with an average of 25 add up to 4 × 25 = 100. Then take away 72.

hints: This is about writing time as a decimal. Minutes are parts of 60, not parts of 100, so the minutes cannot just go after the decimal point.
Keep the 8 whole hours. Then work out what fraction of an hour 45 minutes is, by writing it over 60.
A similar example: 3 hrs 30 min. 30 minutes is 30/60 = 1/2 of an hour, and 1/2 = 0.5. So 3 hrs 30 min is 3.5 hrs.

steps.text: There are 60 minutes in an hour, so 45 minutes is 45 out of 60 of an hour.
Three quarters as a decimal is 0.75.
Add the 8 whole hours.
8 hrs 45 min is 8.75 hrs.
