Example: 1/5 of 35 sweets. Share 35 into 5 equal groups: 35 ÷ 5 = 7. So 1/5 of 35 is 7 sweets.

steps.text: The bottom number is 4, so share the 36 sweets into 4 equal groups.
The top number is 1, so Diya gives away one of these groups.
Diya gives away 9 sweets.

notes.A: Yes! 36 ÷ 4 = 9, and that one group is given away.
notes.B: 27 is how many sweets Diya has left. The question asks how many are given away.
notes.C: 4 is the bottom number of the fraction. It tells you how many equal groups to make, not how many sweets.
notes.D: 36 is all the sweets. Diya gives away only 1/4 of them.

hints: Finding a fraction of a group means sharing it into equal groups. The bottom number tells you how many groups to make. The top number tells you how many groups to take.
Share the 40 sweets into 4 equal groups first. Then think about how many of those groups Rohan gives away.
Example: 3/7 of 14 sweets. Share 14 into 7 equal groups: 14 ÷ 7 = 2. Take 3 of the groups: 2 × 3 = 6. So 3/7 of 14 is 6 sweets.

steps.text: The bottom number is 4, so share the 40 sweets into 4 equal groups.
The top number is 2, so Rohan gives away 2 of these groups.
Rohan gives away 20 sweets.

notes.A: 40 is all the sweets. Rohan gives away only 2/4 of them.
notes.C: Check your working. Divide 40 by 4 first, then multiply the result by 2.
notes.D: This is 2 × 4, the two numbers of the fraction multiplied. Divide 40 by 4 first, then multiply by 2.

hints: Finding a fraction of a group means sharing it into equal groups. The bottom number tells you how many groups to make. The top number tells you how many groups to take.
Share the 96 sweets into 8 equal groups first. Then think about how many of those groups Saanvi gives away.
Example: 3/7 of 14 sweets. Share 14 into 7 equal groups: 14 ÷ 7 = 2. Take 3 of the groups: 2 × 3 = 6. So 3/7 of 14 is 6 sweets.

steps.text: The bottom number is 8, so share the 96 sweets into 8 equal groups.
The top number is 4, so Saanvi gives away 4 of these groups.
Saanvi gives away 48 sweets.

notes.A: This is 4 × 8, the two numbers of the fraction multiplied. Divide 96 by 8 first, then multiply by 4.
notes.B: 96 is all the sweets. Saanvi gives away only 4/8 of them.
notes.C: Check your working. Divide 96 by 8 first, then multiply the result by 4.

hints: Finding a fraction of a group means sharing it into equal groups. The bottom number tells you how many groups to make. The top number tells you how many groups to take.
Share the 24 sweets into 4 equal groups first. Then think about how many of those groups Aarav gives away.
Example: 5/8 of 56 sweets. Share 56 into 8 equal groups: 56 ÷ 8 = 7. Take 5 of the groups: 7 × 5 = 35. So 5/8 of 56 is 35 sweets.

steps.text: The bottom number is 4, so share the 24 sweets into 4 equal groups.
The top number is 3, so Aarav gives away 3 of these groups.
Aarav gives away 18 sweets.

notes.B: 24 is all the sweets. Aarav gives away only 3/4 of them.
notes.C: 6 sweets is one of the 4 equal groups, and it is also what Aarav keeps. Aarav gives away 3 groups.
notes.D: This is 3 × 4, the two numbers of the fraction multiplied. Divide 24 by 4 first, then multiply by 3.

hints: Finding a fraction of a group means sharing it into equal groups. The bottom number tells you how many groups to make. The top number tells you how many groups to take.
Share the 18 sweets into 6 equal groups first. Then think about how many of those groups Arjun gives away.
Example: 5/8 of 56 sweets. Share 56 into 8 equal groups: 56 ÷ 8 = 7. Take 5 of the groups: 7 × 5 = 35. So 5/8 of 56 is 35 sweets.

steps.text: The bottom number is 6, so share the 18 sweets into 6 equal groups.
The top number is 3, so Arjun gives away 3 of these groups.
Arjun gives away 9 sweets.

notes.B: 18 is all the sweets. Arjun gives away only 3/6 of them.
notes.C: Check your working. Divide 18 by 6 first, then multiply the result by 3.
notes.D: 6 is the bottom number of the fraction. It tells you how many equal groups to make, not how many sweets.

hints: To add fractions, the bottom numbers must be the same. After adding, simplify the answer so that its top is 1.
Change 1/9 into eighteenths. What must you multiply 9 by to get 18? Do the same to the top.
Example: 1/4 + 1/12. First 1/4 = 3/12. Then 3/12 + 1/12 = 4/12. Divide the top and bottom by 4 to get 1/3. The box would be 3.

steps.text: Make the bottom numbers the same. Change 1/9 into eighteenths.
Add the tops.
Simplify by dividing the top and bottom by 3.
The box is 6.

notes.B: 18 is the common bottom number, but the sum is 3/18. Simplify it so that the top is 1.
notes.C: This adds the bottom numbers, 9 + 18. Bottom numbers are not added. Change 1/9 to 2/18 first.
notes.D: 1/9 on its own already has 9 below. Adding 1/18 makes the sum bigger than 1/9, so the box must be smaller than 9.

hints: To reduce a fraction, divide the top and the bottom by the same number. Keep going until no number divides both.
Find a number that divides both 117 and 156. Try 3 first: do the digits of each number add to a multiple of 3?
Example: 65/91. Both are in the 13 times table: 65 = 13 × 5 and 91 = 13 × 7. Dividing the top and bottom by 13 gives 5/7.

steps.text: Both numbers are divisible by 3: 117 ÷ 3 = 39 and 156 ÷ 3 = 52.
39 = 13 × 3 and 52 = 13 × 4. Divide the top and bottom by 13.
In lowest terms the fraction is 3/4.

notes.A: The bottom is right, but check the top: 117 ÷ 39 = 3.
notes.B: Yes! Dividing by 3 and then by 13 turns 117/156 into 3/4.
notes.C: 117 ÷ 13 = 9, but 156 ÷ 13 = 12. So the fraction is 9/12, and it can still be made simpler.
notes.D: Check by multiplying back. 13 × 12 = 156, but 6 × 12 = 72, not 117.

hints: The three fractions have the same bottom number, so add the tops. Then change the answer into an equal fraction with 21 below.
Add 2/7 three times. Then ask: 7 times what makes 21? Multiply the top by the same number.
Example: 1/5 + 1/5 + 1/5 = ★/15. The sum is 3/5. Since 5 × 3 = 15, multiply the top by 3 as well: 3 × 3 = 9. The star would be 9.

steps.text: Add the tops. The sum is 6/7.
7 × 3 = 21, so multiply the top by 3 as well.
So 6/7 is the same as 18/21.
The star is 18.

notes.A: 6/7 is the sum, but the new bottom is 21. Change 6/7 into twenty-firsts.
notes.B: This is what two lots of 2/7 give. Add all three, then change the answer into twenty-firsts.
notes.C: Yes! The sum is 6/7, and 6/7 = 18/21.
notes.D: Check: 15/21 = 5/7, but the sum of the three fractions is 6/7.

hints: All the fractions have the same bottom number, so you only need to work with the tops. Change the mixed number first.
Turn 1 11/19 into an improper fraction. One whole is 19/19, so add 19 to 11 to get the new top.
Example: 5/7 + 1 3/7 − 6/7. The mixed number 1 3/7 is the same as 10/7. Tops: 5 + 10 − 6 = 9. The answer is 9/7, which is 1 2/7.

steps.text: Change the mixed number. 1 11/19 is the same as 30/19.
Now work with the tops.
The result is 26/19. Take out one whole, which is 19/19.
The answer is 1 7/19.

notes.A: Yes! The tops give 12 + 30 − 16 = 26, and 26/19 is 1 whole and 7/19.
notes.B: Check the tops: 12 + 30 − 16 = 26. Then 26 − 19 = 7 for the fraction part.
notes.C: Go through the tops slowly: 12 + 30 = 42, then 42 − 16 = 26. Take out 19 for one whole.
notes.D: One of the choices does match. Change 1 11/19 to 30/19 and work with the tops.

hints: All four fractions have the same top number. When the tops are equal, compare the bottoms.
Think of sharing the same cake among more people. Does each person get a bigger piece or a smaller piece?
Example: 1/2, 1/5 and 1/10. The tops are the same. Cutting into 10 parts makes the smallest pieces, so 1/10 is the smallest.

steps.text: W, X, Y and Z are equal, so all four fractions have the same top number.
When the tops are equal, the bigger the bottom number, the smaller the fraction.
The bottom numbers are 23, 29, 17 and 13. The biggest is 29.
The smallest fraction is Y/29.

notes.A: 23 is not the biggest bottom number. More parts means smaller parts, so look for the largest bottom number.
notes.B: Yes! 29 is the biggest bottom number, so those parts are the smallest.
notes.C: 17 is not the biggest bottom number. More parts means smaller parts, so look for the largest bottom number.
notes.D: 13 is the smallest bottom number, so this is the greatest fraction. The question asks for the smallest.

hints: What should be added means: find the gap between the two fractions. That is a subtraction.
Subtract 3/8 from 8/3. First give both fractions the same bottom number. Which number do both 8 and 3 divide into?
Example: what should be added to 1/2 to get 5/3? Use sixths: 5/3 = 10/6 and 1/2 = 3/6. Then 10/6 − 3/6 = 7/6.

steps.text: Subtract 3/8 from 8/3. Both 3 and 8 divide into 24, so use twenty-fourths.
Change 8/3.
Change 3/8.
Subtract the tops.
The fraction to add is 55/24.

notes.B: Check the subtraction on top. It is 64 − 9.
notes.C: Use 24 as the common bottom number, because 3 × 8 = 24. Then subtract the tops.
notes.D: Check 3/8 in twenty-fourths. 3 × 3 = 9, so it is 9/24. Then work out 64 − 9.

hints: The three fractions on the left are equal and all have 14 below. Make the fraction on the right have 14 below too.
126 ÷ 14 = 9. So divide the top and bottom of 162/126 by 9 to turn it into fourteenths.
Example: three equal fractions, each K/10, add up to 36/40. Divide the top and bottom of 36/40 by 4 to get 9/10. Three equal tops add to 9, so K = 9 ÷ 3 = 3.

steps.text: Divide the top and bottom of 162/126 by 9 to get fourteenths.
So the three equal tops must add up to 18.
Share 18 equally among the three fractions.
M is 6.

notes.A: With 8 the sum is 24/14. But 162/126 is 18/14. Three equal tops must add to 18.
notes.B: With 9 the sum is 27/14. But 162/126 is 18/14. Three equal tops must add to 18.
notes.C: With 4 the sum is 12/14. But 162/126 is 18/14. Three equal tops must add to 18.

hints: A quick way to compare is to use one half as a marker. Is each fraction more than half or less than half?
For each fraction, double the top and compare it with the bottom. If double the top is smaller than the bottom, the fraction is less than half.
Example: 3/4, 4/9 and 5/8. Double the tops: 6 is more than 4, 8 is less than 9, and 10 is more than 8. Only 4/9 is less than half, so it is the smallest.

steps.text: Compare each fraction with one half by doubling its top.
For 2/3, 4 is more than 3. For 11/15, 22 is more than 15. For 5/7, 10 is more than 7. These three are more than half.
For 13/29, 13 × 2 = 26, which is less than 29. So 13/29 is less than half.
The smallest fraction is 13/29.

notes.A: 2/3 is more than half, because 2 × 2 = 4 is more than 3. One fraction here is less than half.
notes.B: Yes! 13 × 2 = 26 is less than 29, so 13/29 is the only fraction below half.
notes.C: 11/15 is more than half, because 11 × 2 = 22 is more than 15. One fraction here is less than half.
notes.D: 5/7 is more than half, because 5 × 2 = 10 is more than 7. One fraction here is less than half.

hints: All four fractions have the same top number. When the tops are equal, compare the bottoms.
Think of cutting the same cake into fewer pieces. Is each piece bigger or smaller?
Example: 3/4, 3/5 and 3/8. The tops are the same. Quarters are the biggest pieces, so 3/4 is the greatest.

steps.text: M, N, Q and P are equal, so all four fractions have the same top number.
When the tops are equal, the smaller the bottom number, the greater the fraction.
The bottom numbers are 12, 10, 7 and 8. The smallest is 7.
The greatest fraction is Q/7.

notes.A: 12 is the biggest bottom number, so this is the smallest fraction. The question asks for the greatest.
notes.B: 10 is not the smallest bottom number. Fewer parts means bigger parts, so look for the smallest bottom number.
notes.C: Yes! 7 is the smallest bottom number, so those parts are the biggest.
notes.D: 8 is not the smallest bottom number. Fewer parts means bigger parts, so look for the smallest bottom number.

hints: A fraction needs two counts: how many 2-digit square numbers there are, and how many 2-digit numbers there are in all. Then simplify.
Count all the 2-digit numbers, from 10 to 99. Then list the squares: 4 × 4, 5 × 5 and so on, while the answer still has two digits.
Example: what fraction of the numbers 1 to 30 are square numbers? The squares are 1, 4, 9, 16 and 25. That is 5 out of 30, and 5/30 = 1/6.

steps.text: The 2-digit numbers run from 10 to 99, so there are 90 of them.
The 2-digit squares are 16, 25, 36, 49, 64 and 81. That is 6 numbers.
The fraction is 6 out of 90. Divide the top and bottom by 6.
The fraction is 1/15.

notes.A: 1/5 of 90 would be 18 square numbers. There are only 6. List them from 4 × 4 up to 9 × 9.
notes.B: Yes! There are 6 two-digit squares out of 90 two-digit numbers, and 6/90 = 1/15.
notes.C: 3/10 of 90 would be 27 square numbers. There are only 6. List them from 4 × 4 up to 9 × 9.
notes.D: 2/9 of 90 would be 20 square numbers. There are only 6. List them from 4 × 4 up to 9 × 9.

hints: A quick way to compare is to use one half as a marker. Is each fraction more than half or less than half?
For each fraction, double the top and compare it with the bottom. If double the top is bigger than the bottom, the fraction is more than half.
Example: 2/9, 5/6 and 3/8. Double the tops: 4 is less than 9, 10 is more than 6, and 6 is less than 8. Only 5/6 is more than half, so it is the greatest.

steps.text: Compare each fraction with one half by doubling its top.
For 14/29, 28 is less than 29. For 9/19, 18 is less than 19. For 7/22, 14 is less than 22. These three are less than half.
For 17/21, 17 × 2 = 34, which is more than 21. So 17/21 is more than half.
The greatest fraction is 17/21.

notes.A: Yes! 17 × 2 = 34 is more than 21, so 17/21 is the only fraction above half.
notes.B: 14/29 is just under half, because 14 × 2 = 28 is less than 29. One fraction here is more than half.
notes.C: 9/19 is just under half, because 9 × 2 = 18 is less than 19. One fraction here is more than half.
notes.D: 7/22 is well under half, because 7 × 2 = 14 is less than 22. One fraction here is more than half.

hints: To find what fraction one amount is of another, both must be in the same unit. Change the day into minutes.
1 day = 24 hours and 1 hour = 60 minutes. Work out how many minutes there are in a day. Then put 72 over that number.
Example: what fraction of an hour is 12 minutes? 1 hour = 60 minutes. 12 out of 60 is 12/60 = 1/5, which is 0.2 as a decimal.

steps.text: Find the number of minutes in a day.
72 minutes out of 1440 minutes is 72/1440. Divide the top and bottom by 72.
0.05 is not 0.5, 0.75 or 0.6. So the answer is None of these.

notes.A: 0.5 is half a day, which is 12 hours. 72 minutes is only a little more than 1 hour.
notes.B: 0.75 of a day is 18 hours. 72 minutes is only a little more than 1 hour.
notes.C: 0.6 is 72 out of 120. But a day has 1440 minutes, so use 72 out of 1440.
notes.D: Right! 72 minutes is 1/20 of a day, which is 0.05. That is not in the list.

hints: Fractions with the same bottom number are added by adding their tops. The bottom stays the same.
Add the three top numbers. That total, over the bottom number, must be equal to 2.
Example: two fractions with the same bottom number have tops 4 and 6, and their sum is 2. The tops add to 10. Since 10 ÷ 2 = 5, the bottom number is 5. Check: 10/5 = 2.

steps.text: The bottoms are the same, so add the tops.
The sum is 24 over the bottom number, and it must equal 2.
Find the number that 24 is divided by to give 2.
The denominator is 12.

notes.A: With 4 the sum is 24/4 = 6, not 2. Find the number that goes into 24 exactly 2 times.
notes.B: With 16 the sum is 24/16, which is less than 2. Find the number that goes into 24 exactly 2 times.
notes.C: With 8 the sum is 24/8 = 3, not 2. Find the number that goes into 24 exactly 2 times.
notes.D: Yes! The tops add to 24, and 24/12 = 2.

hints: Multiplying a fraction by a whole number is the same as finding that fraction of the number.
Find one fifth of 10 first by dividing 10 by 5. Then take 3 of those parts.

steps.text: One fifth of 10 is 2.
Three fifths is 3 of these parts.
The answer is 6.

notes.A: 30/5 has the right value, but it is not finished. Do the division 30 ÷ 5 and give the answer as a whole number.
notes.C: 30 is 3 × 10. Remember to divide by the bottom number, 5, as well.
notes.D: This adds 3 and 10. Multiply instead: 3 × 10 = 30, then divide by 5.

hints: The word of here means multiply. To find a fraction of a number, share the number into equal parts and take some of them.
Divide 45 by 3 to find one third. Then think about how many thirds you need.

steps.text: One third of 45 is 15.
Two thirds is 2 of these parts.

notes.B: 15 is one third of 45. You need two thirds, so double it.
notes.C: 22.5 is half of 45. For thirds, divide by 3, not by 2.
notes.D: 90 is 2 × 45. Remember to divide by the bottom number, 3, as well.

hints: Equivalent fractions have the same value. You get one by multiplying the top and the bottom by the same number.
Multiply the top and bottom of 3/4 by 2, then by 3. See which choice appears.
Example: 2/5. Multiply the top and bottom by 3: 2 × 3 = 6 and 5 × 3 = 15. So 6/15 is equivalent to 2/5.

steps.text: To make an equivalent fraction, multiply the top and the bottom by the same number.
Multiply both by 2: 3 × 2 = 6 and 4 × 2 = 8.
The equivalent fraction is 6/8.

notes.A: Yes! 3 × 2 = 6 and 4 × 2 = 8, so 6/8 has the same value as 3/4.
notes.B: Here the top was multiplied by 2 but the bottom by 3. Use the same number for both. 6/12 is one half.
notes.C: Here the top was multiplied by 3 but the bottom by 4. Use the same number for both.
notes.D: This is 3/4 turned upside down. It is more than 1, so it cannot be equal to 3/4.

hints: To simplify a fraction, divide the top and the bottom by the same number. Keep going until no number divides both.
Find the biggest number that divides both 18 and 24. Then divide the top and the bottom by it.
Example: 12/20. The biggest number that divides both is 4. 12 ÷ 4 = 3 and 20 ÷ 4 = 5, so 12/20 = 3/5.

steps.text: The biggest number that divides both 18 and 24 is 6.
Divide the top and bottom by 6: 18 ÷ 6 = 3 and 24 ÷ 6 = 4.
In simplest form the fraction is 3/4.

notes.A: Yes! 18 ÷ 6 = 3 and 24 ÷ 6 = 4, and nothing more divides both 3 and 4.
notes.B: 9/12 is equal to 18/24, but it is not finished. 3 still divides both 9 and 12.
notes.C: 6/8 is equal to 18/24, but it is not finished. 2 still divides both 6 and 8.
notes.D: Check: 2/3 = 16/24, not 18/24. Divide 18 and 24 by 6.

hints: The whole pizza is 5/5. It is split into three parts: what Riya ate, what the others ate and what was left.
Add Riya's share and the leftover share. Then see how many fifths are still missing from 5/5.
Example: Arjun ate 3/8 of a cake and 2/8 was left over. 3/8 + 2/8 = 5/8. The others ate the rest: 8/8 − 5/8 = 3/8.

steps.text: The whole pizza is 5/5.
Add Riya's share and the leftover.
Take this away from the whole pizza.
The others ate 2/5 of the pizza.

notes.A: 3/5 is Riya's share and the leftover added together. Take that away from the whole pizza.
notes.B: Yes! 2/5 + 1/5 = 3/5 is used up, and 5/5 − 3/5 = 2/5 is what the others ate.
notes.C: 1/5 is what was left over. Take both Riya's share and the leftover away from 5/5.
notes.D: 4/5 is everything except the leftover. Riya's 2/5 must come out of that too.

hints: To multiply two fractions, multiply the tops together and the bottoms together. Then simplify.
Multiply 2 by 3 for the new top and 3 by 5 for the new bottom. Then look for a number that divides both.
Example: 3/4 × 2/3. Tops: 3 × 2 = 6. Bottoms: 4 × 3 = 12. Then 6/12 simplifies to 1/2.

steps.text: Multiply the tops and multiply the bottoms: 2 × 3 = 6 and 3 × 5 = 15.
Simplify by dividing the top and bottom by 3.
The answer is 2/5.

notes.A: 6/15 has the right value, but it is not in simplest form. Divide the top and bottom by 3.
notes.B: Yes! The product is 6/15, and 6/15 = 2/5.
notes.C: This adds the tops and adds the bottoms. To multiply fractions, multiply the tops and multiply the bottoms.
notes.D: Check the top: 2 × 3 = 6, and 6 ÷ 3 = 2. So the simplified top is 2.

hints: To add mixed numbers, add the whole numbers and the fractions separately. Then see if the fractions make another whole.
Add the wholes: 2 and 1. Then add the fraction parts, which both have 3 below.
Example: 3 1/4 + 2 3/4. Wholes: 3 + 2 = 5. Fractions: 1/4 + 3/4 = 4/4 = 1. Total: 5 + 1 = 6.

steps.text: Add the whole numbers.
Add the fractions. 3/3 is one whole.
Add the two results.
The answer is 4.

notes.A: The value is right, but 3/3 is one whole. Add it to the 3 and write the answer as a whole number.
notes.B: Yes! The wholes make 3, the fractions make 1 more, and 3 + 1 = 4.
notes.C: Add both fraction parts: 1/3 + 2/3 = 3/3. That makes one more whole.
notes.D: The 1/3 from the first number is missing. 1/3 + 2/3 = 3/3, which makes one more whole.

hints: The reciprocal of a fraction is the fraction turned upside down.
Look at the top and bottom of 5/7. Swap their places.
Example: the reciprocal of 3/8 is 8/3. Check: 3/8 × 8/3 = 24/24 = 1.

steps.text: To find a reciprocal, swap the top and the bottom.
A fraction times its reciprocal is always 1.
The reciprocal of 5/7 is 7/5.

notes.A: Yes! Swapping the top and bottom of 5/7 gives 7/5.
notes.B: This is the same fraction again. For the reciprocal, swap the top and the bottom.
notes.C: A minus sign gives the opposite number, not the reciprocal. Swap the top and the bottom instead.
notes.D: 1 is what you get when you multiply a fraction by its reciprocal. The reciprocal itself is the flipped fraction.

hints: Use one half as a marker. You are looking for a fraction that is less than half.
For each fraction, double the top and compare it with the bottom. If double the top is smaller than the bottom, the fraction is less than half.
Example: is 2/9 between 0 and 1/2? Double the top: 2 × 2 = 4, and 4 is less than 9. So 2/9 is less than half.

steps.text: A fraction is less than half when double its top is smaller than its bottom.
For 3/4, 5/6 and 7/8 the doubled tops are 6, 10 and 14. Each is bigger than the bottom, so these are more than half.
For 1/4, 1 × 2 = 2, which is smaller than 4.
The fraction between 0 and 1/2 is 1/4.

notes.A: 3/4 is more than half, because 3 × 2 = 6 is more than 4. Look for a fraction below half.
notes.B: Yes! 1 × 2 = 2 is less than 4, so 1/4 is less than half.
notes.C: 5/6 is more than half, because 5 × 2 = 10 is more than 6. Look for a fraction below half.
notes.D: 7/8 is more than half, because 7 × 2 = 14 is more than 8. Look for a fraction below half.

hints: A unit fraction is one single part of a whole. Think about what its top number must be.
Look at the top number of each fraction. Which fraction means just one part?
Example: 1/9 is a unit fraction because its top number is 1. 4/9 is not, because its top number is 4.

steps.text: A unit fraction has 1 as its top number. It is one equal part of a whole.
The top numbers here are 2, 1, 3 and 5.
The unit fraction is 1/7.

notes.A: The top number is 2, so this is two parts. A unit fraction is just one part.
notes.B: Yes! 1/7 has 1 on top. It is one of 7 equal parts.
notes.C: Here the 1 is on the bottom. 3/1 means 3 wholes. Look for 1 on the top.
notes.D: 5/5 equals 1 whole, but its top number is 5. A unit fraction has 1 on top.

hints: Some of the tank is used, so this is a subtraction. The two fractions have different bottom numbers.
Take 1/3 away from 3/4. First change both into twelfths, because 4 and 3 both divide into 12.
Example: a jar is 5/6 full and 1/2 of the jar is poured out. In sixths, 1/2 = 3/6. Then 5/6 − 3/6 = 2/6, which is 1/3 of the jar.

steps.text: Subtract 1/3 from 3/4. Use twelfths, because 4 and 3 both divide into 12.
Change 3/4.
Change 1/3.
Subtract the tops.
5/12 of the tank is left.

notes.B: This subtracts the tops and the bottoms separately. Make the bottom numbers the same first, using twelfths.
notes.C: 1/4 is the part that was empty at the start. Take 1/3 away from 3/4 instead.
notes.D: 7/12 is the part of the tank that is now empty. The question asks how much is left.

hints: To compare two fractions with different bottom numbers, change them so the bottoms are the same.
8 and 5 both divide into 40. Change 5/8 and 3/5 into fortieths, then compare the tops.
Example: 2/3 or 3/4? Use twelfths: 2/3 = 8/12 and 3/4 = 9/12. 9 is more than 8, so 3/4 is greater.

steps.text: Use 40 as the common bottom number, because 8 × 5 = 40.
Change 5/8.
Change 3/5.
25/40 is more than 24/40. The greater fraction is 5/8.

notes.A: Yes! 5/8 = 25/40 and 3/5 = 24/40, and 25 is more than 24.
notes.B: In fortieths, 3/5 is 24/40 and 5/8 is 25/40. Compare the tops.
notes.C: They are very close, but not equal. In fortieths they are 25/40 and 24/40.
notes.D: Any two fractions can be compared. Give them the same bottom number, 40, and compare the tops.

hints: A whole number can be written as a fraction. Think about how many thirds make one whole.
One whole is 3/3. Work out how many thirds there are in 4 wholes.
Example: 5 written with denominator 2. One whole is 2/2, so 5 wholes are 5 × 2 = 10 halves. So 5 = 10/2.

steps.text: One whole is 3 thirds.
So 4 wholes are 12 thirds.
Check by dividing. So 4 is 12/3.

notes.A: 4/3 is only 1 whole and 1/3. Each whole needs 3 thirds, so multiply 4 by 3 for the top.
notes.B: Yes! 4 wholes are 4 × 3 = 12 thirds.
notes.C: 3/4 is less than 1, and its bottom number is 4, not 3.
notes.D: This adds 4 and 3. Multiply instead, because each whole is 3 thirds.

hints: To find what fraction one amount is of another, put the part over the whole. Both must be in the same unit.
How many hours are there in a day? Put 8 over that number, then simplify.
Example: what fraction of a day is 4 hours? A day has 24 hours, so it is 4/24. Divide the top and bottom by 4 to get 1/6.

steps.text: A day has 24 hours.
8 hours out of 24 hours is 8/24.
Divide the top and bottom by 8.
8 hours is 1/3 of a day.

notes.A: Yes! 8 out of 24 is 8/24, and 8/24 = 1/3.
notes.B: 1/4 of a day is 6 hours, because 24 ÷ 4 = 6. Start with 8/24 and simplify.
notes.C: 2/3 of a day is 16 hours. 8 hours is the smaller part.
notes.D: This uses 12 hours. A full day has 24 hours, so start with 8/24.

hints: To find a fraction of a length, share the length into equal parts and take some of them.
Divide 20 m by 4 to find one quarter. Then think about how many quarters are used.
Example: a ribbon is 30 m long and 3/5 of it is used. 30 ÷ 5 = 6, and 6 × 3 = 18. So 18 m is used.

steps.text: One quarter of 20 m is 5 m.
Three quarters is 3 of these parts.
15 m of the rope is used.

notes.B: 5 m is one quarter. It is also the part that is not used. Three quarters are used.
notes.C: This is 3 × 4, the two numbers of the fraction multiplied. Divide 20 by 4, then multiply by 3.
notes.D: 16 m is 4/5 of the rope. For quarters, divide 20 by 4.

hints: The two fractions have different bottom numbers. Make the bottoms the same before you add.
15 is a multiple of 3. Change 2/3 into fifteenths by multiplying its top and bottom by 5.
Example: 3/8 + 1/4. Change 1/4 into eighths: 1/4 = 2/8. Then 3/8 + 2/8 = 5/8.

steps.text: 3 × 5 = 15, so change 2/3 into fifteenths.
Add the tops and keep the bottom.
The answer is 23/15.

notes.A: The top is right, but the bottom was doubled. When the bottoms are the same, the bottom stays as 15.
notes.B: This multiplies the tops, 13 × 2. To add, make the bottoms the same first, then add the tops.
notes.C: This is 13/15 − 10/15, a subtraction. The question asks you to add.

hints: The two fractions have different bottom numbers. Make the bottoms the same before you subtract.
15 is a multiple of 5. Change 2/5 into fifteenths by multiplying its top and bottom by 3.
Example: 7/8 − 1/4. Change 1/4 into eighths: 1/4 = 2/8. Then 7/8 − 2/8 = 5/8.

steps.text: 5 × 3 = 15, so change 2/5 into fifteenths.
Subtract the tops and keep the bottom.
The answer is 7/15.

notes.A: 4/3 is more than 1. Taking something away from 13/15 must leave less than 13/15. Change 2/5 to 6/15 and subtract.
notes.B: This multiplies the tops, 13 × 2. To subtract, make the bottoms the same first, then subtract the tops.
notes.C: This adds 13 and 6 on top and doubles the bottom. Subtract the tops and keep the bottom as 15.

hints: The two fractions already have the same bottom number. So only the tops need adding.
Add 3 and 7 for the new top. Keep 10 as the bottom. Then see if the answer can be made simpler.
Example: 2/9 + 4/9. Tops: 2 + 4 = 6. The sum is 6/9, which simplifies to 2/3.

steps.text: Add the tops and keep the bottom.
10 tenths make one whole.
The answer is 1.

notes.A: Yes! 3/10 + 7/10 = 10/10, and ten tenths make 1 whole.
notes.B: This adds the bottoms as well as the tops, giving 10/20. Keep the bottom as 10.
notes.C: This is 7/10 − 3/10, a subtraction. The question asks you to add.
notes.D: This multiplies the tops, 3 × 7. To add, just add the tops: 3 + 7.

hints: The two fractions already have the same bottom number. So only the tops need subtracting.
Take 3 away from 9 for the new top. Keep 10 as the bottom. Then see if the answer can be made simpler.
Example: 7/8 − 3/8. Tops: 7 − 3 = 4. The result is 4/8, which simplifies to 1/2.

steps.text: Subtract the tops and keep the bottom.
Simplify by dividing the top and bottom by 2.
The answer is 3/5.

notes.A: 8/5 is more than 1. Taking 3/10 away from 9/10 must leave less than 9/10. Subtract the tops: 9 − 3.
notes.B: 17/10 is more than 1. Taking 3/10 away from 9/10 must leave less than 9/10. Subtract the tops: 9 − 3.
notes.C: This multiplies the tops, 9 × 3. To subtract, just subtract the tops: 9 − 3.

hints: The two fractions have different bottom numbers. Make the bottoms the same before you subtract.
12 is a multiple of 2. Change 1/2 into twelfths by multiplying its top and bottom by 6.
Example: 9/10 − 1/2. Change 1/2 into tenths: 1/2 = 5/10. Then 9/10 − 5/10 = 4/10, which simplifies to 2/5.

steps.text: 2 × 6 = 12, so change 1/2 into twelfths.
Subtract the tops and keep the bottom.
The answer is 5/12.

notes.A: This adds 11 and 6 on top and doubles the bottom. Subtract the tops and keep the bottom as 12.
notes.C: This multiplies the tops, 11 × 1. To subtract, make the bottoms the same first, then subtract the tops.
notes.D: 13/12 is more than 1. Taking 1/2 away from 11/12 must leave less than 11/12. Change 1/2 to 6/12 and subtract.

hints: The two fractions already have the same bottom number. So only the tops need subtracting.
Take 7 away from 11 for the new top. Keep 12 as the bottom. Then see if the answer can be made simpler.
Example: 8/9 − 2/9. Tops: 8 − 2 = 6. The result is 6/9, which simplifies to 2/3.

steps.text: Subtract the tops and keep the bottom.
Simplify by dividing the top and bottom by 4.
The answer is 1/3.

notes.A: This multiplies the tops, 11 × 7. To subtract, just subtract the tops: 11 − 7.
notes.B: This adds the tops and adds the bottoms, giving 18/24. Subtract the tops and keep the bottom as 12.
notes.C: 1/4 is 3/12. Check the tops: 11 − 7 = 4, so the result is 4/12.

hints: The two fractions have different bottom numbers. Make the bottoms the same before you add.
12 is a multiple of 3. Change 2/3 into twelfths by multiplying its top and bottom by 4.
Example: 5/6 + 1/3. Change 1/3 into sixths: 1/3 = 2/6. Then 5/6 + 2/6 = 7/6.

steps.text: 3 × 4 = 12, so change 2/3 into twelfths.
Add the tops and keep the bottom.
The answer is 19/12.

notes.B: This is 11/12 − 8/12, a subtraction. The question asks you to add.
notes.C: This multiplies the tops, 11 × 2. To add, make the bottoms the same first, then add the tops.
notes.D: The top is right, but the bottom was doubled. When the bottoms are the same, the bottom stays as 12.

hints: Each digit has its own place. In a 5-digit number the places are ten-thousands, thousands, hundreds, tens and ones.
Draw five boxes for the five places. The greatest place is the ten-thousands and the least place is the ones. Put each digit in its box.
Example: a 4-digit number has 3 in the hundreds place, 8 in the greatest place, 2 in the least place and 6 in the tens place. Thousands 8, hundreds 3, tens 6, ones 2. The number is 8362.

steps.text: The greatest place of a 5-digit number is the ten-thousands place, so 6 goes there.
9 is in the thousands place and 7 is in the hundreds place.
1 is in the tens place. 5 is in the least place, which is the ones.
The number is 69715.

notes.A: Here 9 is in the greatest place. The clues say 6 is in the greatest place and 9 is in the thousands place.
notes.B: Here 1 is in the hundreds place and 7 is in the tens place. The clues say 7 hundreds and 1 ten.
notes.C: Here 7 is in the thousands place. The clues say 9 is in the thousands place and 7 is in the hundreds place.
notes.D: Yes! 6 ten-thousands, 9 thousands, 7 hundreds, 1 ten and 5 ones make 69715.

hints: Break the number into thousands, hundreds, tens and ones. Write each part in Roman numerals, biggest part first.
1945 = 1000 + 900 + 40 + 5. Remember that 900 is written as 100 before 1000, and 40 as 10 before 50.
Example: 1494 = 1000 + 400 + 90 + 4. 1000 is M, 400 is CD, 90 is XC and 4 is IV. So 1494 is MCDXCIV.

steps.text: Split the number into its parts.
1000 is M. 900 is CM, which means 100 less than 1000.
40 is XL, which means 10 less than 50. 5 is V.
Put the parts together: MCMXLV.

notes.A: This is not a proper Roman numeral. Start with M for 1000, then write 900, 40 and 5.
notes.B: Yes! M is 1000, CM is 900, XL is 40 and V is 5.
notes.C: This is 1465, because CD is 400 and LX is 60. You need CM for 900 and XL for 40.
notes.D: This is 945. The M for 1000 is missing at the front.

hints: This is about writing a number in Roman numerals. Break the number into thousands, hundreds, tens and ones, and write each part on its own.
Split 1946 into 1000 + 900 + 40 + 6. Now think how each part is written. Remember that 900 and 40 are each written with a smaller letter before a bigger one.
Here is a similar one. To write 1492, split it into 1000 + 400 + 90 + 2. M is 1000, CD is 400, XC is 90 and II is 2. So 1492 is MCDXCII.

steps.text: Split the number into its place value parts.
1000 is M. 900 is CM, because C before M means 100 less than 1000.
40 is XL, because X before L means 10 less than 50. 6 is VI.
Join the parts in order: M, CM, XL, VI. So 1946 is MCMXLVI.

notes.A: This starts with CM, which is 900, and then M. The thousand must come first, so begin with M and then write CM for 900.
notes.B: Yes! M is 1000, CM is 900, XL is 40 and VI is 6, which makes 1946.
notes.C: MM is 2000, so this number is 2146. You need just one M, and then CM for 900.
notes.D: This writes 40 as XXXX. A letter is never repeated four times, so 40 is written XL.

hints: This is a place value problem. The same digit sits in two different places, so it has two different place values. Look at which places the two stars are in.
Count the places from the right. One star is in the tens place and the other is in the ten-thousands place. Think what the difference would be if the star were 1, and how it grows for bigger digits.
Here is a similar one. In 5★3★ let the star be 4. The stars are in the hundreds and ones places, so the place values are 400 and 4. The difference is 400 − 4 = 396.

steps.text: Find the places of the two stars in 6★74★3. From the right, one star is in the tens place and the other is in the ten-thousands place.
If the star were 1, the place values would be 10000 and 10.
So the difference is always the star digit times 9990. Look for an option that is 9990 times a single digit.
The star is 7. Its place values are 70000 and 70, and the difference is 69930.

notes.A: Check this with a star of 5. The place values are 50000 and 50, and 50000 − 50 = 49950, not 49990. Try 9990 times each digit.
notes.B: Yes! With 7 as the star, the place values are 70000 and 70, and 70000 − 70 = 69930.
notes.C: No single digit gives this. A star of 6 gives 60000 − 60 = 59940. Subtract the tens place value from the ten-thousands place value.
notes.D: One of the numbers does fit. Try a star of 7 and subtract its two place values.

hints: When two digits swap places, you get a new number. The question wants the difference between the new number and the old one.
Write 7,02,459 with the 5 and the 0 swapped. The 5 moves to the ten-thousands place and the 0 moves to the tens place. Then subtract the smaller number from the bigger one.
Here is a similar one. Swap 3 and 0 in 4,02,638. The new number is 4,32,608. The difference is 4,32,608 − 4,02,638 = 29,970.

steps.text: Swap the 5 and the 0 in 7,02,459. The new number is 7,52,409.
The new number is bigger, so subtract the old number from it.
The difference is 49950.

notes.A: This is 10000 too many. Line up the digits and subtract again, taking care when you borrow in the ten-thousands place.
notes.B: This is 10000 too few. Line up the digits and subtract again, place by place.
notes.D: This counts only the 5 moving into the ten-thousands place. The tens place also changed from 5 to 0, which takes away 50.

hints: There are two jobs here. First find the greatest number in the list. Then find the place value of the digit 6 in that number.
All five numbers have five digits, so compare the ten-thousands digits first. Two numbers start with 4, so compare their thousands digits next.
Here is a similar one. Of 23815, 38251 and 35128, the greatest is 38251. Its digit 8 is in the thousands place, so the place value of 8 is 8000.

steps.text: Compare the ten-thousands digits. 46749 and 47659 both start with 4, which is the biggest first digit.
Now compare their thousands digits. 7 is more than 6, so 47659 is the greatest number.
In 47659 the digit 6 is in the hundreds place.
The place value of 6 is 600.

notes.A: 6 is the face value, the digit by itself. Place value depends on where the digit sits in the greatest number.
notes.B: Yes! The greatest number is 47659, and its 6 is in the hundreds place, so the place value is 600.
notes.C: The 6 is in the tens place in 12764, but that is not the greatest number. Find the greatest number first.
notes.D: The 6 is in the thousands place in 46749 and 26947, but 47659 is greater than both. Look at the 6 in 47659.

hints: First list the prime numbers that have only one digit. Then build the greatest and the smallest numbers from them, using each digit once.
The one-digit primes are 2, 3, 5 and 7. For the greatest number put the digits from biggest to smallest. For the smallest number put them from smallest to biggest.
Here is a similar one with the digits 1, 4, 6 and 8. The greatest number is 8641 and the smallest is 1468. The difference is 8641 − 1468 = 7173.

steps.text: The one-digit prime numbers are 2, 3, 5 and 7.
For the greatest number, write the digits from biggest to smallest: 7532. For the smallest, write them from smallest to biggest: 2357.
Subtract the smallest from the greatest.
The difference is 5175.

notes.A: 2357 is the smallest number you can make. The question asks for the difference, so subtract it from the greatest number, 7532.
notes.B: Yes! The greatest number is 7532 and the smallest is 2357, and 7532 − 2357 = 5175.
notes.C: Check your digits and your subtraction. 1 and 9 are not prime, so the digits are 2, 3, 5 and 7. Then work out 7532 − 2357 again.
notes.D: This is close. Subtract 2357 from 7532 again, one place at a time, and watch the borrowing.

hints: The two years are written in Roman numerals. Change each one into an ordinary number, and then find how many years lie between them.
Read MCDXLIX in parts: M, CD, XL, IX. Read MDCLXV in parts too. When a smaller letter stands before a bigger one, you subtract it.
Here is a similar one. A shop opened in MCCXL and closed in MCCCLXV. MCCXL is 1240 and MCCCLXV is 1365. 1365 − 1240 = 125, and 125 is CXXV.

steps.text: Read the starting year. M is 1000, CD is 400, XL is 40 and IX is 9.
Read the closing year. M is 1000, DC is 600, LX is 60 and V is 5.
Subtract to find how long the company ran.
216 is 200 + 10 + 6, which is CC, X and VI. The company ran for CCXVI years.

notes.A: Yes! The years are 1449 and 1665, the difference is 216, and 216 is written CCXVI.
notes.B: CDVI is 406. Check how you read the two years. CD is 400 and DC is 600, so the years are 1449 and 1665.
notes.C: MMVI is 2006, which is far too long. Change both years to ordinary numbers and subtract.
notes.D: DCLXVI is 666. Read each year in parts first, 1449 and 1665, and then subtract.

hints: This is about writing a number in Roman numerals. Break the number into thousands, hundreds, tens and ones, and write each part on its own.
Split 2349 into 2000 + 300 + 40 + 9. The parts 40 and 9 are each written with a smaller letter before a bigger one.
Here is a similar one. To write 1294, split it into 1000 + 200 + 90 + 4. M is 1000, CC is 200, XC is 90 and IV is 4. So 1294 is MCCXCIV.

steps.text: Split the number into its place value parts.
2000 is MM and 300 is CCC.
40 is XL, which means 10 less than 50. 9 is IX, which means 1 less than 10.
Join the parts in order. 2349 is MMCCCXLIX.

notes.A: Yes! MM is 2000, CCC is 300, XL is 40 and IX is 9, which makes 2349.
notes.B: Here the tens are LX, which is 60, so this is 2369. For 40 the X must come before the L.
notes.C: This writes 40 as XXXX. A letter is never repeated four times, so 40 is written XL.
notes.D: CCD is not a way to write 300. Three hundreds are simply CCC.

hints: The place value of a digit depends on where it sits in the number. Find the 6 in each number and name its place.
For each number, count the places from the right until you reach the 6: ones, tens, hundreds, thousands. Then compare the four place values.
Here is a similar one with the digit 4. In 2473 the 4 is worth 400. In 54 it is worth 4. In 4012 it is worth 4000. So 4012 has the 4 with the greatest place value.

steps.text: Find the place of 6 in each number. In 34562 it is in the tens place, so it is worth 60.
In 3342654 it is in the hundreds place, worth 600. In 75621 it is also in the hundreds place, worth 600.
In 4256402 it is in the thousands place, worth 6000.
6000 is the greatest, so the number is 4256402.

notes.A: In 34562 the 6 is in the tens place, so it is worth only 60. Look for a 6 further to the left.
notes.B: This is a long number, but its 6 is in the hundreds place, worth 600. Check where the 6 sits, not how big the number is.
notes.C: Yes! In 4256402 the 6 is in the thousands place, so it is worth 6000, the greatest of the four.
notes.D: In 75621 the 6 is in the hundreds place, worth 600. One of the other numbers has its 6 in a higher place.

hints: This compares two place values in the same number. Find the place value of each digit, then see how many times one fits into the other.
In 768459, find the place of the 4 and the place of the 5. Write both place values. Then divide the bigger by the smaller.
Here is a similar one. In 13926, the 9 is worth 900 and the 2 is worth 20. 900 ÷ 20 = 45, so the place value of 9 is 45 times that of 2.

steps.text: In 768459 the 4 is in the hundreds place, so its place value is 400.
The 5 is in the tens place, so its place value is 50.
Divide to see how many times 50 goes into 400.
The place value of 4 is 8 times the place value of 5.

notes.A: Check the two place values. The 4 is worth 400 and the 5 is worth 50. Then divide 400 by 50.
notes.B: Yes! The 4 is worth 400 and the 5 is worth 50, and 400 ÷ 50 = 8.
notes.C: Check the two place values. They are 400 and 50, and 50 goes into 400 more than 6 times.
notes.D: The hundreds place is 10 times the tens place, but the digits are different here. Use 400 and 50, not 100 and 10.

hints: First work out the sum. Then look for the digit 9 in your answer and name its place.
The greatest 4-digit number is 9999. Find the greatest 2-digit prime by checking 99, 98 and 97 in turn. Then add the two numbers.
Here is a similar one. The greatest 3-digit number is 999 and the greatest 1-digit prime is 7. 999 + 7 = 1006. In 1006 the digit 1 is in the thousands place, so its place value is 1000.

steps.text: The greatest 4-digit number is 9999.
The greatest 2-digit prime is 97, because 99 can be divided by 3 and 98 can be divided by 2.
Add them.
In 10096 the digit 9 is in the tens place, so its place value is 90.

notes.A: 9 is the face value of the digit. Place value depends on where the 9 sits in the sum, 10096.
notes.B: Yes! 9999 + 97 = 10096, and the 9 in 10096 is in the tens place, so it is worth 90.
notes.C: 9000 is the value of a 9 in 9999 before adding. Add first, then look for the 9 in the sum.
notes.D: Check the sum. 9999 + 97 = 10096, and there the 9 is in the tens place, not the hundreds place.

hints: The Roman letters are I, V, X, L, C, D and M. You need the greatest and the smallest numbers that use each letter once, and then their difference.
For the greatest number, write the letters from biggest to smallest. For the smallest, keep M first, then pair the others so that a smaller letter stands before a bigger one, like CD.
Here is a similar one with only I, V, X and L. The greatest number is LXVI, which is 66. The smallest is XLIV, which is 44. 66 − 44 = 22, and 22 is XXII.

steps.text: For the greatest number, write all seven letters from biggest to smallest: MDCLXVI.
For the smallest, after M put each smaller letter before a bigger one. That gives M, CD, XL, IV, which is MCDXLIV.
Subtract.
222 is 200 + 20 + 2, which is CC, XX and II. The difference is CCXXII.

notes.A: CCXXXIII is 233. Check the two numbers: the greatest is 1666 and the smallest is 1444.
notes.B: CDXXVI is 426. The smallest number is not just the letters turned around. It is MCDXLIV, which is 1444.
notes.C: CCXLII is 242. Check the subtraction: 1666 − 1444.
notes.D: Yes! The greatest is MDCLXVI, 1666, and the smallest is MCDXLIV, 1444. 1666 − 1444 = 222, which is CCXXII.

hints: When two digits swap places, you get a new number. The question wants the difference between the new number and the old one.
Write 86352 with the 6 and the 5 swapped. The 5 moves to the thousands place and the 6 moves to the tens place. Then subtract the smaller number from the bigger one.
Here is a similar one. Swap 7 and 4 in 27143. The new number is 24173. The difference is 27143 − 24173 = 2970.

steps.text: Swap the 6 and the 5 in 86352. The new number is 85362.
The old number is bigger, so subtract the new number from it.
The difference is 990.

notes.A: This is 100 too many. Line up 86352 and 85362 and subtract again, place by place.
notes.B: Yes! The new number is 85362, and 86352 − 85362 = 990.
notes.C: This is close. Subtract 85362 from 86352 again and take care when you borrow in the tens place.
notes.D: Check the new number first. It should be 85362. Then subtract it from 86352, watching the borrowing.

hints: First find the two numbers in ordinary digits and subtract. Then write the answer in Roman numerals.
The greatest 3-digit number is 999, but it is odd, so step down to the nearest even number. The smallest 3-digit number is 100, but it is even, so step up to the nearest odd number.
Here is a similar one. The greatest 2-digit even number is 98 and the smallest 2-digit odd number is 11. 98 − 11 = 87. 87 is 80 + 7, so it is LXXXVII.

steps.text: The greatest 3-digit even number is 998. The smallest 3-digit odd number is 101.
Subtract.
Split 897 into 800 + 90 + 7. 800 is DCCC, 90 is XC and 7 is VII.
So the answer is DCCCXCVII.

notes.A: CMLXXXVII is 987. Work out 998 − 101 again. The answer has 8 hundreds, not 9.
notes.B: DCCLXXXVII is 787. Work out 998 − 101 again, then write 800 as DCCC and 90 as XC.
notes.C: Yes! 998 − 101 = 897, and 897 is DCCC for 800, XC for 90 and VII for 7.
notes.D: CMXCVII is 997. The smallest 3-digit odd number is 101, so subtract 101 from 998.

hints: The predecessor of a number is the number that comes just before it when you count.
To find the number just before, take away 1 from 10,000. Think what happens to all those zeros when you take 1 away.
Here is a similar one. The predecessor of 1,000 is 1,000 − 1 = 999. All the zeros turn into 9s and the number has one digit fewer.

steps.text: The predecessor is the number just before, so subtract 1.
The predecessor of 10,000 is 9,999.

notes.A: 10,001 comes just after 10,000. That is the successor. The predecessor comes just before, so take away 1.
notes.B: Yes! The number just before 10,000 is 10,000 − 1 = 9,999.
notes.C: 99,999 has five digits and is much bigger than 10,000. Taking 1 away from 10,000 leaves four 9s.
notes.D: This takes away 1,000. The predecessor is only 1 less than the number.

hints: Every digit has a face value and a place value. The face value is the digit itself. The place value depends on where it sits.
Find the place of the 5 in 4,562 to get its place value. Its face value is just 5. Then subtract the face value from the place value.
Here is a similar one. In 3,817 the 8 is in the hundreds place, so its place value is 800. Its face value is 8. The difference is 800 − 8 = 792.

steps.text: In 4,562 the 5 is in the hundreds place, so its place value is 500.
The face value of 5 is just 5.
Subtract the face value from the place value.
The difference is 495.

notes.A: 500 is the place value of 5. The question asks for the difference, so take away the face value, 5.
notes.B: Yes! The place value is 500 and the face value is 5, and 500 − 5 = 495.
notes.C: Check the two values. The place value is 500 and the face value is 5. Subtract the smaller from the bigger.
notes.D: 5 is the face value. Now find the place value, 500, and subtract the face value from it.

hints: To estimate a sum, round each number first and then add the rounded numbers.
Round 4,891 to the nearest thousand by looking at its hundreds digit. Do the same for 3,207. If the hundreds digit is 5 or more, round up.
Here is a similar one. Estimate 1,812 + 4,239. 1,812 rounds up to 2,000 because its hundreds digit is 8. 4,239 rounds down to 4,000 because its hundreds digit is 2. 2,000 + 4,000 = 6,000.

steps.text: Round 4,891. The hundreds digit is 8, which is 5 or more, so round up to 5,000.
Round 3,207. The hundreds digit is 2, which is less than 5, so round down to 3,000.
Add the rounded numbers.
The estimated sum is 8,000.

notes.A: This rounds to the nearest hundred, 4,900 and 3,200. The question asks for the nearest thousand.
notes.B: This rounds 4,891 down to 4,000. Its hundreds digit is 8, so it rounds up to 5,000.
notes.C: This rounds 3,207 up to 4,000. Its hundreds digit is 2, so it rounds down to 3,000.

hints: In the Indian system the commas split a number into periods: ones, thousands, lakhs and crores. Read one period at a time.
Look at the commas in 23,45,678. From the right, the first group is the ones period, the next is thousands and the next is lakhs. Say each group with its period name.
Here is a similar one. 51,06,342 has 51 in the lakhs period, 06 in the thousands period and 342 in the ones period. It is read as fifty-one lakh six thousand three hundred forty-two.

steps.text: Split the number at its commas: 23, 45 and 678.
23 is in the lakhs period, 45 is in the thousands period and 678 is in the ones period.
Read each group with its period name. The number is twenty-three lakh forty-five thousand six hundred seventy-eight.

notes.A: Yes! 23 lakh, 45 thousand and 678 is twenty-three lakh forty-five thousand six hundred seventy-eight.
notes.B: This number has only seven digits, so it does not reach crores. The first group, 23, is in the lakhs period.
notes.C: Million belongs to the international system. In the Indian system the periods are lakhs and thousands.
notes.D: There are no crores here, and the 45 thousand is missing. Read the groups as 23 lakh, 45 thousand, 678.

hints: Even numbers are the ones you say when you count in 2s. Between means the numbers after 11 and before 21.
Write out the numbers from 12 to 20. Then circle the ones that can be split into two equal groups.
Here is a similar one. The even numbers between 3 and 11 are 4, 6, 8 and 10. That makes 4 even numbers.

steps.text: The numbers between 11 and 21 are 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19 and 20.
The even ones are 12, 14, 16, 18 and 20.
Count them. There are 5 even numbers.

notes.A: One even number may have been missed. 20 comes before 21, so it counts too. List them all: 12, 14, 16, 18, 20.
notes.B: Yes! The even numbers between 11 and 21 are 12, 14, 16, 18 and 20, which makes 5.
notes.C: This is one too many. List the even numbers from 12 to 20 and count again.
notes.D: Some even numbers were missed. Write them all out from 12 to 20 and count again.

hints: To read a Roman numeral, break it into parts. When a smaller letter stands before a bigger one, you subtract it.
Split MCMXCIX into M, CM, XC and IX. Work out each part, then add the parts.
Here is a similar one. MCDXLIV splits into M, CD, XL and IV. That is 1000 + 400 + 40 + 4 = 1444.

steps.text: Split MCMXCIX into M, CM, XC and IX.
M is 1000. CM is 900. XC is 90. IX is 9.
Add the parts.
MCMXCIX is 1,999.

notes.A: This is 100 too many. CM is 900, not 1000, because the C stands before the M.
notes.B: This reads XC as 40. X before C means 10 less than 100, which is 90.
notes.C: The XC part is missing here. It is worth 90, so add it in.
notes.D: Yes! M is 1000, CM is 900, XC is 90 and IX is 9, which makes 1,999.

hints: A number that lies between two numbers is bigger than the first and smaller than the second.
The two numbers are the same until the last digits. Look at just the endings, 678 and 680, and think what comes between them.
Here is a similar one. Which number lies between 5,21,348 and 5,21,350? Only the endings differ, 348 and 350. The number between them ends in 349, so it is 5,21,349.

steps.text: Both numbers start with 3,45. Only the endings differ: 678 and 680.
The only whole number between 678 and 680 is 679.
So the number that lies between them is 3,45,679.

notes.A: Yes! 3,45,679 is one more than 3,45,678 and one less than 3,45,680.
notes.B: 3,45,677 comes before 3,45,678, so it is not between the two numbers.
notes.C: 3,45,690 is bigger than 3,45,680, so it is past the second number.
notes.D: 3,45,681 comes just after 3,45,680, so it is past the second number.

hints: Place value depends on where a digit sits. Face value is just the digit itself. Product means you multiply.
Find the place of the 4 in 4,372 to get its place value. The face value of 7 is simply 7. Then multiply the two.
Here is a similar one. In 6,243 the place value of 6 is 6,000 and the face value of 4 is 4. The product is 6,000 × 4 = 24,000.

steps.text: In 4,372 the 4 is in the thousands place, so its place value is 4,000.
The face value of 7 is 7.
Multiply them.
The product is 28,000.

notes.A: Yes! The place value of 4 is 4,000 and the face value of 7 is 7, and 4,000 × 7 = 28,000.
notes.B: This multiplies the two face values, 4 and 7. For the 4 you need its place value, 4,000.
notes.C: This uses 400 for the 4. The 4 is in the thousands place, so its place value is 4,000.
notes.D: This adds 4,000 and 7. Product means multiply, so work out 4,000 × 7.

hints: Think about how a crore is written in digits. Then count its zeros.
Build up step by step: 1 thousand has 3 zeros and 1 lakh has 5 zeros. Keep going to 10 lakh and then 1 crore. Then swap the 1 for a 5.
Here is a similar one. 1 lakh is written 1,00,000, so 3 lakh is 3,00,000. Count the zeros and you get 5.

steps.text: 1 crore is written 1,00,00,000. It is a 1 followed by 7 zeros.
5 crore is written 5,00,00,000. The 1 becomes a 5, and the zeros stay the same.
So 5 crore has 7 zeros.

notes.A: Yes! 5 crore is 5,00,00,000, which is a 5 followed by 7 zeros.
notes.B: 5 zeros make a lakh, as in 5,00,000. A crore is 100 times bigger than a lakh.
notes.C: 8 zeros would make 50 crore. Write 5,00,00,000 and count the zeros one by one.
notes.D: 6 zeros make ten lakh, as in 50,00,000. A crore has one more zero.

hints: Each digit has its own place. Fill in the places in order, from ten-thousands down to ones.
Draw five boxes for ten-thousands, thousands, hundreds, tens and ones. Write each digit in its box. A zero still needs its box.
Here is a similar one. A number has 7 in ten-thousands, 2 in thousands, 0 in hundreds, 5 in tens and 0 in ones. Writing the digits in order gives 72,050.

steps.text: Write the digits in order of their places: 4 in ten-thousands, 0 in thousands, 3 in hundreds, 0 in tens, 8 in ones.
Add up the values of the digits.
The number is 40,308.

notes.A: Here the 8 is in the tens place. The 8 belongs in the ones place and the tens place holds 0.
notes.B: This has only four digits. The 0 in the thousands place still needs its own place, so the number has five digits.
notes.C: Yes! 4 ten-thousands, 3 hundreds and 8 ones make 40,308.
notes.D: Here the 3 is in the thousands place. The 3 belongs in the hundreds place.

hints: To compare two numbers with the same number of digits, start from the left and look for the first place where the digits differ.
Both numbers begin with 65. Now look at the hundreds digits of 65,432 and 65,342 and see which is bigger.
Here is a similar one. Compare 48,715 and 48,175. Both begin with 48. The hundreds digits are 7 and 1, and 7 is bigger, so 48,715 > 48,175.

steps.text: Both numbers have five digits and both start with 65.
The hundreds digits are 4 and 3. Since 4 is more than 3, the first number is bigger.
So 65,432 > 65,342. The sign is >.

notes.A: This sign says the first number is smaller. Compare the hundreds digits: 4 is more than 3, so 65,432 is the bigger one.
notes.B: Any two numbers can be compared. Go from left to right and find the first place where the digits differ.
notes.C: The numbers use the same digits but in a different order. Look at the hundreds place: one has 4 and the other has 3.
notes.D: Yes! Both start with 65, and in the hundreds place 4 is more than 3, so 65,432 is greater.

hints: The number just before is one less. So this is a subtraction of 1.
Take 1 away from 50,00,000. Think what happens to the zeros and to the 5 when you take away 1.
Here is a similar one. The number just before 20,000 is 20,000 − 1 = 19,999. The 2 drops to 1 and every zero becomes a 9.

steps.text: The number just before is 1 less, so subtract 1.
Written with Indian commas, the number just before 50,00,000 is 49,99,999.

notes.A: This has one 9 too few. It is 4 lakh 99 thousand 999, which is far smaller. The answer has seven digits.
notes.B: This is 10 less than 50,00,000. Just before means only 1 less.
notes.C: 50,00,001 comes just after. Just before means 1 less, not 1 more.

hints: This is an order of operations problem. Brackets come first, and inside a bracket multiplication comes before addition.
Work out each part on its own. In the first part, add 2 + 3 before you multiply. In the second part there is no inner bracket, so multiply 3 × 5 before you add.
Here is a similar one: {(1 + 4) × 3} − (1 + 4 × 3). The first part is 5 × 3 = 15. The second part is 1 + 12 = 13. Then 15 − 13 = 2.

steps.text: First part: do the inner bracket, then multiply.
Second part: multiply first, then add.
Subtract the second part from the first.
The value is 8.

notes.A: Check each part again. The first part is 5 × 5 = 25 and the second part is 2 + 15 = 17.
notes.B: This takes away only 15. In the second part, add the 2 as well, so it is 2 + 15 = 17.
notes.C: The two parts look alike, but they are not equal. The second one has no inner bracket, so there you multiply 3 × 5 first.
notes.D: Yes! The first part is 25, the second part is 17, and 25 − 17 = 8.

hints: This sum mixes four operations. Multiplication and division are done before addition and subtraction.
Find the multiplication and the division in the sum and work those two out first. Then go from left to right with what is left.
Here is a similar one: 30 − 4 × 5 + 18 ÷ 6. First 4 × 5 = 20 and 18 ÷ 6 = 3. Then 30 − 20 + 3 = 13.

steps.text: Do the multiplication first.
Do the division next.
Now go from left to right.
The answer is 12.

notes.A: This is too big. Do 2 × 3 and 15 ÷ 3 first, then subtract and add.
notes.C: This is close. After 2 × 3 = 6 and 15 ÷ 3 = 5, work from left to right: 13 − 6, then add 5.
notes.D: This comes from adding 3 + 15 before anything else. Multiply and divide first, then go from left to right.

hints: Work out the value of each side on its own, using the order of operations. Then compare the two values.
On the left there are no brackets, so multiply 3 × 2 before adding. On the right, do the bracket first.
Here is a similar one: 3 + 2 × 4 and 4 × (2 + 3). The left side is 3 + 8 = 11. The right side is 4 × 5 = 20. Since 11 is less than 20, the sign is <.

steps.text: Left side: multiply first, then add.
Right side: bracket first, then multiply.
8 is less than 10, so the sign is <.

notes.A: The two sides are equal only if you add 2 + 3 first on the left. Without a bracket, multiply 3 × 2 first, which gives 8.
notes.B: Check the left side. Multiply first: 2 + 6 = 8. The right side is 2 × 5 = 10, which is bigger.
notes.C: Yes! The left side is 8 and the right side is 10, and 8 is less than 10.
notes.D: One of the signs does fit. Work out both sides and compare 8 with 10.

hints: Dozen and score are names for groups. Change both amounts into plain numbers so that you can compare them.
One dozen is 12 and one score is 20. Multiply to find how many each child has.
Here is a similar one. Mira has 6 dozen, which is 6 × 12 = 72. Jay has 3 score, which is 3 × 20 = 60. Mira has more, by 72 − 60 = 12.

steps.text: One dozen is 12, and Raunak has 12 dozen.
One score is 20, and Shail has 5 score.
Raunak has more. Subtract to find how many more.
Raunak has more, by 44.

notes.A: Yes! Raunak has 144 and Shail has 100, so Raunak has 44 more.
notes.B: A score is 20, so Shail has 5 × 20 = 100. Raunak has 12 × 12 = 144, which is more.
notes.C: Raunak does have more, but check the amounts. 12 dozen is 144 and 5 score is 100.
notes.D: They are not equal. 12 dozen is 144 and 5 score is 100.

hints: This sum mixes four operations. Multiplication and division are done before addition and subtraction.
Find the multiplication and the division in the sum and work those two out first. Then go from left to right with what is left.
Here is a similar one: 5 + 6 × 2 − 9 ÷ 3. First 6 × 2 = 12 and 9 ÷ 3 = 3. Then 5 + 12 − 3 = 14.

steps.text: Do the multiplication first.
Do the division next.
Now go from left to right.
The answer is 30.

notes.A: 27 is only 9 × 3. You still need to add the 7 and take away 8 ÷ 2.
notes.B: This is 7 + 27, but the last part is missing. Take away 8 ÷ 2, which is 4.
notes.C: This is close. After 9 × 3 = 27 and 8 ÷ 2 = 4, work out 7 + 27 − 4.

hints: You have to find which signs make the sum equal 20. Test each set of signs, using the order of operations.
Take one set of signs, put it into the boxes and work it out, doing × and ÷ before + and −. If it does not give 20, try another set.
Here is a similar one: 4 □ 2 □ 5 □ 3 = 11. Try +, × and −. That gives 4 + 2 × 5 − 3 = 4 + 10 − 3 = 11, so those signs fit.

steps.text: Try the signs +, × and −. Multiply first.
Then add and subtract from left to right.
The signs + × − make the sum equal 20.

notes.A: With ÷ at the end you get 21 ÷ 6, which does not divide evenly. Try a different last sign.
notes.B: With − first you would have to take 21 away from 5, which cannot give 20. Try starting with +.
notes.D: One set of signs does fit. Try +, × and −, and remember to multiply first.

hints: A bracket changes which part is done first. Test each bracket and see which one makes the sum equal 41.
Take one of the brackets, put it into 17 − 8 × 4 + 5 and work it out, bracket first. If it does not give 41, try another.
Here is a similar one. Where does a bracket go to make 12 − 2 × 3 + 1 equal to 31? Try (12 − 2). Then 10 × 3 + 1 = 30 + 1 = 31, so that bracket fits.

steps.text: Try a bracket around 17 − 8 and do it first.
Multiply next.
Then add.
The bracket goes around (17 − 8).

notes.A: This bracket changes nothing, because 8 × 4 is done first anyway. You would have to take 32 from 17, which cannot be done.
notes.B: This bracket makes 8 × 4 + 5 = 37, which is more than 17. Try a bracket around the first two numbers.
notes.C: This bracket makes 8 × 9 = 72, which is more than 17. Try a bracket around the first two numbers.

hints: First find the price of one banana. Then see how many bananas the money will buy.
Half a dozen is 6 bananas. Divide Rs.30 by 6 to get the price of one banana.
Here is a similar one. Half a dozen mangoes cost Rs.48. One mango costs 48 ÷ 6 = 8 rupees. For Rs.72 you get 72 ÷ 8 = 9 mangoes.

steps.text: Half a dozen is 6 bananas, and they cost Rs.30.
Find the price of one banana.
Divide the money by the price of one banana.
Rs.85 buys 17 bananas.

notes.A: 15 bananas at Rs.5 each cost only Rs.75. Divide 85 by 5 again.
notes.B: 18 bananas at Rs.5 each would cost Rs.90, which is more than Rs.85. Divide 85 by 5 again.
notes.C: Yes! One banana costs Rs.5, and 85 ÷ 5 = 17.
notes.D: 20 bananas at Rs.5 each would cost Rs.100. First find the price of one banana, then divide 85 by it.

hints: Each statement is a small sum with a sign. Work out both sides of each one and see whether the sign is true.
Start with 240 ÷ 16 and check whether it really is more than 16. Then test the others the same way, multiplying and dividing before adding.
Here is a similar one. Is 5 × 5 + 6 = 4 × 4 + 5 × 3 true? The left side is 25 + 6 = 31. The right side is 16 + 15 = 31. Both sides are 31, so it is true.

steps.text: Is 240 ÷ 16 more than 16? It is 15, so no.
Is 18 + 18 ÷ 2 equal to 18? Divide first. It comes to 27, so no.
Now the long statement. Work out its left side.
Work out its right side.
Both sides are 307, so 17×17+18 = 16×16+17×3 is the true one.

notes.A: 240 ÷ 16 = 15, and 15 is less than 16. So this one is not true.
notes.B: Divide before adding: 18 ÷ 2 = 9, and 18 + 9 = 27, not 18.
notes.C: Yes! Both sides come to 307. The left side is 289 + 18 and the right side is 256 + 51.
notes.D: One of them is true. Work out both sides of the statement that starts with 17 × 17.

hints: First find the number itself. When there is no remainder, the number is the divisor times the quotient.
Multiply 8 by 12 to get the number. Then divide that number by 3.
Here is a similar one. A number divided by 6 gives quotient 10 and remainder 0, so the number is 6 × 10 = 60. Dividing 60 by 4 gives 60 ÷ 4 = 15.

steps.text: The number is the divisor times the quotient.
Now divide the number by 3.
The quotient is 32.

notes.A: Check the division. The number is 96, and 3 × 28 = 84, which is too small.
notes.B: Yes! The number is 8 × 12 = 96, and 96 ÷ 3 = 32.
notes.C: 24 is 8 × 3. First find the number, 8 × 12 = 96, and then divide it by 3.
notes.D: 36 is 12 × 3. The number is 96, and it has to be divided by 3, not multiplied.

hints: A gross is a fixed number of things. Find the cost of one notebook first, then the cost of 68.
One gross is 12 dozen, which is 144. Divide Rs.2592 by 144 to find the price of one notebook.
Here is a similar one. 1 gross of pencils costs Rs.720. One pencil costs 720 ÷ 144 = 5 rupees. So 30 pencils cost 30 × 5 = 150 rupees.

steps.text: One gross is 12 dozen.
Find the cost of one notebook.
Multiply by 68.
68 notebooks cost Rs.1224.

notes.A: Check the multiplication. One notebook costs Rs.18, so work out 68 × 18 again.
notes.B: This is close. One notebook costs Rs.18, and 68 × 18 comes to a little less than this.
notes.C: Rs.1296 is half of Rs.2592, the cost of 72 notebooks. You need 68, so find the cost of one notebook first.
notes.D: Yes! One notebook costs 2592 ÷ 144 = 18 rupees, and 68 × 18 = 1224.

hints: This has a bracket inside a bracket. Start with the innermost bracket and work outwards. The word 'of' means multiply.
Begin inside the round bracket, 35 − 2 × 12. Multiply before you subtract.
Here is a similar one: 100 − [10 + 3 of (20 − 2 × 5)]. Inside, 2 × 5 = 10 and 20 − 10 = 10. Then 3 of 10 is 30, and 10 + 30 = 40. Last, 100 − 40 = 60.

steps.text: Round bracket first. Multiply, then subtract.
6 of 11 means 6 times 11.
Finish the square bracket.
Subtract from 178.
The answer is 97.

notes.A: Check the round bracket. 2 × 12 = 24 and 35 − 24 = 11. Then 6 of 11 is 66.
notes.B: Check each stage. The round bracket is 11, the square bracket is 15 + 66 = 81, and then you subtract 81 from 178.
notes.C: This is close. The square bracket comes to 81. Subtract 81 from 178 again.
notes.D: Yes! The round bracket is 11, 6 of 11 is 66, 15 + 66 = 81, and 178 − 81 = 97.

hints: Work out the value of each side on its own. Then compare the two values.
On each side, multiply first and then add. Start with 17 × 17.
Here is a similar one: 12 × 12 + 10 and 11 × 13 + 20. The left side is 144 + 10 = 154. The right side is 143 + 20 = 163. 154 is less than 163, so the sign is <.

steps.text: Left side: multiply, then add.
Right side: multiply, then add.
334 is more than 313, so the sign is >.

notes.A: Yes! The left side is 289 + 45 = 334 and the right side is 224 + 89 = 313, so the left side is greater.
notes.B: The two sides are not equal. The left side is 334 and the right side is 313.
notes.C: Check the multiplications. 17 × 17 = 289 and 16 × 14 = 224. The left side comes out bigger.
notes.D: The two sides can be compared. Work out each side: 334 and 313.

hints: A bracket changes which part is done first. Test each bracket to see whether the sum becomes 40. It is possible that none of them does.
Take one of the brackets, put it into 16 + 24 ÷ 4 + 6 × 2 and work it out, bracket first. Do the same for the others.
Here is a similar one. Where does a bracket go to make 10 + 20 ÷ 5 + 5 × 2 equal to 16? With (10 + 20) you get 30 ÷ 5 + 10 = 6 + 10 = 16, so that bracket fits. Each bracket must be tested like this.

steps.text: Try (16 + 24). The bracket is 40, and the sum comes to 22.
Try (4 + 6 × 2). The bracket is 16, and 24 ÷ 16 does not divide evenly, so this cannot give 40.
Try (16 + 24 ÷ 4). The bracket is 22, and the sum comes to 34.
No bracket shown makes 40, so the answer is none of these.

notes.A: With this bracket you get 40 ÷ 4 + 12 = 22, not 40. Test the other brackets too.
notes.B: With this bracket you would need 24 ÷ 16, which does not divide evenly. So it cannot make 40.
notes.C: Yes! The brackets shown give 22, a sum that does not divide evenly, and 34. None of them makes 40.
notes.D: With this bracket you get 22 + 12 = 34, not 40. Test the other brackets too.

hints: A bracket changes which part is done first. Test each bracket and see which one makes the sum equal 40.
Take one of the brackets, put it into 3 × 25 − 13 + 4 and work it out, bracket first. See whether it gives 40.
Here is a similar one. Where does a bracket go to make 2 × 15 − 5 + 3 equal to 23? Try (15 − 5). Then 2 × 10 + 3 = 20 + 3 = 23, so that bracket fits.

steps.text: Try a bracket around 25 − 13 and do it first.
Multiply.
Add.
The bracket goes around (25 − 13).

notes.A: One of the brackets does fit. Try putting it around 25 − 13.
notes.B: This bracket makes 25 − 13 + 4 = 16, and 3 × 16 = 48. That is too many.
notes.C: This bracket makes 13 + 4 = 17, and 75 − 17 = 58. That is too many.

hints: There are two steps. First find the sum. Then find what must be taken away from it to leave 1789.
Add 2012 and 689 first. The number to take away is the gap between that sum and 1789.
Here is a similar one. What must be subtracted from the sum of 1500 and 250 to get 1200? The sum is 1750. Then 1750 − 1200 = 550, so subtract 550.

steps.text: Find the sum.
Find the gap between the sum and 1789.
You must subtract 912.

notes.A: This is 20 too many. The sum is 2701. Subtract 1789 from 2701 again, borrowing with care.
notes.B: This is 20 too few. The sum is 2701. Subtract 1789 from 2701 again, borrowing with care.
notes.C: Check the sum first. 2012 + 689 = 2701. Then subtract 1789 from it.

hints: Brackets come first, then multiplication, then addition and subtraction from left to right.
Start inside the round bracket, 8 + 5 − 6. Then multiply that by 2. Also work out 7 × 7.
Here is a similar one: 6 × 6 − 20 + 1 + {(7 + 4 − 5) × 3}. The round bracket is 6, and 6 × 3 = 18. Then 36 − 20 + 1 + 18 = 35.

steps.text: Round bracket first.
Finish the curly bracket.
Do the multiplication at the start.
Now go from left to right.
The answer is 29.

notes.A: This is close. The steps are 49 − 36 = 13, then 13 + 2 = 15, and then you add 14.
notes.B: Yes! 7 × 7 = 49 and the bracket is 14, so 49 − 36 + 2 + 14 = 29.
notes.C: Go from left to right: 49 − 36 = 13, then add 2, then add the bracket, 14.
notes.D: This is too many. Check the bracket: 8 + 5 − 6 = 7, and 7 × 2 = 14.

hints: Work from the innermost brackets outwards. Inside each bracket, do division and multiplication before addition and subtraction.
Start with the inner bracket, 72 ÷ 8 − 5. Do the division first, then the subtraction.
Similar example: 100 ÷ (4 + (18 ÷ 3 − 4) × 3). Inner bracket: 18 ÷ 3 = 6, then 6 − 4 = 2. Next 2 × 3 = 6, then 4 + 6 = 10. Last, 100 ÷ 10 = 10.

steps.text: Inner bracket first: divide, then subtract.
In the outer bracket, multiply before adding.
Now add inside the outer bracket.
Last, divide. The value is 8.

notes.A: Yes! The inner bracket is 4, then 4 × 3 = 12, 12 + 12 = 24, and 192 ÷ 24 = 8.
notes.B: This needs the outer bracket to be 32. Work it step by step: 72 ÷ 8 = 9, 9 − 5 = 4, 4 × 3 = 12, then 12 + 12.
notes.C: This comes from dividing 192 by 12 alone. The whole outer bracket must be worked out first, and it comes to 24.
notes.D: This comes from an outer bracket of 16, which leaves out the multiplying by 3. After 9 − 5 = 4, multiply by 3 before adding 12.

hints: A bracket changes which part is done first. Test each bracket and see which one makes the sum equal 17.
Take one of the brackets, put it into 80 ÷ 10 + 2 × 3 + 12 and work it out, bracket first. See whether it gives 17.
Here is a similar one. Where does a bracket go to make 60 ÷ 5 + 5 × 2 + 3 equal to 7? Try (5 + 5 × 2). The bracket is 5 + 10 = 15. Then 60 ÷ 15 + 3 = 4 + 3 = 7, so that bracket fits.

steps.text: Try a bracket around 10 + 2 × 3. Inside it, multiply first.
Divide 80 by the bracket.
Add 12.
The bracket goes around (10 + 2 × 3).

notes.A: This bracket makes 8 + 2 = 10, then 10 × 3 + 12 = 42. That is too many.
notes.B: Yes! The bracket is 16, 80 ÷ 16 = 5, and 5 + 12 = 17.
notes.C: This bracket changes nothing, because 2 × 3 is done first anyway. You get 8 + 6 + 12 = 26.
notes.D: This bracket makes 3 + 12 = 15, and 8 + 2 × 15 = 38. That is too many.

hints: Work out the value of each side on its own. Then compare the two values.
Add up the six numbers on the left. Pairing them into easy tens and twenties makes it quicker. Then work out 8 × 7.
Here is a similar one: 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 + 9 and 6 × 5. The left side adds up to 25. The right side is 30. 25 is less than 30, so the sign is <.

steps.text: Add the left side.
Work out the right side.
48 is less than 56, so the sign is <.

notes.A: Yes! The left side is 48 and the right side is 56, and 48 is less than 56.
notes.B: Check both sides. The sum on the left is 48, and 8 × 7 = 56, which is bigger.
notes.C: The two sides are close but not equal. The left side is 48 and the right side is 56.
notes.D: One of the signs does fit. Compare 48 with 56.

hints: First find how many seats there are in all. Then take away the empty ones.
Count the rows from A to Q. Multiply by 17 seats to get the total. Then count the rows from A to H to find how many seats are empty.

Here is a similar one. A hall has rows A to J, which is 10 rows, with 12 seats each. That is 10 × 12 = 120 seats. If 2 seats are empty in each of rows A to E, that is 5 × 2 = 10 empty seats. So 120 − 10 = 110 people are seated.

steps.text: Rows A to Q make 17 rows, because Q is the 17th letter of the alphabet.
Find the total number of seats.
Rows A to H make 8 rows, each with 3 empty seats.
Take away the empty seats.
265 people are seated.

notes.A: Check the count of rows. A to Q is 17 rows and A to H is 8 rows. Then subtract 24 from 289.
notes.B: This is close. The empty seats are 8 × 3 = 24. Subtract 24 from 289.
notes.C: Check the total first. 17 × 17 = 289. Then take away the 24 empty seats.
notes.D: Yes! There are 17 × 17 = 289 seats and 8 × 3 = 24 are empty, so 289 − 24 = 265.

hints: You do not need to find the hidden digits. Think about the last digit of the product and about how big the product can be.
Both numbers have three digits. Multiply only their last digits, 7 and 6, to see what the product must end in. Then think how many digits the product of two 3-digit numbers can have.

Here is a similar one. The product of (★3) and (★4) must end in 2, because 3 × 4 = 12. Two 2-digit numbers give a product from 10 × 10 = 100 up to 99 × 99 = 9801. So 1472 could be the product, but 1475 could not.

steps.text: Multiply the last digits. The product must end in 2.
Two 3-digit numbers multiply to at least 100 × 100 = 10000 and to less than 1000 × 1000 = 1000000. So the product has 5 or 6 digits.
1342 has too few digits, 9933012 has too many, and 51276 does not end in 2.
Only 312312 has the right size and ends in 2. For example, 507 × 616 = 312312.

notes.A: This number is too small. Two 3-digit numbers multiply to at least 100 × 100 = 10000, which has five digits.
notes.B: Yes! It ends in 2, as 7 × 6 = 42 says it must, and it has six digits, which fits two 3-digit numbers.
notes.C: This number is too big. Two 3-digit numbers multiply to less than 1000 × 1000 = 1000000, so the product has at most six digits.
notes.D: Look at the last digit. 7 × 6 = 42, so the product must end in 2, and this ends in 6.

hints: This sum mixes subtraction, multiplication and addition. Multiplication is done first.
Work out 3 × 8 first. Then go from left to right with the subtraction and the addition.
Here is a similar one: 40 − 4 × 6 + 5. First 4 × 6 = 24. Then 40 − 24 = 16, and 16 + 5 = 21.

steps.text: Do the multiplication first.
Now go from left to right. Subtract.
Then add.
The answer is 28.

notes.B: This is close. After 3 × 8 = 24, go from left to right: 50 − 24 = 26, then add 2.
notes.C: 26 is what you get after the subtraction. There is still a + 2 to do.
notes.D: This is what you get if you subtract first and then multiply 47 by 8. Do the multiplication first.

hints: There is a bracket in this sum. The bracket is always done first.
Add the two numbers inside the bracket. Then multiply your answer by 3.
Here is a similar one: (12 + 8) × 4. The bracket is 12 + 8 = 20. Then 20 × 4 = 80.

steps.text: Do the bracket first.
Multiply by 3.
The answer is 60.

notes.A: Yes! The bracket is 15 + 5 = 20, and 20 × 3 = 60.
notes.B: This is what you get if you multiply 5 × 3 first. The bracket tells you to add 15 + 5 first.
notes.C: This is 15 × 3. The 5 in the bracket has to be added to 15 before you multiply.
notes.D: 20 is the bracket, 15 + 5. Now multiply it by 3.

hints: This sum has a division and an addition. Division is done before addition.
Work out 36 ÷ 6 first. Then add 14.
Here is a similar one: 48 ÷ 8 + 11. First 48 ÷ 8 = 6. Then 6 + 11 = 17.

steps.text: Do the division first.
Then add 14.
The answer is 20.

notes.A: This is 36 + 14. The first sign is ÷, so divide 36 by 6 first.
notes.B: This is too small. Divide first, 36 ÷ 6 = 6, and then add 14.
notes.C: Check the adding. 36 ÷ 6 = 6, and then you add 14, not 2.

hints: Do the bracket first. After that, division and multiplication are done in order from left to right.
Add inside the bracket. Then divide 48 by that number before you multiply by 2.
Here is a similar one: 36 ÷ (2 + 4) × 3. The bracket is 6. Then 36 ÷ 6 = 6, and 6 × 3 = 18.

steps.text: Do the bracket first.
Go from left to right. Divide.
Then multiply.
The answer is 12.

notes.A: Yes! The bracket is 8, then 48 ÷ 8 = 6, and 6 × 2 = 12.
notes.B: Check the bracket first. 4 + 4 = 8, then 48 ÷ 8 = 6, and then multiply by 2.
