notes.C: 25 × 25 = 625, which is far too big. The two squares add up to 289.
notes.D: 15 is already one of the numbers in the sum. x must be bigger, because x times x is 225 with 64 more added.

hints: A small 2 above a number means multiply the number by itself. Work out the left side first, then find the number whose square matches it.
Find 5 × 5 and 12 × 12 and add them. Then look for a number that gives that total when it is multiplied by itself.
Similar example: 3² + 4² = n². 3 × 3 = 9 and 4 × 4 = 16, and 9 + 16 = 25. Since 5 × 5 = 25, n is 5.

steps.text: Square 5.
Square 12.
Add the two squares.
Find the number that multiplies by itself to make 169. So M is 13.

notes.B: This is 12 take away 5. Square each number first, then add the squares.
notes.C: 169 is M times M. The question asks for M itself, the number that multiplies by itself to make 169.
notes.D: 12 is already one of the numbers in the sum. M must be bigger, because M times M is 144 with 25 more added.

hints: When the number of rows equals the number of chairs in each row, the total is a number multiplied by itself. Think about what kind of number that makes.
The number of men must be a perfect square. Find square numbers close to each choice and see which choice is exactly a number times itself.
Similar example: could 225 children sit this way? 15 × 15 = 225, so yes, in 15 rows of 15. Could 226? 15 × 15 = 225 and 16 × 16 = 256, and 226 lies between them, so no.

steps.text: The rows and the chairs in each row are equal, so the number of men is a number times itself, a perfect square.
Find square numbers near the choices.
131 lies between 121 and 144, and 275 lies between 256 and 289, so neither is a perfect square.
Now try 18.
325 is one more than 324, so it is not a perfect square. The number of men can be 324.

notes.A: 11 × 11 = 121 and 12 × 12 = 144. 131 falls between them, so it cannot be arranged in equal rows and columns.
notes.B: Very close! 18 × 18 = 324, so 325 has one man too many for a square arrangement.
notes.C: 16 × 16 = 256 and 17 × 17 = 289. 275 falls between them, so it is not a number times itself.
notes.D: Yes! 18 × 18 = 324, so there are 18 rows with 18 chairs in each row.

hints: A square number is a number times itself, like 49 or 100. Add each pair and see which total is a square number.
Start by adding the first pair, 91 and 19. Then check whether the total sits exactly on a square, such as 10 × 10 or 11 × 11.
Similar example: is 87 + 57 a square number? 87 + 57 = 144, and 12 × 12 = 144, so yes. Is 60 + 30 a square? 60 + 30 = 90, which lies between 9 × 9 = 81 and 10 × 10 = 100, so no.

steps.text: Add the first pair. 110 lies between 100 and 121, so it is not a square.
Add the second pair.
225 is a square number.
The other two pairs give 59 + 52 = 111 and 76 + 78 = 154. Neither is a square number.
So the pair whose sum is a square number is 157 & 68.

notes.A: 91 + 19 = 110. That lies between 10 × 10 = 100 and 11 × 11 = 121, so it is not a square.
notes.C: 59 + 52 = 111. That lies between 10 × 10 = 100 and 11 × 11 = 121, so it is not a square.
notes.D: 76 + 78 = 154. That lies between 12 × 12 = 144 and 13 × 13 = 169, so it is not a square.

hints: To compare, work out the value of each side first. Then see which side is bigger.
Find 29 × 29 for the left side. For the right side, find 31 × 31 and 10 × 10, then subtract.
Similar example: compare 12² with 13² − 6². The left side is 12 × 12 = 144. On the right, 13 × 13 = 169 and 6 × 6 = 36, and 169 − 36 = 133. 144 is more than 133, so the sign is >.

steps.text: Work out the left side.
On the right side, square 31.
Square 10 to get 100, and subtract it.
841 is smaller than 861, so the left side is less than the right side. The sign is <.

notes.A: Yes! The left side is 841 and the right side is 861, so the left side is smaller.
notes.B: Check the right side. 31 × 31 = 961, and taking away 100 leaves 861, which is more than 841.
notes.C: The two sides are close but not equal. The left side is 841 and the right side is 861.
notes.D: One of the signs does fit. Work out both sides: 841 on the left and 861 on the right.

hints: A perfect square is made of matching pairs of factors. Break the number into its prime factors and look for a factor that has no partner.
Break 28 into prime factors: 28 = 2 × 2 × 7. Which factor is in a pair, and which one is alone?
Similar example: 12 = 2 × 2 × 3. The 2s make a pair but the 3 is alone. Multiply by 3: 12 × 3 = 36, and 36 = 6 × 6, a perfect square.

steps.text: Break 28 into prime factors.
The two 2s make a pair. The 7 has no partner, so one more 7 is needed.
Multiply 28 by 7 and check.
196 is a perfect square, so the smallest number to multiply by is 7.

notes.A: 28 × 12 = 336, and no whole number times itself gives 336. Look for the factor of 28 that has no partner.
notes.B: 28 × 10 = 280, which is not a perfect square. Break 28 into 2 × 2 × 7 and see which factor is alone.
notes.C: Yes! 28 = 2 × 2 × 7, so one more 7 completes the pairs. 28 × 7 = 196 = 14 × 14.
notes.D: 28 × 5 = 140, which is not a perfect square. The factor of 28 without a partner is 7, not 5.

hints: Square each number in a pair, add the two squares, and see whether the total is itself a square number.
Start with the first pair: find 10 × 10 and 15 × 15 and add them. Then check if that total is some number times itself.
Similar example: 9 and 12. 9 × 9 = 81 and 12 × 12 = 144, and 81 + 144 = 225. Since 15 × 15 = 225, the sum of the squares is a square number.

steps.text: Try 10 and 15. 325 is one more than 18 times 18, so it is not a square.
Try 7 and 24. Square each and add.
625 is a square number.
The other two pairs give 64 + 2025 = 2089 and 81 + 625 = 706. Neither is a square number.
So the pair is 7 and 24.

notes.A: 100 + 225 = 325. That is just one more than 18 × 18 = 324, so it is not a square.
notes.C: 64 + 2025 = 2089. That lies between 45 × 45 = 2025 and 46 × 46 = 2116, so it is not a square.
notes.D: 81 + 625 = 706. That lies between 26 × 26 = 676 and 27 × 27 = 729, so it is not a square.

hints: A perfect square is made of factors that all come in pairs. Break 588 into small factors and look for one without a partner.
Start dividing 588 by 2, then by 2 again, and keep going with small prime numbers. Write 588 as a product of primes.
Similar example: 180. Its prime factors are 2 × 2 × 3 × 3 × 5 = 180. The 2s pair up and the 3s pair up, but 5 is alone. Multiply by 5: 180 × 5 = 900, and 30 × 30 = 900.

steps.text: Break 588 into prime factors.
The two 2s make a pair and the two 7s make a pair. The 3 has no partner.
Multiply by 3 to give it a partner.
Check that 1764 is a perfect square.
The least number is 3, which is not among the numbers given. So the answer is None of these.

notes.A: 588 × 2 = 1176. The 2s already had partners and the 3 is still alone, so this is not a square.
notes.B: 588 × 6 = 3528. This gives the 3 a partner but leaves an extra 2 alone, so it is not a square.
notes.C: 588 × 4 = 2352. The 3 still has no partner, so this is not a square.
notes.D: Yes! The lonely factor is 3, and 3 is not listed, so none of the numbers given fits.

hints: Find the square numbers that sit close to 1234. The number to add is the gap up to a square above it.
Try 35 × 35 and 36 × 36. See which one is just above 1234.
Similar example: what must be added to 380 to get a square number? 19 × 19 = 361 is too small, and 20 × 20 = 400 is the next square. 400 − 380 = 20, so add 20.

steps.text: 35 times 35 is a little less than 1234.
So the next square above 1234 is 36 times 36.
Find the gap from 1234 up to 1296. The number to add is 62.

notes.A: 1234 + 45 = 1279. That lies between 35 × 35 = 1225 and 36 × 36 = 1296, so it is not a square.
notes.B: 1234 + 25 = 1259. That lies between 35 × 35 = 1225 and 36 × 36 = 1296, so it is not a square.
notes.C: 1234 + 57 = 1291. That is close, but the next square is 36 × 36 = 1296.

hints: A square number is a number times itself, like 49 or 100. Add each pair and see which total is a square number.
Start by adding the first pair, 159 and 165. Then check whether the total is some number times itself. Try numbers near 18.
Similar example: is 130 + 126 a square number? 130 + 126 = 256, and 16 × 16 = 256, so yes. Is 75 + 50 a square? 75 + 50 = 125, which lies between 11 × 11 = 121 and 12 × 12 = 144, so no.

steps.text: Add the first pair.
324 is a square number.
The other pairs give 198 + 145 = 343 and 189 + 330 = 519. Neither is a square number.
So the pair whose sum is a square is 159 and 165.

notes.B: 198 + 145 = 343. That lies between 18 × 18 = 324 and 19 × 19 = 361, so it is not a square.
notes.C: 189 + 330 = 519. That lies between 22 × 22 = 484 and 23 × 23 = 529, so it is not a square.
notes.D: One pair does work. Add 159 and 165, then compare the total with 18 × 18.

hints: There are two numbers to find before dividing: the smallest square with 4 digits, and the biggest even square with 2 digits.
For the first number, try 31 × 31 and 32 × 32 and see which one first reaches 4 digits. For the second, list the 2-digit squares and pick the biggest even one.

Similar example: divide the smallest 3-digit square by the greatest 1-digit even square. 10 × 10 = 100 is the smallest 3-digit square. The 1-digit squares are 1, 4 and 9, so the greatest even one is 4. 100 ÷ 4 = 25.

steps.text: 31 times 31 has only 3 digits.
So the smallest 4-digit square is 32 times 32.
The 2-digit squares are 16, 25, 36, 49, 64 and 81. The greatest even one is 64.
Divide. The quotient is 16.

notes.A: Check the two numbers first. The smallest 4-digit square is 32 × 32 = 1024, and the greatest 2-digit even square is 8 × 8 = 64.
notes.B: Remember the 2-digit square must be even. 81 is bigger but odd, so use 64, then divide 1024 by it.
notes.C: This is close. Work out 1024 ÷ 64 again. It helps to know that 64 × 10 = 640.
notes.D: Yes! The two squares are 1024 and 64, and 1024 ÷ 64 = 16.

hints: First find the two square numbers the question describes. Then divide the bigger by the smaller and see what is left over.
List the squares that have 2 digits, starting from 4 × 4. The first one in your list and the last one are the two numbers you need.

Similar example: find the remainder when the greatest 3-digit square is divided by the smallest 3-digit square. They are 31 × 31 = 961 and 10 × 10 = 100. Nine 100s make 900, and 961 − 900 = 61. The remainder is 61.

steps.text: The 2-digit squares are 16, 25, 36, 49, 64 and 81. The greatest is 81 and the smallest is 16.
See how many 16s fit into 81. Five of them fit.
Find what is left over. The remainder is 1.

notes.A: Check which squares you used. The greatest 2-digit square is 81 and the smallest is 16.
notes.B: Yes! 5 × 16 = 80, and 81 is just 1 more than 80.
notes.C: This is what is left when 100 is divided by 16, but 100 has 3 digits. The greatest 2-digit square is 81.
notes.D: Check the two squares: 81 and 16. Five 16s make 80, so see how much of 81 is left.

hints: All the numbers look alike in one way, so look for a second property that one number does not share.
Find which number each one is the square of. Then look at whether each number is even or odd.
Similar example: 9, 25, 36, 49, 81. These are the squares of 3, 5, 6, 7 and 9. All of them are odd except 36, so 36 is the odd one out.

steps.text: These are all square numbers: the squares of 12, 13, 14, 16, 18 and 20.
144, 196, 256, 324 and 400 are all even numbers.
169 is the square of 13, and it is an odd number.
So the odd one out is 169.

notes.A: 144 is 12 × 12 and it is even, like most of the others. Look for the one number that is odd.
notes.B: Yes! Every number here is a square, but 169 is the only odd one.
notes.C: 196 is 14 × 14 and it is even, like most of the others. Look for the one number that is odd.
notes.D: 324 is 18 × 18 and it is even, like most of the others. Look for the one number that is odd.

hints: All the numbers look alike in one way, so look for a second property that one number does not share.
Find which number each one is the square of. Then ask what kind of numbers 11, 13, 17, 19 and 23 are.
Similar example: 4, 9, 25, 36, 49. These are the squares of 2, 3, 5, 6 and 7. All of those are prime except 6, because 2 × 3 = 6. So 36 does not belong.

steps.text: These are the squares of 9, 11, 13, 17, 19 and 23.
11, 13, 17, 19 and 23 are prime numbers. Each can be divided only by 1 and itself.
9 is not prime, because it is 3 times 3.
So the number that does not belong is 81.

notes.A: Yes! 81 is 9 × 9, and 9 is not prime. All the others are squares of prime numbers.
notes.B: 529 is 23 × 23, and 23 is a prime number. Look for the square of a number that is not prime.
notes.C: 121 is 11 × 11, and 11 is a prime number. Look for the square of a number that is not prime.
notes.D: 289 is 17 × 17, and 17 is a prime number. Look for the square of a number that is not prime.

hints: A square number is a number times itself, like 49 or 100. Add each pair and see which total is a square number.
Start by adding the first pair, 91 and 19. Then check whether the total sits exactly on a square, such as 10 × 10 or 11 × 11.
Similar example: is 113 + 83 a square number? 113 + 83 = 196, and 14 × 14 = 196, so yes. Is 45 + 25 a square? 45 + 25 = 70, which lies between 8 × 8 = 64 and 9 × 9 = 81, so no.

steps.text: Add the first pair. 110 lies between 100 and 121, so it is not a square.
Add the second pair.
225 is a square number.
The other two pairs give 59 + 52 = 111 and 76 + 78 = 154. Neither is a square number.
So the pair whose sum is a square number is 157 & 68.

notes.A: 91 + 19 = 110. That lies between 10 × 10 = 100 and 11 × 11 = 121, so it is not a square.
notes.C: 59 + 52 = 111. That lies between 10 × 10 = 100 and 11 × 11 = 121, so it is not a square.
notes.D: 76 + 78 = 154. That lies between 12 × 12 = 144 and 13 × 13 = 169, so it is not a square.

hints: The same day of the week comes back every 7 days. Use this to jump backwards from the date you know.
Take 7 away from 17, and then 7 again, to find earlier Saturdays. Then count back the last few days to the 1st.

Similar example: the 20th is a Wednesday. Going back in 7s, the 13th and the 6th are also Wednesdays. Counting back from the 6th: the 5th is Tuesday, the 4th Monday, the 3rd Sunday, the 2nd Saturday and the 1st Friday.

steps.text: Go back 7 days. The 10th is also a Saturday.
Go back 7 more days. The 3rd is also a Saturday.
Count back from the 3rd: the 2nd is a Friday and the 1st is a Thursday.
So the first day of the month was Thursday.

notes.A: Friday is the 2nd, the day before Saturday the 3rd. Go back one more day to reach the 1st.
notes.B: Yes! The 3rd is a Saturday, so the 2nd is Friday and the 1st is Thursday.
notes.C: Check your counting back. The 3rd is a Saturday, so the 2nd is Friday and the 1st is the day before that.
notes.D: Sunday comes after Saturday. Here we go backwards from Saturday the 3rd to reach the 1st.

hints: On a clock the hour hand does not sit still. It creeps forward as the minutes pass. Find where each hand points, then find the gap between them.
The gap between two neighbouring numbers on a clock is 30°. At half past six the minute hand is on 6. Think about where the hour hand is between 6 and 7.

Similar example: at 20 minutes past 8, the minute hand is on 4. In 60 minutes the hour hand moves 30°, so in 20 minutes it moves 10° past the 8. From 4 to 8 is 4 × 30 = 120°. The angle is 120 + 10 = 130°.

steps.text: The 12 numbers on a clock share a full turn of 360°. So each gap between numbers is 30°.
At half past six the minute hand points exactly at 6.
Half an hour has passed since 6 o'clock, so the hour hand has moved halfway from 6 to 7.
Half of one gap is the angle between the hands. The angle is 15°.

notes.A: Yes! The hour hand is half a gap past 6, and half of 30° is 15°.
notes.B: Check the size of one gap. Each gap between clock numbers is 30°, and the hour hand is half a gap past 6.
notes.C: This is one full gap. The hour hand is only halfway from 6 to 7, so the angle is half of this.
notes.D: This is one and a half gaps. The hour hand is only half a gap away from the minute hand at 6.

hints: Change the seconds into minutes first. Then think about how far the minute hand turns in one minute.
There are 60 seconds in a minute, so find 300 ÷ 60. The minute hand goes all the way round, 360°, in 60 minutes.
Similar example: in 900 seconds, 900 ÷ 60 = 15 minutes pass. The minute hand turns 360 ÷ 60 = 6° each minute. So it turns 15 × 6 = 90°.

steps.text: Change 300 seconds into minutes.
The minute hand makes a full turn of 360° in 60 minutes. Find its turn in 1 minute.
In 5 minutes it turns 5 times as much. The minute hand moves 30 degrees.

notes.A: This is half of 300. First change 300 seconds to 5 minutes, then use 6° for each minute.
notes.B: That is the turn in 10 minutes. 300 seconds is only 5 minutes.
notes.C: Yes! 300 seconds is 5 minutes, and 5 × 6 = 30.
notes.D: This is half of the real turn. The minute hand moves 6° every minute, and 5 minutes pass.

hints: An ordinary year has 365 days, which is 52 full weeks and 1 extra day. So the same date moves forward one weekday each year, and two after a leap year.
Go one year at a time from 1st January 2006. Check which of the years 2006, 2007, 2008 and 2009 is a leap year.

Similar example: 1st January 2014 was a Wednesday. 2014 and 2015 are ordinary years, so 1st January 2015 is a Thursday and 1st January 2016 is a Friday. 2016 is a leap year, so the day moves on by 2: 1st January 2017 is a Sunday.

steps.text: An ordinary year is 52 weeks and 1 day, so a date moves on by 1 weekday.
2006 is an ordinary year, so 1st January 2007 is a Monday. 2007 is ordinary too, so 1st January 2008 is a Tuesday.
2008 is a leap year with 366 days, so the day moves on by 2. 1st January 2009 is a Thursday.
2009 is an ordinary year. So 1st January 2010 is a Friday.

notes.A: This moves one day too many. Only 2008 is a leap year, so the day moves 1 + 1 + 2 + 1 = 5 days on from Sunday.
notes.B: This moves 4 days, one for each year. 2008 is a leap year, so it adds one extra day.
notes.C: That is the day one year later, in 2007. Keep going for all four years.
notes.D: Yes! The day moves 1 + 1 + 2 + 1 = 5 days on from Sunday, which is Friday.

hints: Each gap between numbers on a clock is 30°. Remember that the hour hand creeps forward as the minutes pass. Test each time.
Start with the half-past times. The minute hand is on 6 and the hour hand is halfway between two numbers. Count the gaps between the hands.

Similar example: what is the angle at 3:30? The minute hand is on 6 and the hour hand is halfway between 3 and 4. From the hour hand to 4 is half a gap, 15°. From 4 to 6 is 2 × 30 = 60°. The angle is 15 + 60 = 75°.

steps.text: Each gap between clock numbers is 30°.
At 7:30 the minute hand is on 6. The hour hand is halfway between 7 and 8.
From 6 to 7 is one gap of 30°. From 7 to the hour hand is half a gap, 15°.
Add them. The angle is 45°, so the time is 07:30.

notes.A: At 1:15 the minute hand is on 3 and the hour hand is a little past 1. That angle is more than 45°. Try a half-past time.
notes.B: At 2:30 the hands are three and a half gaps apart, which is 105°. Look for hands one and a half gaps apart.
notes.C: At 8:30 the hands are two and a half gaps apart, which is 75°. Look for hands one and a half gaps apart.
notes.D: Yes! At 7:30 the hands are one and a half gaps apart, and 30 + 15 = 45.

hints: Change minutes into hours, hours into days, and days into weeks. Take it one unit at a time.
First multiply out the product to get the number of minutes. Then divide by 60 to change the minutes into hours.
Similar example: how many weeks are in 20160 minutes? 20160 ÷ 60 = 336 hours. 336 ÷ 24 = 14 days. 14 ÷ 7 = 2 weeks.

steps.text: Multiply out the minutes.
Change minutes to hours.
Change hours to days.
Change days to weeks. There are 4 weeks.

notes.A: Yes! 40320 minutes is 672 hours, which is 28 days, and 28 ÷ 7 = 4.
notes.B: Check the last step. The minutes make 28 days, and 28 ÷ 7 gives the weeks.
notes.C: Check the multiplication first. The product is 40320 minutes, which is 672 hours.
notes.D: This is one week too many. The minutes make 28 days, and 7 days make a week.

hints: One full turn of the minute hand takes one hour. So count the turns as hours and move the clock forward.
30 turns means 30 hours. Split 30 hours into one full day of 24 hours and the hours left over.
Similar example: it is 9:00 am on 3rd May and the minute hand turns 28 times. That is 28 hours, and 24 + 4 = 28. After 24 hours it is 9:00 am on 4th May. Four more hours make it 1:00 pm on 4th May.

steps.text: Each full turn of the minute hand is 1 hour. So 30 turns is 30 hours.
Split 30 hours into 1 day and some hours.
24 hours after 4:30 pm on 15th April is 4:30 pm on 16th April.
6 hours after that is 10:30 pm. So it is 10:30pm, 16th April.

notes.A: Yes! 30 turns is 30 hours: one full day and 6 hours more.
notes.B: After full turns the minute hand is back where it started, on the 6. So the time must end in 30 minutes.
notes.C: This adds 42 hours. 30 turns is 30 hours: one full day and 6 more hours.
notes.D: This moves on many days. 30 turns of the minute hand is only 30 hours, a little more than one day.

hints: Change the minutes into hours and minutes. Then see whether the hours go past one full day.
Divide 2023 by 60 to get the hours and the leftover minutes. Remember that a day has 24 hours.
Similar example: 1500 minutes after 12:00 am on 5th June. 1500 ÷ 60 = 25 hours. 24 hours takes us to 12:00 am on 6th June, and 1 more hour makes it 1:00 am on 6th June.

steps.text: 60 minutes make an hour. 33 hours use up 1980 minutes.
Find the minutes left over. So 2023 minutes is 33 hours 43 minutes.
Split 33 hours into 1 day and some hours.
24 hours after 12:00 am on 2nd March is 12:00 am on 3rd March.
9 hours 43 minutes later it is 3rd March 9:43 am.

notes.A: Yes! 2023 minutes is 33 hours 43 minutes: one full day, then 9 hours 43 minutes more.
notes.B: That is only 21 hours 43 minutes after midnight. 2023 minutes is 33 hours 43 minutes, more than a full day.
notes.C: The date is right, but 9 hours after midnight is still morning.
notes.D: This goes one day too far. 33 hours is one full day and 9 hours.

hints: On a clock the hour hand does not sit still. It creeps forward as the minutes pass. Find where each hand points, then count the gaps between them.
Each gap between clock numbers is 30°. At 8:30 the minute hand is on 6. Think about where the hour hand is between 8 and 9.
Similar example: at 2:30 the minute hand is on 6 and the hour hand is halfway between 2 and 3. From the hour hand to 3 is half a gap, 15°. From 3 to 6 is 3 × 30 = 90°. The angle is 15 + 90 = 105°.

steps.text: Each gap between clock numbers is 30°.
At 8:30 the minute hand is on 6. The hour hand is halfway between 8 and 9.
From 6 to 8 is two gaps.
The hour hand is half a gap, 15°, past 8.
The angle is 75°, which is not listed. So the answer is none of these.

notes.A: Yes! The angle is 60° + 15° = 75°, and 75° is not one of the angles given.
notes.B: Check the half gap. The hour hand is 15° past 8, and the two full gaps make 60°.
notes.C: This counts three full gaps, as if the hour hand were on 9. At 8:30 it is only halfway from 8 to 9.
notes.D: Check the adding. Two gaps make 60°, and the half gap adds 15° more.

hints: Republic Day is 26th January. Each ordinary year the day moves forward by 1, and by 2 when a 29th February falls in between.
Go year by year from 26th January 2023. Watch for the leap year 2024: its extra day, 29th February, comes after Republic Day 2024.
Similar example: 26th January 2015 was a Monday. In 2016 it is a Tuesday. From January 2016 to January 2017 we pass 29th February 2016, so it moves 2 days to a Thursday. In 2018 it is a Friday.

steps.text: Republic Day is 26th January. In an ordinary year the same date moves on by 1 weekday.
From 2023 to 2024 there is no leap day in between. So 26th January 2024 is a Friday.
From 2024 to 2025 we pass 29th February 2024, so the day moves on by 2. 26th January 2025 is a Sunday.
Then 2026 gives Monday and 2027 gives Tuesday.
So Republic Day falls on a Tuesday in 2027.

notes.A: In 2026 it falls on a Monday. Go one more year.
notes.B: Yes! The days go Friday, Sunday, Monday, Tuesday for 2024, 2025, 2026 and 2027.
notes.C: In 2028 it falls on a Wednesday. That is one year too far.
notes.D: In 2025 it falls on a Sunday. Keep moving forward one day each year.

hints: One full turn of the minute hand takes one hour. So count the turns as hours and move the clock forward.
42 turns means 42 hours. Split 42 hours into one full day of 24 hours and the hours left over.

Similar example: it is 7:00 am on 10th July and the minute hand turns 40 times. That is 40 hours, and 24 + 16 = 40. After 24 hours it is 7:00 am on 11th July. Sixteen more hours make it 11:00 pm on 11th July.

steps.text: Each full turn of the minute hand is 1 hour. So 42 turns is 42 hours.
Split 42 hours into 1 day and some hours.
24 hours after 10:30 am on 21st April is 10:30 am on 22nd April.
12 hours more makes it 10:30 pm on 22nd April. There are still 6 hours to add.
6 hours after 10:30 pm is 4:30 am the next day. So it is 23rd Apr 4:30am.

notes.A: This goes too far. 42 hours is one full day and 18 hours, which ends early on the 23rd.
notes.B: The time is right but the date is one day too late. 42 hours is less than two full days.
notes.C: This adds only 34 hours. 42 turns of the minute hand is 42 hours.
notes.D: Yes! 42 hours is one full day and 18 hours more, which reaches 4:30 am on the 23rd.

hints: Independence Day is 15th August. Each ordinary year the day moves forward by 1, and by 2 when a 29th February falls in between.
Go year by year from 15th August 2024. Watch for the next leap year, 2028: its 29th February makes the day jump by 2.
Similar example: 15th August 2014 was a Friday. In 2015 it is a Saturday. From August 2015 to August 2016 we pass 29th February 2016, so it moves 2 days to a Monday. In 2017 it is a Tuesday.

steps.text: Independence Day is 15th August. In an ordinary year the same date moves on by 1 weekday.
So 2025 gives Friday, 2026 gives Saturday and 2027 gives Sunday.
From August 2027 to August 2028 we pass 29th February 2028, so the day moves on by 2. 15th August 2028 is a Tuesday.
One more year gives Wednesday. So Independence Day falls on a Wednesday in 2029.

notes.A: In 2028 it falls on a Tuesday, because the leap day makes the day jump on from Sunday. Go one more year.
notes.B: In 2030 it falls on a Thursday. That is one year too far.
notes.C: In 2031 it falls on a Friday. Count on from Thursday one year at a time, with a jump of 2 for 2028.
notes.D: Yes! The days go Friday, Saturday, Sunday, Tuesday, Wednesday for 2025 to 2029.

hints: List the bus times one after another. The next bus is the first one that leaves after you arrive.
Start at 7:00 am and keep adding 36 minutes: 7:36 am, and so on. Stop when you pass 8:50 am.
Similar example: buses leave every 25 minutes from 6:00 am, and you arrive at 7:20 am. The buses leave at 6:00, 6:25, 6:50, 7:15 and 7:40. The 7:15 bus has gone, so the next bus is at 7:40 am.

steps.text: The buses leave at 7:00 am, 7:36 am, 8:12 am and 8:48 am.
The 8:48 am bus has just left when you arrive at 8:50 am.
Add 36 minutes to 8:48 am. 48 and 36 make 84 minutes, which is 1 hour 24 minutes.
So the next bus is at 9:24 am.

notes.A: This is not one of the bus times. List them from 7:00 am, adding 36 minutes each time.
notes.B: Yes! The bus before leaves at 8:48 am, and 36 minutes later is 9:24 am.
notes.C: Check your list of bus times. After 8:48 am, add 36 minutes to find the next one.
notes.D: This is too late. A bus leaves at 8:48 am, and the next one is only 36 minutes after that.

hints: The two times are in different units. Change them to the same unit before you divide.
Half an hour is 30 minutes. Find how many pictures are printed in 1 minute first.
Similar example: a machine takes 15 seconds to fill a bottle. In 1 minute it fills 60 ÷ 15 = 4 bottles. In a quarter of an hour, which is 15 minutes, it fills 15 × 4 = 60 bottles.

steps.text: Find the pictures printed in 1 minute, which is 60 seconds.
Half an hour is 30 minutes.
Multiply the pictures per minute by 30. So 180 pictures can be printed.

notes.A: 30 is the number of minutes in half an hour. In each of those minutes 6 pictures are printed.
notes.B: This multiplies 60 by 10. Divide instead: 60 ÷ 10 gives 6 pictures a minute, then multiply by 30 minutes.
notes.C: Yes! 6 pictures a minute for 30 minutes makes 6 × 30 = 180.
notes.D: This is 30 × 10. Each minute gives 6 pictures, so multiply 30 by 6.

hints: Count the gaps between rings, not the rings. The first ring happens at the start, before any gap has passed.
From the 1st ring to the 5th ring there are 4 gaps. Find how many minutes 4 gaps of 35 minutes make.
Similar example: a bell rings every 25 minutes, first at 8:00 am. The 4th ring comes after 3 gaps: 3 × 25 = 75 minutes, which is 1 hour 15 minutes. So it rings for the 4th time at 9:15 am.

steps.text: From the 1st ring to the 5th ring there are 4 gaps.
Find the time for 4 gaps.
140 minutes is 2 hours 20 minutes.
2 hours 20 minutes after 9:00 am is 11:20 am.

notes.A: Yes! 4 gaps of 35 minutes make 140 minutes, which is 2 hours 20 minutes after 9:00 am.
notes.B: Write the ring times: 9:00, 9:35, 10:10, 10:45 and then the 5th. Each is 35 minutes after the one before.
notes.C: Check the ring times one by one. Add 35 minutes four times, starting from 9:00 am.
notes.D: This adds 5 gaps of 35 minutes. From the 1st ring to the 5th there are only 4 gaps.

hints: First find how long the journey really took. Then compare it with how long it should take.
Write the times as clock times: quarter past eight is 8:15 am and quarter to 1 is 12:45 pm. Find the time between them.

Similar example: a bus leaves at quarter past nine and arrives at half past twelve. From 9:15 to 12:15 is 3 hours, and 15 minutes more makes 3 hours 15 minutes. If the trip should take 2 hours 45 minutes, the bus is 30 minutes late.

steps.text: Quarter past eight is 8:15 am. Quarter to 1 is 12:45 pm.
From 8:15 am to 12:15 pm is 4 hours. Then 30 minutes more takes us to 12:45 pm. The journey took 4 hours 30 minutes.
Change to minutes. 4 hours 30 minutes is 270 minutes.
The journey should take 3 hours 40 minutes, which is 220 minutes.
Subtract. The train was late by 50 min.

notes.A: Check the journey time. From 8:15 am to 12:45 pm is 4 hours 30 minutes. Then take away 3 hours 40 minutes.
notes.B: Check the subtraction. 4 hours 30 minutes is 270 minutes and 3 hours 40 minutes is 220 minutes.
notes.C: Yes! The journey took 270 minutes instead of 220 minutes, and 270 − 220 = 50.
notes.D: Quarter to 1 means 15 minutes before 1 o'clock, which is 12:45. Find the journey time from 8:15 to 12:45.

hints: A fast watch shows a later time than the real time. A slow watch shows an earlier time. Find the real time first.
Kriya's watch is 5 minutes fast, so the real time is 5 minutes before 3:45 pm. Work that out first.
Similar example: Ravi's watch is 10 minutes fast and shows 6:20. So the real time is 6:10. Meena's watch is 15 minutes slow, so it shows 15 minutes before 6:10, which is 5:55.

steps.text: Kriya's watch is 5 minutes fast. So the real time is 5 minutes before 3:45 pm, which is 3:40 pm.
Priya's watch is 10 minutes slow. So it shows 10 minutes before the real time.
Take 10 minutes from 3:40 pm. Priya's watch shows 3:30 pm.

notes.A: This adds both amounts. A fast watch is ahead, so go back 5 minutes for the real time, then back 10 more for the slow watch.
notes.B: This is the real time. Priya's watch is 10 minutes behind it.
notes.C: Yes! The real time is 3:40 pm, and a watch that is 10 minutes slow shows 3:30 pm.
notes.D: This adds 5 minutes. Kriya's watch is fast, so the real time is earlier than 3:45 pm.

hints: A clock that loses time falls further behind every hour. Find how many hours pass, then how much time is lost in total.
Count the hours from 1:00 am to 6:00 am. The clock loses 10 minutes in each of those hours.
Similar example: a clock loses 6 minutes every hour and is set right at 2:00 pm. At 7:00 pm, 5 hours have passed. It has lost 5 × 6 = 30 minutes, so it shows 6:30 pm.

steps.text: Count the hours from 1:00 am to 6:00 am.
The clock loses 10 minutes in each hour.
The clock is 50 minutes behind 6:00 am. So it shows 5:10 am.

notes.A: This adds the 50 minutes. A clock that loses time is behind, so go back 50 minutes from 6:00 am.
notes.B: Yes! In 5 hours the clock loses 50 minutes, and 50 minutes before 6:00 am is 5:10 am.
notes.C: This is only 10 minutes behind. The clock loses 10 minutes in each of the 5 hours.
notes.D: This is 60 minutes behind. Only 5 hours pass, so the clock loses 5 × 10 = 50 minutes.

hints: A watch that gains time runs ahead. In one real hour it moves forward more than 60 minutes. Think about how far the watch moves in each real hour.
In 1 real hour this watch moves 65 minutes. From noon to quarter past three the watch has moved 3 hours 15 minutes. Change that to minutes.

Similar example: a watch gains 10 minutes every hour and is set right at noon. In each real hour it moves 70 minutes. When it shows 2:20 pm it has moved 140 minutes, and 140 ÷ 70 = 2. So 2 real hours have passed and the real time is 2:00 pm.

steps.text: In 1 real hour the watch moves 5 minutes extra.
From noon to quarter past three, the watch has moved 3 hours 15 minutes.
See how many lots of 65 minutes fit in 195 minutes.
So 3 real hours have passed since noon. The actual time is 3:00 pm.

notes.A: Yes! In 3 real hours the watch gains 15 minutes, so it shows 3:15 pm when the real time is 3:00 pm.
notes.B: This takes off only 5 minutes. The watch gains 5 minutes in every hour, and 3 hours have passed.
notes.C: This takes off 30 minutes. In 3 real hours the watch gains 3 × 5 = 15 minutes.
notes.D: This adds 5 minutes. A watch that gains time is ahead, so the real time is earlier than 3:15 pm.

hints: A leap year comes once every 4 years, and its number divides by 4 exactly. The word between means the two end years are not counted.
Find the first year after 1990 that divides by 4 exactly. Then keep adding 4, stopping before 2004.
Similar example: leap years between 2010 and 2030. The first is 2012, then 2016, 2020, 2024 and 2028. That makes 5 leap years.

steps.text: 1990 does not divide by 4 exactly, but 1992 does.
Keep adding 4 years: 1992, 1996, 2000. The next one would be 2004.
2004 is an end year, so it is not between 1990 and 2004.
The leap years between them are 1992, 1996 and 2000. That is 3 leap years.

notes.A: Yes! The leap years between 1990 and 2004 are 1992, 1996 and 2000.
notes.B: This also counts 2004. The word between leaves out the end years, so stop at 2000.
notes.C: This counts too many. Leap years come once every 4 years: 1992, 1996 and 2000.
notes.D: This counts every second year. Leap years come once every 4 years, starting here with 1992.

hints: Count the days month by month: the days left in April, all of May, and the days in June. Remember how many days each month has.
April has 30 days. Count the vacation days in April from the 17th to the 30th, and include the 17th itself.
Similar example: a camp runs from 20th June to 5th July. June has 30 days, so June gives 30 − 20 + 1 = 11 days. July gives 5 days. The camp lasts 11 + 5 = 16 days.

steps.text: April has 30 days. From the 17th to the 30th, counting the 17th too, there are 14 days.
May has 31 days.
June gives 3 days, from the 1st to the 3rd.
Add the three parts. The vacation was 48 days.

notes.A: Check the days in each month. April gives 14 days, May gives 31 and June gives 3.
notes.B: This leaves out the first day. The 17th of April is part of the vacation, so April gives 14 days, not 13.
notes.C: Yes! 14 days in April, 31 in May and 3 in June make 14 + 31 + 3 = 48.
notes.D: This is one day too many. Check that May has 31 days and June gives just 3.

hints: Count the vacation days month by month. The school reopens on the day after the last vacation day.
April has 30 days. Count the vacation days in April from the 22nd to the 30th, including the 22nd. Then see how many of the 40 days are left for May.

Similar example: a holiday begins on 25th June and lasts 20 days. June has 30 days, so June gives 30 − 25 + 1 = 6 days. That leaves 20 − 6 = 14 days in July, so the last holiday is 14th July. School reopens on 15th July.

steps.text: April gives the days from the 22nd to the 30th, counting the 22nd too.
Find how many vacation days are left after April.
May has exactly 31 days, so the last day of the vacation is 31st May.
The school reopens the next day, on 1st June.

notes.A: Yes! The 40 days end on 31st May, so school reopens the next day.
notes.B: 31st May is the last day of the vacation. School reopens the day after.
notes.C: This is one day late. Count 22nd April as the first vacation day, so April gives 9 days.
notes.D: This goes backwards from April. The vacation moves forward 40 days, through May.

hints: The 12th birthday is two years after the 10th. Each ordinary year moves the day forward by 1, and a 29th February in between moves it by 2.
Go from 15th April 2019 to 15th April 2020 first. Check whether 29th February 2020 falls in between.

Similar example: a girl turns 8 on 10th May 2015, a Sunday. From May 2015 to May 2016 we pass 29th February 2016, so her 9th birthday is 2 days on, a Tuesday. The next year is ordinary, so her 10th birthday is a Wednesday.

steps.text: The 12th birthday is on 15th April 2021, two years later.
From April 2019 to April 2020 we pass 29th February 2020. So the day moves on by 2, from Monday to Wednesday.
From April 2020 to April 2021 there is no leap day. So the day moves on by 1, from Wednesday to Thursday.
The 12th birthday falls on a Thursday.

notes.A: Yes! The day moves 2 days in the first year and 1 day in the second, from Monday to Thursday.
notes.B: This moves only 1 day. Two years pass, and one of them includes 29th February 2020.
notes.C: That is the day of the 11th birthday. One more year moves it on again.
notes.D: This goes backwards. Days move forward each year: 2 days in the first year and 1 in the second.

hints: Each year the same date moves forward by 1 weekday, or by 2 when a 29th February falls in between. Follow the birthdays one year at a time.
Start with 3rd August 2015, the 6th birthday. Then check whether a leap day comes before 3rd August 2016.

Similar example: Asha's 4th birthday is on 10th September 2018, a Monday. Her 5th birthday in 2019 is a Tuesday. Before September 2020 comes 29th February 2020, so her 6th birthday is 2 days on, a Thursday. Her 7th birthday in 2021 is a Friday.

steps.text: The 6th birthday is on 3rd August 2015. No leap day comes in between, so it is 1 day on: a Monday.
The 7th birthday is on 3rd August 2016. We pass 29th February 2016, so it is 2 days on: a Wednesday.
The 8th birthday is on 3rd August 2017. It is 1 day on: a Thursday.
So the 8th birthday falls on a Thursday.

notes.A: The 9th birthday, in 2018, is a Friday. Thursday comes one year earlier.
notes.B: The 10th birthday, in 2019, is a Saturday. Count on year by year from 2014.
notes.C: Yes! The birthdays fall on Monday, Wednesday and then Thursday, which is the 8th birthday.
notes.D: The 7th birthday, in 2016, is a Wednesday. One more year reaches Thursday.

hints: The three angles of a triangle always add up to 180°. Find the missing angle, then look at all three to name the triangle.
Add 48° and 66°, and take the total away from 180° to get the third angle.
Similar example: a triangle has angles 35° and 55°. 35 + 55 = 90, and 180 − 90 = 90. The third angle is 90°, a right angle, so it is a right-angled triangle.

steps.text: Add the two angles you know.
Take this from 180° to get the third angle.
The angles are 48°, 66° and 66°. Two of them are equal.
A triangle with two equal angles has two equal sides. So it is an Isosceles triangle.

notes.A: An equilateral triangle has three angles of 60° each. Here the angles are 48°, 66° and 66°.
notes.B: A right-angled triangle needs one angle of 90°. Here the third angle is 66°.
notes.C: Yes! The third angle is 66°, so two angles are equal and the triangle is isosceles.
notes.D: An obtuse-angled triangle needs one angle bigger than 90°. Here every angle is less than 90°.

hints: The three angles of any triangle add up to exactly 180°. Add each set and look for the one that does not make 180°.
Start with the first set: add 70, 60 and 40. Then do the same for the other sets.
Similar example: can 50°, 65° and 55° be the angles of a triangle? 50 + 65 + 55 = 170, which is not 180, so they cannot. Can 50°, 65° and 65°? 50 + 65 + 65 = 180, so they can.

steps.text: Add the first set.
This total is 10° short of 180°, so these cannot be the angles of a triangle.
The other three sets each add up to 180°: 75 + 55 + 50 = 180, 45 + 45 + 90 = 180 and 30 + 80 + 70 = 180.
So the angles that cannot make a triangle are 70°, 60°, 40°.

notes.A: Yes! 70 + 60 + 40 = 170, which is not 180, so no triangle can have these angles.
notes.B: 75 + 55 + 50 = 180, so these can be the angles of a triangle. Look for the set that does not add up to 180.
notes.C: 45 + 45 + 90 = 180, so these can be the angles of a triangle. Look for the set that does not add up to 180.
notes.D: 30 + 80 + 70 = 180, so these can be the angles of a triangle. Look for the set that does not add up to 180.

hints: The area of a triangle is half the area of a rectangle with the same base and height.
Multiply the base by the height: 6 × 4. Then remember that a triangle takes up only half of that.
Similar example: a triangle has base 10 cm and height 3 cm. 10 × 3 = 30, and half of 30 is 15, so the area is 15 sq cm.

steps.text: Multiply the base by the height.
A triangle is half of that rectangle, so divide by 2.
The area of triangle BED is 12 sq.cm.

notes.A: 6 cm is the length of the base. Area needs base times height, then half of that, and it is measured in square centimetres.
notes.B: Area is measured in square centimetres, not centimetres. Work out half of 6 × 4.
notes.C: 24 is base times height, which is the area of the whole rectangle. A triangle is half of that.
notes.D: Yes! Half of 6 × 4 is 12, so the area is 12 square centimetres.

hints: The area of a right triangle is half the area of the rectangle with the same base and height. Watch the unit too.
Multiply the base by the height first. Then remember that the triangle takes up only half of that.
Similar example: a right triangle has base 14 cm and height 10 cm. 14 × 10 = 140, and half of 140 is 70. Its area is 70 cm.sq.

steps.text: Multiply the base by the height.
The triangle is half of this rectangle.
The sides are in centimetres, so the area is 152 cm.sq.

notes.A: The number is right, but look at the unit. The sides are in centimetres, so the area is in square centimetres, not square metres.
notes.B: Check the multiplication. 19 × 16 = 304, and half of 304 is a little more than this.
notes.C: Yes! Half of 19 × 16 is 152, and the unit is square centimetres.
notes.D: This is base times height, the area of the whole rectangle. The triangle is half of it.

hints: An isosceles triangle has two equal angles. Use the fact that all three angles add up to 180° to find the third angle of each pair.
For the first pair, add 63 and 54 and take the total from 180. See whether the third angle matches one of the two given.
Similar example: can 50° and 80° be two angles of an isosceles triangle? 50 + 80 = 130, and 180 − 130 = 50. The third angle is 50°, the same as one already there, so yes.

steps.text: Add the first pair.
Find the third angle.
The angles are 63°, 54° and 63°. Two are equal, so this triangle is isosceles.
The other pairs give third angles of 60°, 51° and 68°, which match nothing in their pairs.
So the pair is 63°, 54°.

notes.A: Yes! The third angle is 180 − 117 = 63, which matches the 63° already there.
notes.B: 75 + 45 = 120, so the third angle is 60°. All three angles are different, so it is not isosceles.
notes.C: 49 + 80 = 129, so the third angle is 51°. That is close to 49° but not equal.
notes.D: 59 + 53 = 112, so the third angle is 68°. All three angles are different, so it is not isosceles.

hints: In any triangle, two sides together must be longer than the third side. Use this to see how long the third side can be.
Add the two sides you know, 20 and 15. The third side must be shorter than this total. Then find the third side for each perimeter.

Similar example: two sides of a triangle are 10 cm and 8 cm. 10 + 8 = 18, so the third side must be shorter than 18 cm. Can the perimeter be 40 cm? The third side would be 40 − 18 = 22 cm, which is too long. So 40 cm is not possible.

steps.text: Add the two sides you know.
The third side must be shorter than 35 cm, or the two sides could not reach across it.
So the perimeter must be less than 70 cm.
For a perimeter of 72 cm the third side would be 37 cm, which is too long.
So the perimeter cannot be 72cm.

notes.A: 52 − 35 = 17, so the third side would be 17 cm. That is shorter than 35 cm, so this triangle can be made.
notes.B: 67 − 35 = 32, so the third side would be 32 cm. That is shorter than 35 cm, so this triangle can be made.
notes.C: Yes! The third side would be 72 − 35 = 37 cm, longer than the other two sides put together.
notes.D: 62 − 35 = 27, so the third side would be 27 cm. That is shorter than 35 cm, so this triangle can be made.

hints: An isosceles triangle has two equal angles. Use the fact that all three angles add up to 180° to find the third angle of each pair.
For each pair, add the two angles and take the total from 180. See whether the third angle matches one of the two given.
Similar example: can 70° and 40° be two angles of an isosceles triangle? 70 + 40 = 110, and 180 − 110 = 70. The third angle is 70°, the same as one already there, so yes.

steps.text: Try the pair 68° and 44°. Add them.
Find the third angle.
The angles are 68°, 44° and 68°. Two are equal, so this triangle is isosceles.
The other pairs give third angles of 57.5° and 63°, which match nothing in their pairs.
So the pair is 68° & 44°.

notes.A: 64 + 58.5 = 122.5, so the third angle is 57.5°. That is close to 58.5° but not equal.
notes.B: Yes! The third angle is 180 − 112 = 68, which matches the 68° already there.
notes.C: 62.5 + 54.5 = 117, so the third angle is 63°. That is close to 62.5° but not equal.
notes.D: One pair does work. Find the third angle for 68° and 44° and compare it with them.

hints: Find the area of the square first. Then find the area of each triangle and look for the one that matches.
The square has side 9 cm, so its area is 9 × 9. A triangle's area is half of its base times its height.
Similar example: a square has side 4 cm, so its area is 4 × 4 = 16 sq cm. A triangle with base 8 cm and height 4 cm has 8 × 4 = 32, and half of 32 is 16 sq cm. The two areas are equal.

steps.text: Find the area of the square.
A triangle's area is half of base times height. So base times height must be twice 81, which is 162.
Check base 27 and height 6.
Half of 162 is the triangle's area.
So the triangle with B=27, H=6 has the same area as the square.

notes.A: Half of 12 × 4 is 24. The square's area is 9 × 9 = 81, so this triangle is too small.
notes.B: Half of 18 × 8 is 72. That is close, but the square's area is 9 × 9 = 81.
notes.C: Half of 12 × 14 is 84. That is close, but the square's area is 9 × 9 = 81.
notes.D: Yes! Half of 27 × 6 is 81, the same as 9 × 9.

hints: This is a fact about every triangle, whatever its shape. Think about what you get when you put its three corners together.
Picture tearing the three corners off a paper triangle and placing them side by side. They fit along a straight line. Think how many degrees a straight line makes.
Similar example: think of a rectangle. It has 4 corners, and each is a right angle of 90°. 4 × 90 = 360, so the angles of a rectangle add up to 360°.

steps.text: Put the three corners of any triangle side by side. Together they make a straight line.
A straight line is half of a full turn, and a full turn is 360°.
Half of 360° is the angle on a straight line.
So the sum of all angles of a triangle is 180°.

notes.A: Yes! The three angles of any triangle always add up to 180°.
notes.B: 360° is a full turn, and the angle sum of a four-sided shape. A triangle's corners make only a straight line.
notes.C: 90° is one right angle. The three angles of a triangle together make two right angles.
notes.D: 270° is three right angles. The three angles of a triangle together make two right angles.

hints: Triangles get their names from how many of their sides are equal. Think about the names you know.
Rule out the names you are sure about. Scalene means no sides are equal, and isosceles means just two sides are equal.
Similar example: a triangle has sides 5 cm, 5 cm and 8 cm. Exactly two sides are equal, so it is called an isosceles triangle.

steps.text: Triangles are named by their sides. If no sides are equal it is scalene, and if two sides are equal it is isosceles.
When all three sides are equal, the name comes from words meaning equal sides.
A triangle with all sides equal is called Equilateral.

notes.A: Yes! Equilateral means equal sides, and all three sides are the same length.
notes.B: An isosceles triangle has only two equal sides. Here all three sides are equal.
notes.C: A scalene triangle has no equal sides at all. Here all three sides are equal.
notes.D: Right-angled tells us about an angle of 90°, not about the sides. Look for the name that means equal sides.

hints: Triangles get their names from how many of their sides are equal. Think about the names you know.
Rule out the names you are sure about. Scalene means no sides are equal, and equilateral means all three sides are equal.
Similar example: a triangle has sides 4 cm, 6 cm and 7 cm. No two sides are equal, so it is called a scalene triangle.

steps.text: Triangles are named by their sides. If no sides are equal it is scalene, and if all three are equal it is equilateral.
The name for exactly two equal sides comes from words meaning equal legs.
A triangle with two equal sides is called Isosceles.

notes.A: Yes! An isosceles triangle has exactly two equal sides.
notes.B: An equilateral triangle has all three sides equal. Here only two sides are equal.
notes.C: A scalene triangle has no equal sides. Here two sides are equal.
notes.D: Obtuse tells us about an angle bigger than 90°, not about the sides. Look for the name that means two equal sides.

hints: The three angles of a triangle always add up to 180°. Two are given, so find what is left for the third.
First add the two angles you know, 50° and 60°. Then think about how far that total is from 180°.
Similar example: two angles of a triangle are 40° and 65°. 40 + 65 = 105, and 180 − 105 = 75. The third angle is 75°.

steps.text: Add the two angles you know.
All three angles of a triangle add up to 180°.
Take the total away from 180°. The third angle is 70°.

notes.B: This is 10° too big. The two angles add up to 110°, so take 110 from 180 once more.
notes.C: A triangle does not need a 90° angle. Add 50 and 60, then take the total from 180.
notes.D: 60° is one of the angles already given. Add 50 and 60, then take the total from 180.

hints: Triangles can also be named by their biggest angle. Think about the special name for an angle of 90°.
Rule out the names you are sure about. Acute means every angle is less than 90°, and obtuse means one angle is more than 90°.
Similar example: a triangle has angles 30°, 40° and 110°. One angle is more than 90°, so it is called an obtuse-angled triangle.

steps.text: An angle of exactly 90° is called a right angle. It looks like the corner of a book.
A triangle is named after its biggest angle: acute if all are less than 90°, obtuse if one is more than 90°.
A triangle with one angle of 90° is called Right-angled.

notes.A: Yes! A 90° angle is a right angle, so the triangle is right-angled.
notes.B: In an acute triangle every angle is less than 90°. Here one angle is exactly 90°.
notes.C: An obtuse triangle has one angle more than 90°. Here the angle is exactly 90°.
notes.D: An equilateral triangle has three angles of 60°. It can never have a 90° angle.

hints: An isosceles triangle has two equal angles. The 80° angle could be one of the equal pair, or it could be the angle on its own. Try both cases.
First suppose 80° is one of the two equal angles. Then the angles are 80°, 80° and one more. Find that one using 180°.

Similar example: one angle of an isosceles triangle is 30°. If 30° is one of the equal pair, the third angle is 180 − 30 − 30 = 120. If 30° is the angle on its own, the other two share 180 − 30 = 150, so each is 150 ÷ 2 = 75. The other angles can be 30°, 120° or 75°.

steps.text: Case 1: 80° is one of the equal pair. The angles are 80°, 80° and one more.
Case 2: 80° is the angle on its own. The other two angles share what is left.
They are equal, so each is half of 100°.
So the other angles can only be 80°, 20° or 50°.
The measure that cannot appear is 70°.

notes.A: 20° is possible. The angles can be 80°, 80° and 20°, which add up to 180°.
notes.B: 50° is possible. The angles can be 80°, 50° and 50°, which add up to 180°.
notes.C: Yes! The other angles can only be 80°, 20° or 50°, so 70° can never appear.
notes.D: 80° is possible. The 80° angle can be one of the equal pair: 80°, 80° and 20°.

hints: An isosceles triangle has two equal sides and one other side. Any two sides together must be longer than the third. List the triangles in an orderly way.
Two equal sides plus the third side make 23. Start with equal sides of 11 and find the third side. Then try equal sides of 10, and keep going.

Similar example: perimeter 11. Sides 5, 5, 1 work. Sides 4, 4, 3 work. Sides 3, 3, 5 work, because 3 + 3 = 6 is more than 5. Sides 2, 2, 7 do not, because 2 + 2 = 4 is less than 7. So there are 3 triangles.

steps.text: Two equal sides plus the third side make 23. Twice a whole number is even, so the third side must be odd.
List them from the longest equal sides: 11, 11, 1 then 10, 10, 3 then 9, 9, 5 then 8, 8, 7 then 7, 7, 9 then 6, 6, 11.
Each of these can be made. The last one just fits, because 12 is more than 11.
The next would be 5, 5, 13. The equal sides are too short to reach across 13.
So there are 6 different isosceles triangles.

notes.A: There are more than this. Try equal sides of every length from 11 down to 6 and find the third side each time.
notes.B: Some are missing. The third side may be longer than the equal sides, as in 7, 7, 9 and 6, 6, 11.
notes.C: Yes! The equal sides can be 11, 10, 9, 8, 7 or 6, which gives 6 triangles.
notes.D: Some of these cannot be made. With equal sides of 5 or less, the two together are too short to reach across the third side.

hints: An isosceles triangle has two equal angles. Use the fact that all three angles add up to 180° to find the third angle of each pair.
For each pair, add the two angles and take the total from 180. See whether the third angle matches one of the two given.
Similar example: can 50° and 80° be two angles of an isosceles triangle? 50 + 80 = 130, and 180 − 130 = 50. The third angle is 50°, the same as one already there, so yes.

steps.text: Try the pair 55° and 70°. Add them.
Find the third angle.
The angles are 55°, 70° and 55°. Two are equal, so this triangle is isosceles.
The other pairs give third angles of 40°, 60° and 80°, which match nothing in their pairs.
So the pair is 55° & 70°.

notes.A: 90 + 50 = 140, so the third angle is 40°. All three angles are different, so it is not isosceles.
notes.B: 80 + 40 = 120, so the third angle is 60°. All three angles are different, so it is not isosceles.
notes.C: Yes! The third angle is 180 − 125 = 55, which matches the 55° already there.
notes.D: 60 + 40 = 100, so the third angle is 80°. All three angles are different, so it is not isosceles.

hints: Grams and milligrams are linked by thousands. Change the milligrams into a part of a gram, then join it to the whole grams.
1 gram is 1000 milligrams, so 1 mg is one thousandth of a gram. Write 15 mg as a decimal with three places after the point.
Similar example: 3 g 45 mg. Since 1000 mg make 1 g, 45 mg is 45 thousandths of a gram, written 0.045 g. So 3 g 45 mg is 3 + 0.045 = 3.045 g.

steps.text: 1000 milligrams make 1 gram.
Change 15 mg into grams by dividing by 1000.
Add this to the 5 whole grams. The ring weighs 5.015 gm.

notes.A: This has four places after the point, as if 10000 mg made a gram. 1000 mg make a gram, so use three places.
notes.B: This treats 15 mg as 15 hundredths. Milligrams are thousandths of a gram, so 15 mg is 0.015 g.
notes.C: The 5 whole grams have slipped behind the decimal point. Keep 5 as the whole number and add 0.015.

hints: The three lengths are in different units. Change them all into centimetres before adding.
1 m is 100 cm and 1 dm is 10 cm. Change 2 m and 2 dm into centimetres first.
Similar example: 3 m + 4 dm + 12 cm. 3 m is 3 × 100 = 300 cm and 4 dm is 4 × 10 = 40 cm. Then 300 + 40 + 12 = 352 cm.

steps.text: Change 2 m into centimetres.
Change 2 dm into centimetres.
Add all three lengths. The total is 235 cm.

notes.A: This just writes the numbers 2, 2 and 15 side by side. Change each length to centimetres, then add.
notes.B: This is 10 cm short. Check that 2 dm is 20 cm, then add 200, 20 and 15.
notes.D: Check each change. 2 m is 200 cm and 2 dm is 20 cm, and there are 15 cm more.

hints: The two weights are in different units. Change the kilograms to grams, then see how many beans fit.
Half a kilogram is 500 grams. Now think how many beans of 2.5 grams make up 500 grams.
Similar example: each marble weighs 2.5 grams and the bag weighs 100 grams. Two marbles weigh 5 grams, and 100 ÷ 5 = 20 pairs. So there are 20 × 2 = 40 marbles.

steps.text: Change 0.5 kg into grams.
Two beans weigh 5 grams together.
Find how many pairs of beans make 500 grams.
Each pair is 2 beans. There are 200 beans.

notes.A: Yes! 500 grams holds 100 pairs of beans, which is 200 beans.
notes.B: 500 is the weight in grams, not the number of beans. Each bean weighs 2.5 grams, so there are fewer beans than grams.
notes.C: Check the division. Two beans weigh 5 grams, so 500 grams holds 100 pairs of beans.
notes.D: 1000 is the number of grams in a whole kilogram. The bag weighs half a kilogram, and each bean is 2.5 grams.

hints: Kilograms and grams are linked by thousands. Change the grams into a part of a kilogram, then join it to the whole kilograms.
1 kilogram is 1000 grams, so 1 g is one thousandth of a kilogram. Write 11 g as a decimal with three places after the point.
Similar example: 7 kg 25 g. Since 1000 g make 1 kg, 25 g is 25 thousandths of a kilogram, written 0.025 kg. So 7 kg 25 g is 7 + 0.025 = 7.025 kg.

steps.text: 1000 grams make 1 kilogram.
Change 11 g into kilograms by dividing by 1000.
Add this to the 11 whole kilograms. The weight is 11.011 kg.

notes.A: This treats 11 g as 11 hundredths. Grams are thousandths of a kilogram, so 11 g is 0.011 kg.
notes.C: The whole kilograms should stay as 11. Only the grams go after the decimal point, as 0.011.
notes.D: 0.101 kg would be 101 grams. For 11 grams, the three places after the point are 0, 1, 1.

hints: First find out how much a decalitre is in millilitres. Then see how many lots of 250 ml fit into it.
Deca means ten, so 1 decalitre is 10 litres. Change 10 litres into millilitres.
Similar example: 3 lemons give 100 ml of juice. How many lemons give 1 litre? 1 litre is 1000 ml, and 1000 ÷ 100 = 10 lots. Each lot needs 3 lemons, so 10 × 3 = 30 lemons.

steps.text: 1 decalitre is 10 litres. Change it to millilitres.
Find how many lots of 250 ml fit in 10000 ml.
Each lot needs 4 mangoes. So 160 mangoes are needed.

notes.A: 40 is the number of 250 ml lots. Each lot needs 4 mangoes, so multiply by 4.
notes.B: Check the size of a decalitre. It is 10 litres, which is 10000 ml, and that holds 40 lots of 250 ml.
notes.C: Check the last step. There are 40 lots of 250 ml, and each lot needs 4 mangoes.
notes.D: Yes! 10000 ml holds 40 lots of 250 ml, and 40 × 4 = 160.

hints: Deci and deca sound alike but mean very different things. Change each amount into grams before adding.
A decigram is one tenth of a gram, so 10 decigrams make 1 gram. A decagram is 10 grams. Change 100 decigrams into grams first.
Similar example: 50 decigrams + 20 decagrams. 50 ÷ 10 = 5 grams, and 20 × 10 = 200 grams. Together that is 5 + 200 = 205 grams.

steps.text: 10 decigrams make 1 gram. Change 100 decigrams into grams.
1 decagram is 10 grams. Change 300 decagrams into grams.
Add the two amounts.
The total is 3010 grams, which is not listed. So the answer is none of these.

notes.A: This adds 10 and 300 without changing the decagrams. 300 decagrams is 300 × 10 = 3000 grams.
notes.B: This counts 100 decigrams as 100 grams. Ten decigrams make 1 gram, so 100 decigrams is only 10 grams.
notes.C: This leaves out the decigrams. 100 decigrams add 10 more grams.
notes.D: Yes! 10 + 3000 = 3010 grams, and 3010 is not one of the numbers given.

hints: Gross and score are names for fixed counts. Find the price of one egg, then the price of the smaller group.
A gross is 12 dozen, which is 144, and a score is 20. Divide Rs.864 by 144 to get the price of one egg.
Similar example: 1 score of pens costs Rs.100. A score is 20, so one pen costs 100 ÷ 20 = 5 rupees. A dozen is 12, so a dozen pens cost 12 × 5 = 60 rupees.

steps.text: A gross is 12 dozen.
Find the price of one egg in rupees.
A score is 20. Find the price of 20 eggs.
So 1 score of eggs costs Rs.120.

notes.A: This uses 8 rupees for each egg. A gross is 144 eggs, and 864 ÷ 144 = 6.
notes.B: This is the cost of 22 eggs. A score is 20 eggs.
notes.C: Yes! One egg costs 6 rupees, and 20 × 6 = 120.
notes.D: This uses 7 rupees for each egg. A gross is 144 eggs, and 864 ÷ 144 = 6.

hints: Change the length one unit at a time: decameters to metres, then metres to centimetres.
Deca means ten, so 1 decameter is 10 metres. Change 29 decameters into metres first.
Similar example: 7 decameters. 7 × 10 = 70 metres, and 70 × 100 = 7000 centimetres.

steps.text: 1 decameter is 10 metres.
1 metre is 100 centimetres.
So 29 decameters is 29000 centimeters.

notes.A: This multiplies by 100 only. First change decameters to metres by multiplying by 10, then change to centimetres.
notes.B: Yes! 29 decameters is 290 metres, and 290 × 100 = 29000.
notes.C: This is ten times too big. 1 decameter is 10 m and 1 m is 100 cm, so multiply by 1000 in all.
notes.D: This is the length in metres. Multiply by 100 to change metres into centimetres.

hints: Score and dozen are names for fixed counts. Find the price of one orange and one apple, then work out the cost of what is bought.
A score is 20 and a dozen is 12. Divide Rs.130 by 20 to find the price of one orange.

Similar example: 1 score of bananas costs Rs.90 and 1 dozen pears cost Rs.120. One banana costs 90 ÷ 20 = 4.50 rupees and one pear costs 120 ÷ 12 = 10 rupees. So 10 bananas cost Rs.45 and 5 pears cost Rs.50. Together that is 45 + 50 = 95 rupees.

steps.text: A score is 20. Find the price of one orange in rupees.

A dozen is 12. Find the price of one apple.
Find the cost of 17 apples.
Add the two costs.
The cost is Rs.333, which is not listed. So the answer is None.

notes.A: Check each part. 12 oranges cost Rs.78 and 17 apples cost Rs.255.
notes.B: Check the price of one fruit. An orange costs 130 ÷ 20 = 6.50 rupees and an apple costs 180 ÷ 12 = 15 rupees.
notes.C: This is close. Add Rs.78 for the oranges and Rs.255 for the apples carefully.
notes.D: Yes! 78 + 255 = 333, and Rs.333 is not one of the amounts given.

hints: The rice is given in hectograms but the answer is wanted in grams. Change the unit first, then share equally.

Similar example: 90 hectograms of sugar shared among 20 people. 1 hectogram is 100 grams, so 90 × 100 = 9000 grams. Each person gets 9000 ÷ 20 = 450 grams.

steps.text: 1 hectogram is 100 grams. Change 160 hectograms into grams.
Share 16000 grams equally among 25 people.
Each person gets 640 grams, which is not listed. So the answer is None of these.

notes.A: Check the division 16000 ÷ 25. There are four 25s in every 100, so work out 160 × 4.
notes.B: This is too big. 160 hectograms is 16000 grams, and 25 people share it equally.
notes.C: This is close. 25 × 600 = 15000, which leaves 1000 grams still to share.
notes.D: Yes! 16000 ÷ 25 = 640 grams, and 640 is not one of the numbers given.

hints: Different things are measured with different units. Decide what kind of thing a perimeter is: a length, a weight or an amount of liquid.
The perimeter is the distance all the way round the classroom. Think about which unit measures distance.
Similar example: which unit suits the milk in a jug? Milk is a liquid, and the amount of a liquid is measured in litres. So the litre is the suitable unit.

steps.text: The perimeter of a classroom is the distance all the way round its walls. It is a length.
Litres measure liquids and kilograms measure weight. Neither can measure a length.
Lengths of rooms are measured in metres. So the suitable unit is the metre.

notes.A: Litres measure how much liquid something holds. A perimeter is a length.
notes.B: Yes! A perimeter is a length, and the length of a room is measured in metres.
notes.C: Kilograms measure how heavy something is. A perimeter is a length.
notes.D: Each unit measures one kind of thing only. A perimeter is a length, so only a length unit fits.

hints: Check each numeral against the rules of Roman numerals: how many times a letter may repeat, and which letters may be placed before a bigger letter to subtract.
A letter is never written more than three times in a row, and V, L and D are never placed before a bigger letter to subtract. Test each numeral against these two rules.
Similar example: is XXXXVI written correctly? No, because X appears four times in a row. Forty is written XL, so the number 46 is written XLVI.

steps.text: A letter may repeat at most three times in a row. MCCCCIV has C four times in a row, so it breaks this rule.
V, L and D are never put before a bigger letter to subtract. CDVLII has V before L, so it breaks this rule.
Read CDLXVI part by part: CD is 400, L is 50, X is 10, V is 5 and I is 1. Every part follows the rules.
So the numeral that is correctly written is CDLXVI.

notes.A: Count the letter C here. It appears four times in a row, but a letter can repeat only three times. Four hundred is written CD.
notes.B: Look at the V placed before L. V is never used to subtract. Forty-seven is written XLVII.
notes.C: Yes! CD is 400, L is 50, X is 10, V is 5 and I is 1, so this is 466 and every rule is followed.
notes.D: One of the numerals does follow every rule. Check each one for a letter repeated four times, or a V placed before a bigger letter.

hints: Add the journey time to the starting time. Add the hours and the minutes separately, and remember that 60 minutes make 1 hour.
Start by adding the 4 hours to 09:45. Then add the 35 minutes, and watch what happens when the minutes go past 60.
Similar example: a bus leaves at 10:50 and takes 2 hours 25 minutes. 10:50 plus 2 hours is 12:50. Then 50 + 25 = 75 minutes, which is 1 hour 15 minutes. So the bus arrives at 13:15, which is 1:15 PM.
